Technical Validation

As demonstrated in Fig. 1, we conducted intermediate validation at various stages to ensure the quality of the processed data. We consider it essential for maintaining the transparency and reproducibility of the proposed workflow, and potentially useful for identifying the cause of data bias. To brief, the below subsections report simple statistics of detected stay points which form the trajectories; validated detected home and work locations against census data; and tested the usability of O-D flows via two common applications in urban geography.
Simple statistics of processed data

Statistical overview of processed data. (a) Average hourly activity counts in November 2021. (b) Displacement of activity locations fitting into a truncated power law. (c) LAD-Level Correlation between the number of residents detected from Mobile Phone App Data and reported from Census Data.

Figure 2(a) presents a simple statistical overview of processed points data (i.e., stay points without labelling activity types). The average counts of activities were summarised by starting time for each day of the week. All weekdays (Monday through Friday) show similar activity patterns with two peaks: one around 8-9 AM and another around 3-5 PM. In contrast, weekend activity patterns have one peak around midday. While Saturday presents slightly higher activity counts, the lowest activity counts are captured on Sunday throughout the day. The following three sub-sections present the validations introduced in Fig. 1.
Distance distribution between each consecutive stays

Infostop generates stays by aggregating stationary points even though sensitivity analysis was performed to ensure that optimised parameters were set. We further validated that the generated stay points collectively follow the universal distribution. For this purpose, we measured the displacement distance between each consecutive stay, denoted as Deltad. This distribution of displacement shall distinguish different types of diffusion processes, such as Levy flights and random walk models. Although log-normal and exponential distributions have also been reported to fit well in specific datasets, the power-law distribution has proven more suitable for describing movement patterns over substantial distances. Pioneering studies utilising banknote tracking and mobile phone call records (CDRs) have demonstrated that a truncated power-law can approximate displacement distribution. In our analysis (plotted in Fig. 2(b)) the distances ranged from 1 km to 1000 km, and the fitted beta value of 1.24 aligns with the empirical range summarised in a detailed research review. This consistency underscores the robustness of our findings in characterising human movement patterns.
Correlation with usual residents, England: Census 2021

Figure 2(c) illustrates the Local Authority Districts (LAD)-level Pearson correlation between two datasets, namely the number of users with home locations identified from the mobile app data and the number of usual residents estimated in the UK census 2021 (https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/sources/census_2021_bulk). The Pearson correlation coefficient is 0.905, indicating a decent representation. However, when we zoom into smaller areas, the correlation decreases to 0.52. The limitation is somewhat anticipated. The detected home locations are based on simple rules, which makes it especially challenging to capture full working scenarios (e.g., night-time workers and mobile workers). Tuning the parameters used in the rule-based identification may slightly decrease/increase the numbers. Still, our sensitivity analysis shows no significant improvement. Figure S3 has further discussed the issue and bias with statistics of hourly user counts of stay location type for each day of the week. The diversity and variability of working patterns have grown significantly in recent years, particularly post-COVID. Developing a comprehensive approach to identifying irregular home and working patterns will be one of the key topics in our improvements.

passages.text: Pearson correlation and Ratio between travel-to-work trip detected from mobile app data and census data at LADs in England.

We compared our derived travel-to-work O-D matrix with multiple correlation measurements (Pearson, Spearman, and ratio as a measure of population penetration) at two levels - the Local Authority District (LAD) and the Middle layer Super Output Areas (MSOAs). The census travel-to-work data was collected through a combination of self-reported responses to specific questions related to commuting patterns and details about the time and distance. The Pearson correlation of the O-D matrix aggregated at the LAD level is 0.95, which shows good data representativeness. For MSOA level validation, we took the entire England area but grouped MSOAs by upper-level LADs to understand the variabilities across areas. In total, 331 LADs were broken down into 7264 MSOAs. To stabilise variance and handle zero values, a log1p transformation (log(1 + x)) was applied prior to correlation analysis (See Figure S5). This transformation prevents undefined values for zeros while preserving the distributional properties of the data. As reported in the Table 1, for the LDAs (311 areas out of a total of 331 LADs) with significant data records and more than one MSOA, the Pearson correlation shows decent results that range between 0.38 and 0.87 with an average of 0.7. Figure 3 provides further information about the spatial distribution. A further investigation to examine how mobility intensity relates to population is provided in Figure S6, where we applied a simple scaling index that relates the distribution of users/trips to population at the MSOA level. The spatial pattern is consistent with urban structure and data generation.
Validation in the context of example urban applications: spatial interaction model
Plotting R2 for different models presents the trends and consistency of goodness of fit across different models.

The processed data, while not perfectly valid as documented, proves to be highly beneficial for various urban applications, especially at aggregated scales covering large areas. Here, we compared the travel-to-work data from the mobile app and census in the context of spatial interaction application. The four variants of the spatial interaction model were employed, including (unconstrained) gravity, production-constrained, attraction-constrained, and doubly constrained models. The model parameters (k: balancing factor, mu: production, alpha: attraction, beta: for distance decay) were estimated, with two forms of distance decay functions (i.e., power and exponential) using two sets of travel-to-work data. As shown in Fig. 4, the performance of these models, measured by the R2 values, exhibits a strong correlation between the mobile app-derived flows and the census-based flows. This consistency suggests that, despite inherent biases in mobile app data, the spatial interaction models capture comparable trip distribution patterns across both datasets, reinforcing the dataset's utility for large-scale mobility modelling.
Validation in the context of example urban applications: spatial structure
Modularity-based community detection was applied to O-D data of all trips, delineating urban functional zones at different spatial scales.

Another commonly implemented application is to detect functional spatial structures based on flow data using community detection. In network science, a community refers to a sub-network that is dense internally and sparse externally; revealing these communities allows us to understand the urban structure more intuitively. A further intuitive assumption is that urban networks are organised into hierarchically distinct communities, meaning that any given scale of community can be subdivided into smaller communities, which can be further subdivided, and so on. One of the most widely used and arguably most universal methods is modularity maximisation. In this study, we apply modularity-based community detection to the mobility network at three different resolutions (Fig. 5). The identified communities demonstrate clear clustering patterns of urban spatial units, which largely align with known administrative boundaries and socio-economic divisions. Importantly, this analysis serves a dual purpose: (1) it illustrates a practical application of the dataset in uncovering meaningful urban structures, and (2) it provides an internal validation of the data's ability to capture coherent spatial patterns consistent with expected urban morphology. The coherence between detected communities and established city boundaries supports the dataset's structural plausibility for spatial interaction research.
Limitation and future work

Automatically collected human location data inherently contains biases rooted in how it is generated, particularly when sourced from mobile apps. Users of the shared datasets should carefully consider these limitations, in addition to complying with GDPR requirements. First, mobile app location data is recorded only when users consent, location services are enabled, and specific apps are actively used. Unlike vehicle GPS trackers with continuous coverage, mobile app data result in fragmented and irregular trajectories. These datasets should be treated as a sample of activities and trips, not as complete travel diaries. As such, derived mobility patterns reflect user behaviour selectively and may underrepresent specific groups, such as older adults, individuals with lower smartphone usage, or those residing in rural areas. Second, spatial representativeness varies across different levels of aggregation. Our validation indicates that data reliability improves at higher spatial scales (e.g., LAD level), while greater bias and variability are observed at finer resolutions (e.g., MSOA level), particularly in less populated or socioeconomically distinct areas. This should be considered when applying the data to small-area mobility analyses or when interpreting regional disparities. Third, it is worth emphasising that each step in the workflow can be improved and should be updated as data (e.g., mobile app data, census data, other supplementary data sets) of better quality, new techniques and methods emerge and are tailored for specific applications. The parameters and methods we demonstrated may serve basic needs, but are not always optimised. For instance, using hourly time windows may not be effective for travel mode detection, which requires finer temporal resolution. Fourth, to protect privacy, we have applied spatial and temporal aggregation to avoid re-identification risks. While this reduces granularity, it enables safe use for mobility research, urban planning, and comparative analysis across cities. Finally, despite these limitations, we believe the dataset contributes to promoting open science in mobility research. We will continue updating the dataset and sharing improvements via our GitHub page to enhance transparency and utility for the broader research community.

passages.text: Molecular Insights into the Functional Roles of Variants in the FADS Gene Cluster on Omega-3 Long-Chain Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Synthesis
Abstract
Background

Omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (n3-LCPUFAs) have strong triglyceride-lowering and anti-inflammatory properties, and high levels of these fatty acids have been associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease. The synthesis of n3-LCPUFA, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), and n6-LCPUFA, arachidonic acid, share a common pathway mediated by fatty acid desaturase genes, FADS1 and FADS2. LCPUFA synthesis is regulated by both modifiable and non-modifiable factors. Of particular interest is the role of genetic variants in the FADS gene cluster, which are associated with altered FADS1 and FADS2 expression, as well as LCPUFA levels. However, the specific functional variants and the precise molecular mechanisms by which these variants regulate FADS gene expression remain to be elucidated. Variation in the FADS gene cluster is thought to have arisen through natural selection and changing dietary patterns. Available evidence suggests these variants, either individually or as a haplotype, may alter FADS gene expression by modifying DNA methylation in regulatory regions, as well as microRNA and transcription factor binding sites.
Summary

This review explores the current state of knowledge regarding the functional roles of these variants on LCPUFA synthesis and how these new insights will help support precision nutrition strategies aimed at improving an individual's n3-LCPUFA status and health.
Key Messages

Identifying specific functional variants in or near the FADS gene cluster and elucidating the mechanisms by which these variants impact LCPUFA synthesis requires further investigation. However, hypothesis generating in vitro studies have revealed roles for epigenetics, non-coding RNAs, and modification of transcription factor binding sites. This knowledge will generate new insights that will help improve our understanding of the genetic basis underlying LCPUFA synthesis and how this may differ across populations.
Introduction

In the mid-1970s, Danish physicians made the seminal discovery that high levels of the marine omega-3 fatty acids eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) in the diet of Greenlandic Inuit were associated with reduced mortality from cardiovascular disease (CVD). Over the past 50 years, epidemiological and clinical studies have demonstrated that higher levels of EPA and DHA in the body have beneficial effects on numerous CVD risk factors, including triglyceride concentrations, blood pressure, inflammation, endothelial function, and platelet coagulability. Furthermore, many studies have reported that increased omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (n3-LCPUFAs) can reduce the risk of congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke, and sudden cardiac death. Due to the myriad of benefits associated with EPA and DHA, there is widespread interest to better understand the various modifiable and non-modifiable factors that can influence their levels in the body.

EPA and DHA are primarily obtained through the consumption of fatty fish, seafood, and algae; however, the level of intake of these marine products is low in many populations around the world. Indeed, this was recently demonstrated by Schuchardt et al. who released a world map showing that n3-LCPUFA status is low to very low in most populations of the 48 countries and regions included in their analysis. Notable exceptions were countries like Japan, South Korea, Finland, Norway, Iceland, and Greenland due to their high consumption of fish and seafood. While the direct consumption of EPA and DHA from marine foods represents the primary way by which these beneficial fatty acids accumulate in the body, they can also be endogenously synthesized from alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in a pathway regulated by fatty acid desaturase and elongase enzymes. Although the amount of ALA converted into EPA and DHA is widely considered to be low compared to their direct dietary intake, this pathway is important for individuals who do not consume EPA and DHA directly.

Numerous modifiable and non-modifiable factors such as diet, biological sex, age, and genetics, among others, can modify the endogenous synthesis of EPA and DHA. Of specific relevance is the role of variants in fatty acid desaturase (FADS) and elongase (ELOVL) genes that have been associated with LCPUFA profiles in plasma, serum, erythrocytes, adipose tissue, and breast milk. Since the landmark study by Schaeffer et al. and a genome-wide association study (GWAS) by Tanaka et al., variants in the FADS genes in particular are now recognized to have a significant influence on LCPUFA levels. These same single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) have also been associated with various health and disease outcomes, such as CVD and various cancers. There are numerous SNPs located in and near the FADS genes, with the rs174537 SNP in FADS1 emerging as one of the most studied due to its consistently strong association with fatty acid profiles. Although investigations into the functional role(s) of SNPs in the FADS gene cluster are limited and the majority comprise hypothesis generating in vitro studies, emerging evidence suggests they modify FADS gene expression through epigenetic mechanisms and differential binding of transcription factors. The present narrative review collates this existing evidence to provide an update on the current state of knowledge regarding SNPs in the FADS gene cluster and the molecular mechanisms by which they can impact LCPUFA synthesis. Understanding the functional roles of SNPs in the FADS genes is germane given the interest to potentially use these genetic variants for precision nutrition strategies aimed at improving an individual's n3-LCPUFA status and, ultimately, their health.
Overview of LCPUFA Synthesis

The synthesis of both n3- and n6-LCPUFA occurs through a pathway comprising several sequential desaturation and elongation steps. Desaturase enzymes insert a cis-double bond at specific positions in a fatty acyl chain through a reaction that requires molecular oxygen, NAD(P)H cytochrome b5 reductase, and cytochrome b5. In contrast, elongases lengthen a fatty acyl chain by 2 carbons as part of 4 sequential reactions that depend on fatty acyl CoA, malonyl CoA, and NAD(P)H. As depicted in Figure 1, ALA (18:3n-3) and linoleic acid (18:2n-6) are first converted into stearidonic acid (SDA, 18:4n-3) and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA, 18:3n-6), respectively, by the rate-limiting delta-6 desaturase (D6D) enzyme. Subsequently, elongase 5 (ELOVL5) adds 2 carbons to these acyl chains, resulting in the synthesis of eicosatetraenoic acid (20:4n-3) from SDA and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3n-6) from GLA. Next, the delta-5 desaturase (D5D) inserts another double bond into the acyl chain, converting eicosatetraenoic acid into EPA (20:5n-3) and DGLA into arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4n-6). Both EPA and AA can undergo further modification through either a peroxisomal route or FADS2-mediated delta-4 desaturation to generate DHA (22:6n-3) and docosapentaenoic acid (DPAn-6, 22:5n-6), respectively.
LCPUFA synthesis pathway. Key fatty acids are highlighted in red, while enzymes are in grey boxes (created in BioRender. Mutch, D. [2025] https://BioRender.com/sjd7saa).

It is notable that this pathway converts both ALA and LA into more highly unsaturated LCPUFA, thus creating a competition for flux through this pathway (Fig. 1). Previous kinetic studies using microsomes isolated from rat liver and human fetal liver suggest a higher D6D activity with ALA compared to LA, thus pointing to ALA as its preferred substrate. However, a series of microsomal studies by Brenner and Peluffo revealed that D6D conversion of ALA into SDA is inhibited by LA, while LA conversion to GLA is inhibited by ALA. Consequently, the levels of ALA and LA in the background diet can have a significant impact on the flux of substrates through the pathway and, consequently, tissue fatty acid profiles. This substrate competition is notable given the high n6/n3 ratio in the typical Western diet has been associated with increased risk of chronic diseases characterized by dyslipidemia and/or inflammation.

Of further relevance is that ALA conversion into EPA and DHA is generally considered low in humans. Indeed, past studies in which conversion efficiency was examined with stable isotopes have reported that ~8% of ALA is converted to EPA, and <1% is converted to DHA, with these estimates varying with sex and age. These studies used blood samples (e.g., serum, plasma, or erythrocytes) as opposed to tissues to determine the percent composition of EPA and DHA; however, recent investigations using compound-specific isotope analysis suggest that measuring conversion efficiency using blood fatty acids may be underestimating EPA and DHA synthesis at the tissue level. As such, continued investigation of the various factors that can influence ALA conversion into downstream n3-LCPUFA is warranted as this pathway is the primary means by which people who do not consume marine foods accumulate EPA and DHA.
Genetic Variants Associated with n3-LCPUFA Levels

Since the first GWAS by Tanaka et al. revealed that variants in FADS and ELOVL genes were associated with circulating levels of ALA, EPA, and DHA, there remains a high interest to further elucidate the genetic network that can influence EPA and DHA levels in the body. Most GWASs examining how genetic variation affects n3-LCPUFA levels have been conducted in populations of European ancestry; however, more recent studies have begun to explore candidate genetic variants in other ethnicities. Lemaitre et al. conducted a meta-analysis comprising ~9,000 subjects of European ancestry and revealed two loci that were strongly associated with n3-LCPUFA. The first was located on chromosome 11q12.2, which contained the FADS gene cluster, C11orf9/10 and FEN1, and the second was located at chromosome 6p24.2, which contained ELOVL2 and SYPC2L. These authors then replicated selected SNPs in samples of African, Chinese, and Hispanic ancestry. While the allelic frequency varied between the different ethnicities, the relationships between these two SNPs and n3-LCPUFA were similar. The association between SNPs in the FADS gene cluster and ELOVL genes are generally robust and consistent across different studies. Population-specific GWAS have uncovered new associations between circulating LCPUFA levels and SNPs located near other genes; however, these associations require independent replication. Nevertheless, the development of polygenic risk scores that consider SNPs from the FADS gene cluster, ELOVL genes, and newly discovered variants may prove valuable to further clarify the variability in circulating n3-LCPUFA between different populations. However, the remainder of the discussion will focus on variants in the FADS gene cluster.
Fatty Acid Desaturase Genes

The cloning, chromosomal location, and genomic structure of human fatty acid desaturase enzymes was first described by Marquardt et al.. The FADS gene cluster, located on chromosome 11 (11q12-q13.1), comprises three genes: FADS1, FADS2, and FADS3. The FADS1 and FADS2 genes are located head to head, while the FADS3 gene is located tail to tail with FADS2. Due to the highly similar exon organization of the three FADS genes, Marquardt et al. postulated these genes arose through gene duplication events. Through amino acid sequence comparison, it was determined that the FADS genes contained three histidine motifs that are characteristic of other membrane-bound desaturases. Further, these genes appear to be highly conserved among different species, with high sequence identity reported with mouse and rat desaturases. FADS1 encodes for D5D and FADS2 encodes for D6D, while the function of FADS3 remains poorly understood.

LCPUFA synthesis is generally presumed to be highest in the liver; however, FADS1 and FADS2 genes are also expressed in many other tissues. Reynolds et al. used data from the GTEx Project to investigate desaturase gene expression in 44 human tissues collected from deceased individuals enrolled in a rapid autopsy program. Expression levels for FADS1 and FADS2 ranged across tissues, with blood and skeletal muscle having very low levels and the brain and adrenal gland having the highest levels. The implications for varying levels of FADS1 and FADS2 gene expression on the tissue-specific synthesis of LCPUFA remains to be clarified.
Role of Ancestry on Variation in the FADS Gene Cluster

Studies over the past decades have uncovered that the efficiency of LCPUFA synthesis is determined, in part, by an individual's genetic background. The FADS gene cluster spans a region of approximately 100 kb that contains many SNPs in high linkage disequilibrium (LD). Genetic investigations suggest that variants in the FADS gene cluster have been shaped by natural selection and environmental pressures, potentially contributing to ethnic-specific susceptibilities to chronic diseases. Ameur et al. used SNP-array genotype data from five European cohorts to identify the presence of two major LD blocks in the FADS gene cluster. The first block spanned FADS1 and part of FADS2, while the second block spanned the remaining region of FADS2. Strong associations between block 1 and the levels of a phosphatidylcholine (PC36:4) species were found, with a set of 28 SNPs in particular distinguishing individuals with low and high levels of PC36:4. The most common haplotype was associated with high lipid levels and denoted the derived haplotype, while the less common haplotype was associated with low lipid levels and denoted the ancestral haplotype. Further investigations revealed that individuals homozygous for the derived haplotype had low plasma levels of ALA and LA and higher levels of EPA, DHA, and AA, suggesting a greater conversion efficiency. In contrast, individuals homozygous for the ancestral haplotype showed the opposite fatty acid profile, suggesting lower conversion efficiency. The higher conversion efficiency observed with the derived haplotype was reflected by a higher FADS1 gene expression in liver. Analyses using data from the Human Genome Diversity Panel revealed these haplotypes exhibit geographic variability, thus providing intriguing insights into the evolutionary pressures that helped shape this region of the genome. Specifically, the derived haplotype is nearly fixed in African populations, while this region is more polymorphic in European and Asian populations, and the ancestral haplotype is nearly fixed in Indigenous Americans. Furthermore, comparative genomic analyses found that rhesus macaques and African apes, as well as Neanderthals, have haplotypes resembling the ancestral haplotype, leading to the hypothesis that the derived haplotype emerged with modern humans. Independent of these haplotypes, a 22-bp insertion/deletion (indel; rs66698963) in FADS2 was reported by Kothapalli et al. to be under positive selection in South Asians compared to Europeans. Indeed, the frequency of the I/I allele (associated with higher conversion efficiency) was approximately 70% in South Asians compared to 17% in Europeans, thus providing additional evidence of geographical variation in the FADS gene cluster.

Several groups have postulated that selection of FADS alleles was driven by changes in the consumption of dietary fatty acids. Specifically, the emergence of agricultural practices and plant-based diets containing high levels of the precursors ALA and LA support the premise that variants in FADS genes that favour an increased capacity for LCPUFA biosynthesis (i.e., the derived haplotype or I/I allele) are under positive selective pressure. It is therefore intriguing that specific populations such as the Greenland Inuit, Siberian populations, and Indigenous Americans are nearly fixed for the ancestral haplotype. Fumagalli et al. hypothesized that the ancestral haplotype may help with cold weather adaptation and stem from the high consumption of n3-LCPUFA directly from marine foods, thus diminishing the need for their endogenous synthesis. We refer readers to several previously published papers that delve deeper into the impact of ancestry and FADS genetic variation. Given the health benefits associated with higher EPA and DHA levels in the body, there is considerable interest to elucidate whether variants in the FADS gene cluster modify n3-LCPUFA synthesis to alter chronic disease development.
Genetic Variants in the FADS Gene Cluster

Several review papers have documented the associations between SNPs in the FADS gene cluster and fatty acid profiles in serum, plasma, erythrocytes, adipose tissue, and maternal breast milk. Unsurprisingly, the direction of these associations is similar for many of the SNPs in the FADS gene cluster due to the high LD (r2 > 0.8) that exists within this region. In most, but not all, cases, individuals carrying minor alleles show higher levels of precursor fatty acids (ALA, LA) and lower levels of product fatty acids (EPA, DHA, and AA), demonstrating reduced conversion efficiency (i.e., aligning with the ancestral haplotype). Results from individual candidate gene studies are further supported by several recent meta-analyses for specific SNPs, such as rs174547 and rs174556 in FADS1 and rs174575 in FADS2. For rs174547, Wang et al. also showed that minor allele carriers of this SNP had lower fatty acid desaturase indices (i.e., estimates of desaturase activity). Collectively, the evidence currently available overwhelmingly demonstrates that minor alleles in the FADS gene cluster are generally associated with lower desaturase activity compared to major alleles.

One of the most widely studied SNPs in the FADS gene cluster is rs174537 (G/T), which maps to an open reading frame 14.4 kb upstream of FADS1. This SNP has repeatedly been shown to have a robust association with LCPUFA levels in genetic association studies and can be used as proxy for the derived and ancestral haplotypes previously discussed, with the major G allele corresponding to the derived haplotype and the minor T allele corresponding to the ancestral haplotype. Indeed, Mathias et al. analysed rs174537 in 52 populations in the Human Genome Diversity Panel and showed that the G allele is nearly fixed in the African population and the T allele is nearly fixed in Central American populations, thus aligning with previous haplotype analyses. Given the consistent and reproducible associations reported between rs174537, fatty acid profiles, and estimated desaturase activities, many of the functional studies conducted to date have either focused on this SNP directly or related SNPs in high LD (Fig. 2).
Pairwise LD d' and r2 plots for SNPs discussed in the manuscript. The heatmap matrix of pairwise LD was built using 1000G data (Genome Build GRCh37) for the CEU population with the LDmatrix Tool.
Impact of Variants on FADS Gene Expression

SNPs in the FADS gene cluster influence FADS1 and FADS2 gene expression to varying degrees. For example, Wang et al. examined the relationship between 6 SNPs in the FADS gene cluster, including rs174537, and the expression of hepatic FADS genes. Five of the 6 SNPs were in high LD. The authors reported that minor alleles for all 6 SNPs were significantly associated with lower hepatic FADS1 gene and protein expression, but the associations with FADS2 expression were weaker and did not reach statistical significance.

Independently, Reynolds et al. comprehensively explored the relationship between SNPs and FADS1/FADS2 gene expression in 44 tissues from the GTEx Project and uncovered numerous expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) in several tissues. Briefly, the authors used rs174548 as the representative functional eQTL due to previously reported associations with FADS1 and FADS2 gene expression, as well as specific LCPUFA. The rs174548 SNP is in moderate LD with rs174537 (r2 = 0.76; Fig. 2). Interestingly, rs174548 was associated with FADS1 and FADS2 expression but not always in a consistent manner. For example, the minor (G) allele for rs174548 was associated with lower FADS1 expression in the brain, liver, and adipose tissue, while this same minor allele was associated with higher FADS2 expression in adipose tissue and showed no association in the brain or liver. Further investigations are necessary to understand the basis for the differential relationship between eQTLs and FADS1/FADS2 gene expression in different tissues. This study represented one of the first whole-body analyses to examine the relationships between SNPs in the FADS gene cluster and FADS gene expression.

Several other targeted SNP studies also showed that minor alleles in or near the FADS gene cluster are associated with altered gene expression. For example, Klingel et al. and Wang et al. reported that minor allele carriers for rs174537 had lower FADS1 gene expression in different adipose tissue depots. He et al. showed that rs174570, which is in low LD with rs174537 (r2 = 0.34; Fig. 2), was associated with similar changes in both FADS1 and FADS2 expression in visceral adipose tissue. Using in vitro functional assays in cultured liver cells, Hermant et al. and Lee et al. reported reductions in luciferase activity in cells containing the minor allele for rs174546 (C/T), which is in high LD with rs174537 (r2 = 0.98; Fig. 2). Given the high LD that exists between SNPs in this genomic region, the causative functional SNP remains to be clarified.
Molecular Mechanisms Underlying eQTLs in the FADS Gene Cluster

Depending on the genomic location, there are several mechanisms by which SNPs can regulate gene expression. For example, SNPs located in a transcriptional regulatory element can impact mRNA expression, SNPs located within a gene can disrupt mRNA splicing and translation, and non-synonymous SNPs in the coding region of a gene can lead to a change in amino acid that modifies protein activity. Additionally, SNPs in non-coding regions of the genome may impact gene expression through epigenetic mechanisms, such as disrupting DNA methylation and non-coding RNA binding sites. Although the molecular mechanisms linking eQTLs with altered LCPUFA synthesis are not fully elucidated, emerging evidence suggests important roles for epigenetics and altered transcription factor binding (Table 1).

DNA Methylation

Genome-wide allele-specific methylation analyses have shown that variants in the FADS gene cluster may influence DNA methylation, thereby regulating the efficiency of LCPUFA synthesis. For example, Howard et al. found that hepatic FADS1 activity is regulated by DNA methylation in an enhancer region of the FADS gene cluster. Focusing on rs174537, these authors identified a significant association with a methylation probe (cg27386326) located in close proximity to the FADS1 transcription start site in both European Americans and African Americans, with higher methylation observed in individuals homozygous for the minor T allele. This aligned with a lower liver D5D index (i.e., ratio of AA/DGLA). While this site was determined to be susceptible to histone modifications and lie near various predicted transcription factor binding sites (TFBS), the authors did not conduct functional studies. Subsequent bisulfite sequencing in this region was performed for a deeper analysis and confirmed the relationship between rs174537 and the methylation status of cg27386326 in the liver. This association was similarly reported in prostate cancer tissue. Taken together, these studies provide evidence that rs174537 (or a SNP in high LD) may serve as a genetic marker for methylation sites in the liver. Separately, He et al. explored the methylation status in and near the FADS1 and FADS2 promoter regions in visceral adipose tissue. In this study, the authors identified both positive and negative associations between rs174570, methylation status, and gene expression levels. A mediation analysis revealed that the effect of this SNP on FADS1 gene expression was indeed mediated by DNA methylation; however, the authors did not replicate the findings from previous independent studies. This is not unexpected given that methylation patterns are known to differ between tissues. As such, further investigations are necessary to characterize the relationship between SNPs in the FADS gene cluster, DNA methylation, and gene expression in different tissues.

Interestingly, Hoile et al. revealed that the methylation status of the 5' regulatory regions of FADS2 was generally higher with the increased consumption of n3-LCPUFA in both males and females. The changes in methylation status were correlated with FADS2 gene expression, but no changes were observed with FADS1 expression. While this study suggests that dietary fatty acids may influence DNA methylation in a manner that impacts FADS2 gene expression, the authors did not examine genetic variants. A future n3-LCPUFA intervention study examining the interaction between methylation status and conversion efficiency in individuals stratified according to their FADS genotype will provide additional insight.
Non-Coding RNAs

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding molecules that can regulate gene expression. A few in vitro studies have examined whether SNPs in the FADS gene cluster may modify miRNA binding efficiency. Hermant et al. performed an in silico analysis and found that rs174546 could modify 4 predicted miRNA binding sites within the 3'UTR of FADS1. The authors transfected cultured liver cells with luciferase reporter constructs related to rs174546 (rs174546C major allele; rs174546T minor allele), with or without these various miRNAs. Only cells co-transfected with the rs174546T minor allele and miR-149-5p showed a reduction in luciferase activity. In contrast, there was no effect on luciferase activity in cells transfected with the rs174546C major allele. Importantly, the authors confirmed that miR-149-5p was expressed in the human liver. These results suggests that the rs174546T minor allele may create a binding site for miR-149-5p that contributes to reduced FADS1 expression. In a separate analysis, Lee et al. showed that this same minor allele was also found to enhance binding with another miRNA, miR-6728-3p, that reduced FADS1 expression. Taken together, these two studies have uncovered an additional mechanism that may contribute to the lower conversion efficiency observed in minor allele carriers.
Modification of TFBS

Hepatic FADS gene expression is under the control of several key transcription factors, including sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP-1c) and peroxisome proliferator activated receptors (PPARs), among others. Several in vitro studies have revealed that SNPs in the FADS gene cluster may differentially modify TFBS that regulate FADS gene expression.

Lattka et al. conducted functional analyses related to two SNPs located in the FADS promoter region: rs3834458 and rs968567. These SNPs were not only selected due to their genomic location, but they are also located in a CpG-rich region and contain putative binding sites for both SREBP1 and PPAR, among others. Using luciferase reporter gene assays to measure FADS2 promoter activity in different cell lines, constructs with the minor T allele in rs968567 showed increased activity. Several TFBS were predicted to overlap with rs968567, including that of the ELK1 activator (a member of the ETS domain transcription factor family). The authors showed that expression levels of FADS2 and ELK1 were correlated in whole blood samples and that ELK1 binding to the promoter was only observed with the minor T allele in rs968567. While rs968567 is in low LD with rs174537 (r2 = 0.38, Fig. 2), rs3834458 is in high LD (r2 = 0.98, Fig. 2); however, the authors did not measure FADS1 expression.

Reardon et al. identified eQTLs associated with FADS1 gene expression in lymphoblasts collected from Japanese participants in the HapMap Project. Specifically, minor alleles in a region located in the first intron in FADS2 were associated with reduced FADS1 expression. Bioinformatic analysis of this region identified binding sites for both SREBP and PPARgamma. Using agonists targeting SREBP-1c, the authors reported that minor allele carriers showed a stronger response on FADS1 and FADS2 expression than major allele carriers, an effect not seen with a synthetic PPARgamma agonist. Subsequent sequencing of the SREBP-1c binding site in FADS1 led to the discovery of the aforementioned indel (rs66698963). Although this study did not provide an explanation for the lower FADS1 expression observed in minor allele carriers, it did highlight a differential response to SREBP-1c activation that may relate to changes in the binding of other transcription regulators in this region.

Finally, Pan et al. explored functional variants related to desaturase activity between the derived and ancestral haplotypes. Analyses in HepG2 liver cells revealed that constructs containing the rs174557 located in intron 1 of FADS1, which is in moderate LD with rs174537 (r2 = 0.76, Fig. 2), showed strong enhancer activity on several histone modifications that differed between the two alleles (referred to as A and D by the authors, with the A allele corresponding to the ancestral haplotype and the D allele corresponding to the derived haplotype). Subsequent in silico analyses examined potential transcription factors predicted to bind differently to rs174557 and showed that PATZ1 (POZ/BTB and AT hook containing zinc finger 1) binds preferentially to the A allele. Interestingly, overexpressing PATZ1 strongly suppressed the enhancer activity in the A allele compared to the D allele. This genomic region was also shown to be important for SREBP-1c and SP1 binding, which work together to activate gene expression. Through a series of eloquent experiments, the authors demonstrated a direct competition between PATZ1 and SP1 binding in this region, with PATZ1 favouring the A allele and SP1 favouring the D allele. Consequently, the enhancer activity associated with this region is higher with the D allele, thereby favouring increased FADS1 expression. As such, individuals with the derived haplotype (aligning with major allele carriers) may have higher FADS1 gene expression due to lower PATZ1 binding.

Collectively, these studies have taken important first strides to unravel the transcriptional consequences of genetic variants in the FADS gene cluster. Which eQTL is causal remains to be fully elucidated; however, these three studies suggest that variants may regulate transcription factor binding in this genomic region.
Precision Nutrition and FADS Genes

There is considerable interest amongst healthcare practitioners, the general population, and direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing companies towards the use of genetic information to personalize diets. While variants in the FADS gene cluster have garnered particular interest for precision nutrition strategies due to their highly reproducible association with LCPUFA levels in blood and tissues, their association with disease risk remains equivocal. Indeed, links between SNPs in the FADS gene cluster and various health outcomes, including CVD, type-2 diabetes, and cancer, have been previously discussed in the literature; however, the direction of these associations is not always consistent. For example, a recent review by Gittess et al. highlighted that individuals carrying minor alleles in FADS variants were generally found to show a degree of protection from coronary heart disease but that the relationships varied depending on the SNP analysed. A protection in minor allele carriers of FADS variants may initially seem paradoxical given that these individuals would have lower n3-LCPUFA synthesis; however, the desaturase and elongase enzymes that control n3-LCPUFA synthesis also control n6-LCPUFA synthesis. The proportionally greater abundance of n6-LCPUFA in the Western diet compared to n3-LCPUFA means higher synthesis of AA compared to EPA and DHA. Consequently, more AA is available for the production of pro-inflammatory oxylipins that can contribute to the development of chronic diseases. Therefore, minor allele carriers on a background diet with a high n6/n3 ratio would benefit from a lower production of AA and pro-inflammatory oxylipins compared to major allele carriers. While such a tailored nutrition strategy appears straightforward, it is notable that most studies examining the links between SNPs in the FADS gene cluster and disease development have been observational. As such, there is a continued need for prospective studies that control for both background dietary fatty acid composition and FADS genotype to support the development of effective precision nutrition strategies targeting an individual's n3-LCPUFA status and, ultimately, their health.

Although scarce, a few nutrigenetic studies in which dietary fat composition was controlled provide strong support for further investigations in larger and ethnically diverse cohorts. For example, Gillingham et al. conducted a small crossover intervention in 36 hyperlipidemic subjects to examine the effects of three diets (high in flaxseed oil or high in high-oleic acid canola oil compared to a Western diet) on plasma fatty acids and whether responses to these diets were modified by SNPs in the FADS gene cluster. It was reported that FADS minor allele carriers (including rs174537) consuming the diet enriched with flaxseed oil had higher EPA compared to major allele carriers with the other two diets. Furthermore, the authors examined conversion efficiency using a [U-13C]ALA tracer and found that major allele carriers for FADS SNPs had a 3-4-fold higher plasma [13C]EPA compared to minor allele carriers. To the best of our knowledge, this is the only study conducted to date in which an ALA tracer was used to examine conversion efficiency in individuals stratified by their FADS genotype who consumed diets for which fatty acid composition was controlled.

Other nutrigenetic studies have examined the interaction between fish oil supplementation and FADS genotype in young and adult populations. For example, Meldrum et al. conducted an exploratory study in which infants were randomized to receive either fish oil or a placebo between birth to 6 months of age. Fish oil supplementation in infants who were homozygous for FADS1 minor alleles (including rs174537) increased blood DHA levels more than major allele carriers, although no changes were observed in EPA levels. Independently, Al-Hilal et al. showed that adult men and women carrying the minor allele for rs174537 had lower D5D activity compared to major homozygote carriers. However, only minor allele carriers showed an increase in D5D activity with increasing dosage of EPA and DHA, as reflected by a higher AA:DGLA ratio. Together, these studies suggest that individuals with FADS minor alleles may be more responsive to fish oil supplementation and may therefore experience greater health benefits associated with higher EPA and DHA; however, additional prospective studies in larger cohorts with background diets varying in the n6/n3 ratio are necessary.

Understanding the molecular mechanisms by which SNPs in the FADS gene cluster modify FADS1/FADS2 gene expression may help better refine future precision nutrition strategies to improve n3-LCPUFA status. Martinez-Zaldivar et al. examined the effect of combined fish oil and 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) supplementation in mothers during pregnancy on LCPUFA concentrations in offspring stratified according to their FADS genotype. The authors reported a potential interaction between maternal supplementation and genotype on offspring DPAn-6 levels in children. Although DNA methylation was not examined in this study, 5-MTHF is a methyl donor that could promote epigenetic modifications in or near the FADS gene cluster. In conjunction with the recent mechanistic insights demonstrating that FADS gene expression is modified by DNA methylation in a SNP-dependent manner, this study supports the need for additional trials examining the interactions between dietary fatty acids and methyl donors on n3-LCPUFA synthesis.

Collectively, these nutrigenetic studies provide encouragement regarding the use of SNPs in the FADS genes to develop personalized nutrition recommendations related to n3-LCPUFA that may be particularly beneficial for specific demographic groups in the general population. For example, individuals carrying minor alleles (i.e., the ancestral haplotype) may benefit from a diet high in preformed EPA and DHA due to their lower conversion efficiency. Additionally, individuals who adhere to vegan or vegetarian diets could benefit from the consumption of algal products rich in preformed EPA and DHA, or increased levels of ALA-rich seeds and dietary oils, to maximize the levels of these important fatty acids in the body. While these scenarios appear straightforward, a primary challenge remains the implementation and adherence of individuals to changes in dietary patterns. For example, we conducted a trial to examine if free-living participants who received their personal FADS1 genotype (for rs174537) altered their n3-LCPUFA intake. Although participants who received their genetic information showed increased awareness of n3-LCPUFA terminology, no changes in food intake or erythrocyte fatty acids were observed. While findings from nutrigenetics research provide encouragement regarding the value of precision nutrition, translating this basic knowledge into actionable and sustainable plans for a given individual remains a challenge.
Conclusion

Although identifying the specific functional variant and elucidating the mechanisms by which variants in or near the FADS gene cluster impact LCPUFA synthesis remain in their infancy, the work accomplished in the field to date has proved both promising and exciting. Indeed, the hypothesis generating in vitro studies that have explored epigenetic modifications in regulatory regions, the role of non-coding RNAs, and variants that modify transcription factor binding affinity in the FADS gene cluster have generated important new insights that will help improve our understanding of the genetic basis underlying LCPUFA synthesis and how this may differ across populations. Continued investigations in this area are needed to translate this basic research to humans to support future precision nutrition initiatives targeting n3-LCPUFA status and the reduction of chronic disease risk.

passages.text: Community co-design of contextually relevant rheumatic heart disease primary prevention
Abstract
Introduction

Primary prevention of rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is aimed at timely diagnosis and treatment of superficial Group A Streptococcal infections, most commonly Strep sore throat. However, uptake and delivery of primary prevention for RHD-endemic regions has room for improvement. Community co-design is an important aspect of intervention development to increase sustainability and reach.
Methods

Group-level assessment (GLA) sessions were used to understand the community's priorities and insights around sore throat. Personas, or user archetypes, were then developed to capture the behaviours and characteristics of diverse future users of primary prevention in the district. Finally, these personas were used in community design workshops to identify barriers and facilitators to potential interventions, generate creative solutions to overcome identified barriers and prioritise implementation models based on impact and feasibility. The final list of implementation strategies was presented by workshop participants to the broader community for additional validation and feedback.
Results

The GLA sessions identified five priority areas: (1) need for improved access to care, closer to home; (2) importance of mothers as caregivers; (3) strong influence of community leaders; (4) importance of community health workers and (5) role of traditional providers and practices. Five personas were created, including: hands-on caregiver, restricted caregiver, removed family decision-maker, helpful neighbour and influential leader. Design workshops identified the highest-rated interventions as: decentralisation of care delivery into the community (strategy 1), use of community health workers as key implementing partners (strategy 2) and streamlining sore throat services at public healthcare facilities (strategy 3). Participants proposed potential practical applications of these interventions.
Conclusions

Community-based participatory research identified novel implementation strategies for an RHD primary prevention programme in Uganda. The value set and strategies developed in this study can now be used as guideposts to develop and test a package of implementation strategies for improving RHD primary prevention in Uganda.
WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

Primary prevention of rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is inadequate in low-income and middle-income countries, home to the majority of the 55 million people living with RHD. Scalable, sustainable models are urgently needed to address this global issue. Community co-design is crucial for developing culturally and contextually appropriate interventions, ensuring greater sustainability and reach.
WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

This study identifies key community priorities for RHD primary prevention, including improved access to care, the role of mothers and community leaders, and the involvement of community health workers and traditional providers. It highlights three high-impact interventions: decentralising care delivery, using community health workers and streamlining sore throat services in public health facilities. These findings provide a foundation for testing scalable and culturally appropriate primary prevention strategies in Uganda.
HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

This study offers valuable insights into community-driven strategies for improving RHD primary prevention, which could inform the development of more effective, culturally tailored interventions in similar settings. Its findings may influence policy decisions to integrate community health workers and decentralise care delivery, enhancing the scalability and sustainability of RHD prevention efforts.
Background

Without treatment, up to 3% of children with Group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis are at risk of developing acute rheumatic fever (ARF), an immunological response that can damage heart valves and lead to chronic rheumatic heart disease (RHD). Early diagnosis of GAS pharyngitis and appropriate antibiotic treatment within 9 days of symptom onset can prevent up to 80% of RHD cases. However, despite the availability of effective primary prevention, the adoption of these measures remains alarmingly low in many low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), where over 90% of the 55 million people with RHD reside.

Implementing RHD primary prevention in LMICs has been challenging due to barriers such as the high cost of bacteriological diagnosis and low health-seeking behaviour for sore throat. The RESET study (Reducing New Cases of Rheumatic Heart Disease through a Community Streptococcal Treatment Program), conducted from 2019 to 2023 in a Ugandan district, tested a pragmatic, multicomponent intervention to address these challenges (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05276999).

RESET focused on simplified GAS diagnosis using a clinical decision rule, healthcare worker training on guideline-based treatment and extensive community education about sore throat. The aim was to reduce implementation barriers such as diagnostic costs, insufficient provider training and low health-seeking behaviour. 2 years into the study, our evaluation found that while the programme significantly increased healthcare worker knowledge and community awareness of sore throat, it did not notably improve healthcare centre presentations for childhood sore throat. This gap highlighted the need for a more community-informed approach to understand and address current practices.

In this paper, we describe the process and outcomes of deep community consultation using a community-based participatory research (CBPR) approach. We engaged participants with two participatory research methods to identify key implementation elements for a successful childhood sore throat treatment programme. Using a group-level assessment (GLA) method, we identified community priorities and then incorporated these insights into a series of participatory design workshops. These workshops explored alternative ways to deliver sore throat education, diagnosis and treatment, ensuring a future programme would be contextually and culturally relevant to the community.
Methods
Patient and public involvement
When and how were patients/public first involved in the research?

The public was first involved in the research during the recruitment phase, when they were invited either as a key stakeholder (local village chairman, religious leader, herbalist, nurse, teacher, parent and community healthcare worker) or by the key stakeholders.
How were the research question(s) developed and informed by their priorities, experience and preferences?

The research questions were informed by a previous study in which extensive health worker and community education was employed, but did not improve diagnosis and treatment. The research questions were codeveloped with partners in Uganda to increase our understanding of current community practices in Tororo district, as explained by the community members living there.
How were patients/public involved in
The design and conduct of the study?

Patients were involved in the design and conduct of the study by participating in the GLAs and design workshops. In the GLAs, participants engaged in real-time thematic analysis of sore throat needs and priorities, which led to the distilling of top community priorities. In the design workshops, participants identified barriers and facilitators to a sore throat programme and generated solutions to overcome these barriers.
Choice of outcome measures?
The public was not involved in this step.
Recruitment to the study?
Participating community stakeholders invited two additional community members to participate in the GLAs. The participants of the design workshops were hand-selected by the local research team.
How were (or will) patients/public be involved in choosing the methods and agreeing plans for dissemination of the study results to participants and linked communities?
The public was not involved in this step.
Study setting

This study was conducted with community members in Tororo District, where the parent RESET study was conducted. Tororo District is located in a region with a poverty rate of 35.7% and is around 200 kilometers east of the Ugandan capital city, Kampala. The district has approximately 609 000 residents, more than half of whom are less than 15 years of age.
Community-based participatory research

This was a two-part CBPR study where the research team partnered directly with community members in each phase of the research process. CBPR, an approach to research that builds on community strengths and resources to generate relevant research goals and increase sustainability, was used as the guiding approach for the project. GLAs, design workshops and personas were used to engage Tororo community members in cocreating a childhood sore throat treatment programme. Participants signed written informed consent for participation. All sessions were conducted in English, with side-by-side translation employed for the minority of participants who preferred another language. Sessions had a lead facilitator and two cofacilitators (members of the research team), as well as 10 community members that supported small group activities during the sessions and provided translation when necessary. Community-driven real-time analysis was integrated throughout the research process.
Part 1: GLA

GLA is a large group qualitative and participatory method intended to engage diverse groups of people with varying lived experiences. Within the GLA process, participants are viewed as the experts of their lives and communities, and accordingly, generate, assess and prioritise data using their own expertise. For this study, we conducted two GLA sessions, each with a distinct set of community members.

Snowball sampling was used to recruit GLA participants (figure 1). A list of key stakeholders was generated that included the roles of local village chairman, religious leader, herbalist, nurse, teacher, parent and community healthcare worker. These stakeholder roles were selected to ensure a wide variety of input from different sectors of the community. For each of two sessions, a research nurse confirmed participation of one community member for each category and then invited that participant to bring two additional community members, for a total of 21 invited participants per session (42 in total).

The GLA invitation process. Seven participants were directly invited for each GLA session. These seven participants represented various stakeholders. Each of the directly invited participants was asked to bring along two more participants (from the same stakeholder division) except one who was asked to bring along one more person each. These indirectly invited participants were also supposed to be future beneficiaries of a sore throat treatment programme and willing to contribute to the workshop. This process was repeated twice (once for each GLA session). GLA, group-level assessment; VHTs, village health teams.

GLA sessions were conducted through six discrete steps (figure 2). In step 1 (climate setting), warmth builders and get-to-know-you questions encouraged attendees to engage with the people around them. In step 2 (generating), participants were asked to walk around the room and were given markers to write responses on flip charts that contained open-ended prompts such as "The best sore throat treatment program would include...,", "People who treat childhood sore throat in our community need to know..." or "The biggest barriers to treatment of childhood sore throat in our community are..." (online supplemental appendix 1) . An example of a completed flip chart can be found in figure 3. In step 3 (appreciating), participants were prompted to move around the room and observe what others had written, and (step 4, reflecting) note any ideas that caught their attention by circling or starring ideas on the flip chart. In step 5 (understanding), smaller groups were formed, assigned ~5 flip chart prompts and instructed to identify three common themes/patterns across the charts. A representative was nominated from each small group to report common themes back to the whole group in a 'round-robin' format, with the facilitator recording the major themes on a new flip chart. Finally, in step 6 (selecting), each participant identified their top priority from the major themes. These themes formed the basis for understanding community needs and priorities for development of primary prevention strategies in the subsequent design workshops. Themes and priorities across the two GLA sessions were distilled by the research team.
Steps of the GLA process. GLA, group-level assessment.
GLA flip chart. An example of a completed flip chart, where participants answered the bolded prompt at the top of the page.
Part 2: Design Workshops

Design workshops are community-engaged events where stakeholders harness collective community knowledge to identify barriers and facilitators to a discrete issue and generate contextually appropriate solutions. In this study, three primary prevention design workshops were conducted over 2 days. Purposeful sampling, using the same key stakeholder roles outlined for the GLA sessions, was used to recruit 10 community participants who were asked to participate in all workshop sessions.

Workshop 1 started with a warmth builder to encourage participant interaction. Following this, participants reviewed the five community priorities developed in the GLA sessions. Next, the facilitator introduced the patient journey map (figure 4) which outlined the core patient points of any primary prevention strategy including: awareness (knowing sore throats need treatment), diagnosis (determining the cause of the sore throat) and treatment (obtaining and administering the correct medication).
Journey map. The journey map illustrates the three key patient points along the patient journey that this programme will aim to address.

Participants were then introduced to the concept of personas, community archetypes that participants used to walk through the patient journey map. For this study, five personas were designed by the local research team, based on the research team's experience working within the community and scenarios and people described in interviews. Each includes outlined barriers, facilitators, vehicles for engagement and motivators. The five personas include: the hands-on caregiver, the restricted caregiver, the removed family decision maker, the helpful neighbour and the influential leader. The remainder of workshop 1 was spent in small groups, with participants walking these personas through the patient journey map by imagining how the personas would experience each step, to identify facilitators and barriers to each patient point (awareness, diagnosis and treatment).

During workshop 2, participants worked individually, and then in small groups, to imagine possible solutions to the barriers identified in workshop 1. Participants generated innovative interventions for each point on the patient journey map. Using a process of sharing and iterative revision, small groups compared and combined ideas and then reported these out to the larger group, which then ranked each solution in terms of impact and feasibility using sticky notes that were placed on a large matrix (figure 5). A list of the three highest-ranked solutions for each journey map element was then generated. Using a structured worksheet, each participant then took one of these lists home and was instructed to consult with members of their community (friends, family, neighbours) and ask them to rank the proposed solutions in order from most to least desirable, allowing for broader community validation and input. Results from this community consultation were brought back to workshop 3 (figure 6).
Design workshop flip chart. Solution ranking matrix, where participants ranked proposed solutions in terms of feasibility and impact.
Top ranked solutions from design workshop 2.

In workshop 3, the final design workshop, participants were led by facilitators in thinking through the practical applications of the highest-rated solutions. Attendees were prompted to identify the 'who', 'where' and 'when' for each intervention, as well as to identify each solution's most critical component for success.
Results
Part 1: GLAs

Of the 42 invited, 38 participants attended a GLA session. The median age of participants was 45.5 (IQR 17.8) and 53% male. There was substantial geographic representation with participation from 13 of 17 subcounties in the district. The GLA participants identified five key community priorities that should be considered in the development of childhood sore throat programmes. Priorities included (1) the need for improved access to care closer to home, (2) the importance of mothers as caregivers and decision-makers, (3) the strong influence of community leaders, (4) the importance of community health workers (CHWs) and (5) the role of traditional providers and practices.
Need for improved access to care, closer to home

Responses alluding to a lack of access to personal and public resources to seek sore throat treatment were frequent in both GLA sessions. Feedback from attendees explained that long distances to treatment were deterrents to sore throat diagnosis and treatment, related to poverty and need to avoid out-of-pocket direct (transportation, medication) and indirect (missed work) expenses. Most community members were aware of the recommendation to seek formal evaluation for children who had sore throat (recent RESET campaign); however, many expressed that seeking sore throat treatment was not practical due to long distances to healthcare centres. Participants suggested that a programme addressing geographical proximity, or bringing care closer to where children live, would be more likely to be successful.
Importance of mothers as caregivers

During the GLAs, the idea of mother figureheads (mothers, grandmothers, mothers-in-law, etc) as staples in the identification of child illness was emphasised. Mothers were noted as the most likely first person to notice a child's sore throat. Additionally, there was an identified cultural emphasis on mothers turning to their mothers and mothers-in-law for health advice. However, the ability of women to make medication decisions for these children, including if they should seek formal diagnosis, was mixed. Some mother figureheads expressed that they could make executive decisions about child healthcare, some indicated they needed permission from the paternal figureheads before acting. Participants explained that empowering mothers as decision-makers could lead to a shift in approaches to treating childhood sore throat.
Strong influence of community leaders

GLA participants vocalised the importance of involving community leaders in mobilising people to seek treatment for their children through sore throat education and awareness. They specifically identified local chairmen (elected village leaders), religious leaders, CHWs and parents. They described the respect and attention community leaders garner, and the importance of leveraging their platforms to educate the community and raise awareness of new programmes. In particular, the group felt strongly that these community leaders could combat misinformation in the community and influence uptake and belief in messaging around the importance of sore throat.
Importance of CHWs

A consistent theme was the need for CHWs, as those closest in proximity to where people live, to be trained to diagnose and provide treatment for sore throat. The strong trust between CHWs and the populations they serve was repeatedly identified. CHWs were the primary answer to prompts such as: "The most trusted health advice in my community comes from..."; "People who are likely to treat childhood sore throat are..." and "If we really want to engage our community in childhood sore throat care we need to..."
The role of traditional providers and practices

There were mixed feelings in the group about the importance of traditional practices and providers in a community sore throat management strategy. Some participants strongly favoured formal government healthcare centres and expressed they were the first line of healthcare services for their family. All, however, agreed that when there is a sore throat in the community, it is common for members to turn to local herbs and religion (ie, prayer). Answers to the prompt "I have seen my friends and family treat sore throat in children by..." included things like using local herbs and drinking waragi (a locally produced gin-like alcohol product). Explanations included that traditional methods are less expensive and closer to home than formal healthcare. Participants also expressed that it was important to align the teachings of traditional healers, which were strong community motivators, that currently conflicted with those in the public health campaign. Resolving these differences and working together with traditional health practitioners was seen as a facilitator to a successful programme.
Part 2: Design Workshops

Of the 10 invited participants, 9 attended the three-workshop series, median age of participants was 55 years (IQR: 24 years), and 89% were male. There was broad geographic representation, with participants from 9 of the 17 Tororo subcounties.

Workshop 2 narrowed ideas down and mapped them to relevant points on the sore throat journey map. Community consultation further prioritised these strategies, with the final identified strategies including decentralisation of care delivery into the community (strategy 1), use of CHWs as key implementing partners (strategy 2) and streamlining sore throat services at public healthcare facilities (strategy 3). The need for continued education and awareness, in part by engaging local leaders to effectively communicate new approaches, was emphasised across all strategies.
Strategy 1: decentralisation of care delivery into the community

The first strategy focused on the key theme of increased access for primary prevention, closer to home. Outreach events were seen to have a dual purpose for education and awareness as well as for diagnosis. Workshop participants identified district health outreach budgets and potentially central implementation partners, such as the Uganda Heart Institute, as funders for such events. Other potential access points were also identified, including school-based sore throat programmes and a model of enhanced pharmacy-delivered diagnosis and treatment. This strategy also tied back to mothers as decision makers, with note that mothers may find it more feasible to seek care for childhood sore throat if access was expanded.
Strategy 2: engage community healthcare workers as key implementing partners

The identification of a key strategy to engage CHWs as key implementing partners reflects the theme that emerged during the GLAs. Again, workshop participants emphasised that CHWs were trusted health professionals who were close to the community. Healthcare centres were seen as the best place for training, as each CHW has a 'home' healthcare centre and could serve as an extender for this healthcare centre in the community. Training was felt best delivered by the district health team and national trainers of trainees, a model identified as effective for other diseases by workshop participants. Using a focused algorithm approach, a variety of implementation strategies were identified including community outreach events led by CHWs to raise awareness and identify cases of childhood sore throat, CHWs integrating sore throat evaluation and referral into routine work that included home visits, and village health teams taking on new scope of practice, including diagnosing childhood sore throat in the community and giving out antibiotic treatment. This final approach was identified to have possible regulatory challenges, as medication prescription is outside of a typical CHW practice scope. However, the community thought this could be possible for limited-scope indications. Under this strategy, workshop participants also emphasised adaptability, with the idea that outreach would be needed regularly. Outreach would be prioritised if a health centre notices an increase in sore throat cases, which participants identified as common during the rainy seasons.
Strategy 3: streamline primary prevention care at public health facilities

Streamlining care for childhood sore throat was also a popular strategy among many of the workshop participants. Participants felt that reducing the time spent waiting for care and providing more assurance that care will be available would be highly feasible and would increase care-seeking behaviour. Ultimately, this strategy could be important to decision makers who must weigh the decision to spend often long wait times at a healthcare centre for diagnosis or seek less formal care closer to home. A disease-specific focal person was one implementation model raised. In this solution, a disease-specific champion takes on additional responsibilities such as leading trainings, organising outreach events and tracking data on care delivery for their focal area, a model that has been used for other high-endemic diseases such as tuberculosis and HIV.
Discussion

There is an important opportunity to improve the uptake and delivery of RHD primary prevention globally. This study used CBPR to identify a community value set and package of high-priority strategies that could help close the 'know-do' gap for childhood sore throat care. The strongest message was that access points need to be expanded, and care needs to be available closer to home. We need to strengthen delivery of primary prevention through public healthcare centres and develop innovative solutions to integrate CHWs into RHD primary prevention. These strategies will require further stakeholder co-design to develop implementation strategies that are both acceptable in the population and feasible within the current resource limitations of the Ugandan public healthcare system.

By engaging with the community to identify core values, we gained an understanding of existing community strengths that could facilitate successful primary prevention programmes. This included the key role of CHWs to facilitate health in the community. While CHWs have not, to our knowledge, been involved in RHD primary prevention in sub-Saharan Africa, they have been leveraged to improve care in other regions. In Aboriginal communities in Northern Australia, CHWs are at the centre of an RHD primary prevention programme that includes elements of health literacy, community empowerment, housing and environmental support and health navigation. A relatively small impact study of this approach showed an encouraging trend towards increasing health-seeking behaviour and eventual fall in incidence of superficial GAS infections and ARF over the 3-year study period. In Uganda, it will be important to work with stakeholders to understand how CHWs can best facilitate RHD primary prevention. Important feasibility considerations will include boundaries on scope of practice and how to best integrate alongside other CHW-delivered programmes to conserve resources.

An identified value that requires further exploration is the importance of traditional healers and practices in the community. This topic has recently gained global attention, with a 2023 WHO Summit focused on integration of traditional medicine into the African healthcare system. Recommendations included increased collaboration through programmes such as bonus systems for appropriate referrals between traditional and conventional practitioners, formal training programmes in traditional medicine to increase quality and standardise practice, and increasing formal disease-specific collaborations to improve community reach. Additional work with stakeholders in Uganda will be needed to see if there are ways to include this key group into implementation models for RHD primary prevention.

This study has limitations. This is a formative, community-led study that focused on identification of new strategies to deliver RHD primary prevention in a single Ugandan district that had been sensitised to the importance of childhood sore throat through a prior programme. The identified approaches require further testing for impact, real-world feasibility and uptake using rigorous implementation science methodology. Furthermore, additional work is also needed to ensure women are appropriately represented in the co-design of implementation strategies. Despite intentions to ensure gender balance, women were underrepresented in the design workshops due to unintentional skewing during participant selection and attendance, which may limit the diversity of perspectives reflected in the findings.
Conclusions

Primary prevention is an evidence-based RHD control strategy that has not reached its global potential. Locally co-designed programmes are needed to develop innovative and sustainable implementation strategies to maximise the benefit of RHD primary prevention. The value set and strategies developed in this study can now be used as guideposts to develop and test a package of implementation strategies for improving RHD primary prevention in Uganda.
