passages.text: The effect of particles on static crystallisation in suspensions: sucrose vs inulin

The crystallisation of lipids in suspensions is influenced by the presence of the suspended material, in contrast to crystallisation in bulk lipids. In this research, the impact of carbohydrate particles on the crystallisation of palm oil was studied. Refined crystalline sucrose and glassy inulin were chosen as particulate materials added at a 10 wt% concentration. Suspensions were studied either without additives or together with sucrose ester (HLB 6) at a 0.5% concentration as dispersing agent. Suspensions were crystallized while cooling at 20  C/min to 20  C or 25  C under static conditions. A multiscale analysis of the fat crystal network was conducted where simultaneous wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering were used to study the polymorphism, chain length stacking and crystal nanoplatelet (CNP) thickness. Ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering and cryo-scanning electron microscopy provided insights in the CNP size and shape. Polarized light microscopy and Raman spectroscopy revealed the microscale structure of the fat crystal network. Results show that both crystalline and amorphous particles act as surfaces for heterogeneous nucleation, facilitating nucleation. Polymorphic pathways and lamellar spacings remained unchanged, while CNP size decreased compared to crystallisation in the bulk lipids. The effects of the particle nature were subordinate to those of the dispersing agent.
Introduction

Many food products derive their texture from the presence of a lipid phase, composed of a complex multiscale network of triacylglycerol (TAG) crystals dispersed in a continuous oil phase. The fat crystal network is hierarchically formed via TAG molecules, lamellae, crystal nanoplatelets (CNPs), clusters, and flocs. These multiscale arrangements are weakly linked and their formation depends on the molecular composition, cooling rate, shear rate, and aging time.

Understanding the impact of composition and processing on network structure is of particular interest, because it is of key importance to design tailor-made fat formulations and to decrease saturated fat levels in food products while retaining texture and mouthfeel. In suspensions, i.e., a dispersion of solid particles in a continuous lipid phase, the particles provide surfaces at which lipids can nucleate heterogeneously. In addition, the dispersed phase induces changes in the mobility of the TAGs-affecting the crystal growth. The impact of dispersed solids on fat nucleation and crystal growth has been studied in chocolate model systems, real chocolate, and sugar/palm fat dispersions using standard techniques.

Sucrose (C12H22O11), commonly called "sugar", is a disaccharide consisting of the monosaccharides glucose and fructose, connected via an alpha-1,2-glycosidic bond. It is produced by leaching the sucrose from sugar beet or by pressing the juice from sugarcane. The watery excess is then evaporated, and the sugar crystallizes. In most confectionery products, sucrose is a main ingredient next to lipids, due to its early, clean, and intense sweet taste. Next to being a source of energy (394 kcal/100 g), it provides bulkiness and textural properties such as hardness and mouthfeel. Furthermore, sucrose can act as a flavour enhancer or even as preservative. Having multiple functionalities, sucrose replacement in food products is challenging.

Inulin, a soluble fiber, is a widely used sucrose replacer. Inulin is a bulk sweetener, valued in confectionery for its mild sweetness, which is only 10-30% of that of sucrose. At low concentrations, it is nearly tasteless, odourless, and has no aftertaste. Unlike crystalline sucrose, inulin is a hygroscopic glassy solid. It belongs to the fructans and consists of beta-2,1-linked fructose units with a terminal glucose, typically extracted from chicory or Jerusalem artichoke. After leaching, purification, and spray-drying, it has a degree of polymerization (DP) ranging from 3 to 60, averaging 10. Its solubility increases with shorter chains and more branching, while high-DP inulin (>=23) can gel food matrices. Furthermore, inulin is widely used as a gelling agent, texture modifier, fibre, prebiotic, and sugar/fat replacer.

Inulin is minimally digested in the small intestine (less than 15%) due to the absence of human enzymes capable of breaking beta-2,1-glycosidic bonds. As a result, inulin primarily reaches the colon, where it serves as a substrate for the gut microbiota. Its fermentation, along with that of other soluble fibers, may contribute to increased fecal bulk. Consequently, inulin provides only 40-50% of the energy value of sucrose. According to EU Directive 2008/100/EC, inulin is assigned a caloric value of 2 kcal/g.

Additionally, inulin is recognized as a prebiotic because it stimulates the growth of beneficial Bifidobacteria. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has approved a health claim stating that a daily intake of 12 grams of inulin supports bowel function. However, consuming more than 20 grams per day may lead to undesirable effects such as bloating, flatulence, and a laxative response.

When adding sucrose to cocoa butter, it was suggested that the surfaces of sucrose crystals act as nucleation sites. Crystals will be smaller if nucleation is fast, preventing grainy food textures. Furthermore, crystalline sucrose seems to suppress crystal growth and beta' crystal formation in palm oil (PO), and appears to alter the crystal morphology. Furthermore, there is an indication that the solid state of the dispersed phase also has an impact on fat crystallisation. Bricknell and Hartel observed that chocolate formulated with glassy sucrose was less susceptible to fat bloom than the counterpart comprising crystalline sucrose. The authors attributed the difference to the smooth surface and rounded shape of glassy sugar, ensuring fewer active sites for recrystallisation and a closer packed system, ultimately delaying oil migration responsible for betaVI crystal growth.

Next to particles, studying the effect of additives remains crucial, since fat-based suspensions need to be stabilized by dispersing agents to maintain their structural properties. In the case of sucrose esters (SEs), it was shown earlier that they enhance nucleation and polymorphic transitions, without altering the polymorphic form of PO. The SE modified the CNP size in case of PO, but not when added to anhydrous milk fat. The microstructure was found to be finer and denser whenever a SE was added. Until today and to the best of our knowledge, no studies have been presented regarding the effect of a SE on the fat crystal network in the presence of a dispersed phase. In general, the role of processing and the presence of a dispersion on fat crystallisation and network formation remains largely unanswered.

This study aimed to study the effects of sucrose replacement by inulin on fat crystallization in model suspensions. Therefore, the effect of sucrose and inulin addition (10 wt%) on the fat crystal network of palm oil at 20  C and 25  C. The combined addition with 0.5 wt% of SE was also studied. Suspensions were refined to study industrial conditions. X-ray scattering (WAXS, SAXS, USAXS) was applied to study the nano- and mesoscale. The meso- and microscale were visualized by means of polarized light microscopy (PLM), cryo-scanning electron microscopy (cryo-SEM) and Raman spectroscopy.

A view of the native particle shape was provided by means of cryo-SEM (Fig. 1). Unrefined sucrose particles appear as rugged particles, having sharp edges and a flat surface. The carbohydrate particles are widely differing in size, which is confirmed by the particle size distribution (PSD, Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). A volume mean diameter D4,3 of 112.9 microm was found. The Sauter mean diameter D3,2, related to the volume-to-surface area ratio, on the other hand, was around 34 microm. Dv,0.1, Dv,0.5, and Dv,0.9 amounted to 14.0, 66.1, and 291.4 microm, respectively, equally underpinning the presence of a wide variety of particle sizes. In comparison, Van de Walle et al. found a D4,3 of 51 microm and Dv,0.9 of 114 microm, suggesting that the sucrose particles might have aggregated due to the presence of some moisture (and the lack of starch to prevent moisture absorption). In contrast to other studies, the absence of starch was aimed important to solely study the effect of sucrose in suspensions. After all, the study of Mattice and Marangoni showed that fat crystallisation is affected by its matrix. The authors studied the crystallisation behaviour of a shortening in bulk and when applied in croissants. The differences in crystallisation behaviour were ascribed to the presence of the flour (mainly starch) in the croissants.

The melting behaviour of sucrose is characterized by a steep melting peak at 191.5 +- 0.3  C (Supplementary Fig. 2). The solid state of sucrose is reflected in its WAXS profile (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is dominated by a high number of narrow and intense peaks. In the range of 1 A-1 < q < 1.8 A-1, sucrose creates multiple intense peaks. A consequence thereof is that in a suspension with fat and a high concentration of sucrose, the sucrose peaks will obscure the fat peaks and thus make it impossible to distinguish the fat polymorph. In the range of SAXS, no peaks were detected. Therefore, the use of SAXS, without the need for sugar washing, enables to continue studying the fat polymorph. The structure of sucrose is described in detail by Olsson and Swenson and Perez.

The inulin particles have rounded edges and generally appear to be larger than sucrose particles (Fig. 1). The round appearance is typical for spray-dried materials. The drying process might create open pores and even hollow particles. The particle size of inulin was characterized by a volume mean diameter D4,3 of 87.2 microm. The Sauter mean diameter was around 34 microm, indicating a similar volume-to-surface area ratio to sucrose. Dv,0.1, Dv,0.5, and Dv,0.9 were 28.9, 79.8 +- 0.2, and 157.6 +- 1.6 microm (Table 1). The narrow PSD obtained is typical for spray-dried materials.

Inulin, known to be in a glassy solid state, did not show melting peaks. A small shift in the baseline, corresponding to the glass transition was found at 158.9 +- 0.1  C (Supplementary Fig. 2). The broad bump centred around 90  C is believed to be the result of water evaporation from the sample. A higher heating rate (20  C/min instead of 5  C/min) removed this broad feature and showed a clear glass transition with its midpoint around 88.9 +- 1.5  C, in line with the results of Van de Walle et al.. WAXS and SAXS analysis of inulin confirmed its amorphous nature (Supplementary Fig. 3), with a molecular arrangement that is disordered in comparison to the crystalline state.

Both for sucrose and inulin, over 50% of the carbohydrate particles exceeded the size of 30 microm. This size is believed to be the oral cavity detection limit, where larger particles might be perceived as gritty or coarse. In order to more closely resemble industrial conditions and to equalize the particle size of sucrose and inulin, the carbohydrate particles (in suspension) were refined. After refinement, almost all particles were found to be <100 microm and the size distributions obtained for sucrose and inulin were very similar (Supplementary Fig. 1). The extent of sucrose and inulin refinement was found to be only slightly larger than the data obtained by Van de Walle et al., who reported ranges of 14-20 mum for D4,3 and 33-40 microm for Dv,0.9 for different refined sweeteners in suspensions containing skimmed milk powder and palm-/palm kernel-based fat.

As refining might influence the particle size and morphology and particle surface, the refined carbohydrate particles were equally visualized with cryo-SEM (Fig. 1). Inulin particles presented a more noticeable change regarding shape and size, showing sharper sides and a smaller diameter. In sucrose, the PSD is still wider than in inulin, which is in line with the bigger differences found for D4,3 compared to D3,2 (Table 1). Nonetheless, based on the distributions in Supplementary Fig. 1, the PSDs were rather similar after refining.
Static crystallisation of palm oil suspensions

The palm fat crystal network typically adopts a multi-length-scale hierarchical organization. The PO fat crystal network as affected by 10 wt% sucrose or inulin addition and the combined addition with 0.5 wt% SE as dispersing agent, is discussed from the nano-, over the meso- to the microscale.

Crystallisation (top) and melting (bottom) thermograms for palm oil (PO)-based suspensions with 10 wt% sucrose (POS) or inulin (POI) without and with 0.5 wt% of sucrose ester SP30 HLB-6 (POSE, POIE) as obtained with differential scanning calorimetry.
Samples crystallized by cooling from 70  C to 20  C (FC20) or 25  C (FC25) at 20  C/min. Profiles are vertically shifted for readability. Data are available in Supplementary Table 1.

Differential scanning calorimetry was used to study the nanoscale. Figure 2 displays the crystallisation and melting thermograms for palm oil and palm oil-based suspensions with and without SE. Supplementary Table 1 reports data obtained from the DSC profiles. From the DSC profiles, different effects can be deduced. First, for FC20 (Fig. 2, inset and Supplementary Table 1), it was found that compared to the bulk oil, the onset of crystallisation was accelerated most upon the addition of the SE (with or without the carbohydrate particles) and less upon the addition of sucrose or inulin. Sucrose and inulin enable heterogeneous nucleation. The availability of these foreign surfaces requires fewer liquid-state TAGs to assemble and form a nucleus of critical size, and hence nucleation proceeds more readily. For sucrose, this effect has been documented in cocoa butter.

The addition of the SE (POE) seems more beneficial to enhance nucleation than the addition of carbohydrate particles (POS, POI), and the combined additions (POSE, POIE) seem equally beneficial. The SE forms small nuclei, which then accelerate the TAG nucleation as they are more compatible compared to the foreign object. It is believed that, at least for the sucrose particle, the hydrophilic moiety of the dispersing agent coats the dispersed carbohydrate particles, while the hydrophobic part protrudes into the fat phase. No differences have been found between the POSE and POIE samples, which indicates that the behaviour of the ester in these mixtures is similar for the crystalline (sucrose) and glassy (inulin) particles. A second thermal event, the polymorphic transition of alpha to beta', appeared sooner and over a shorter period of time whenever the SE was added (POE, POSE, POIE, Supplementary Table 1). Combined addition of SE and a carbohydrate particle rendered the transition the shortest. The addition of sucrose or inulin without SE did not modify the transition. The melting profile was barely affected, in line with the results of Yoshikawa et al., although the end temperature of the melting range slightly decreased for POSE and POIE compared to PO.

For FC25, the onset was accelerated more for sucrose (POS) and inulin (POI) addition, compared to the combined addition of carbohydrate particles and SE (POSE, POIE). Combined addition was still found more effective than SE addition alone (POE). No other peaks were encountered. For FC25, it was clear that the melting profiles had increased 'intensity' with the additions, indicating a higher melting enthalpy and suggesting that more fat was crystallized upon the additions. The melting point decreased equally with all additions.

Despite their different morphology and solid state, no differences were found between sucrose and inulin particles. Yoshikawa et al. compared the effect of talc particles with modified hydrophobicity and concluded likewise that these modifications had no effect on the fat crystallisation. To conclude this section, we must stress that the results obtained depend on the combined action of the systems' composition and the temperature and cooling rate effects.

Synchrotron radiation X-ray scattering profiles obtained during simultaneous wide- and small-angle scattering (WAXS and SAXS) can be found in Supplementary Fig. 4. From the WAXS and SAXS figures, it can be seen that upon cooling to 20  C or 25  C, the alpha-2L to beta-2L polymorphic pathway was followed. In WAXS, this is illustrated by a peak shift from q = 1.58 A-1 to q = 1.50, 1.55, and 1.67 A-1. In SAXS, the polymorphic transition can be seen as a change in peak position from q = 0.13 A-1 to q = 0.15 A-1. The extent of alpha-2L formation is more limited at 25  C compared to at 20  C. The addition of carbohydrate particles or SE did not change the polymorphs formed. Nonetheless, the crystallisation in suspensions was found to start sooner and the polymorphic transitions were accelerated with SE addition, in agreement with DSC data (Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 1). For suspensions containing SE, an extra peak at q = 0.12 A-1 was found. It has been identified in earlier publications as a reflection related to the (lamellar or cubic) structure of the SE.

Yoshikawa et al. reported that certain particles might cause direct crystallisation into the most stable beta polymorph. This effect has not yet been, however, attributed to sugar or inulin. On the contrary, most authors state that particles do not affect the polymorphism. Mattice and Marangoni found that in croissants prepared with a non-hydrogenated shortening, fat started to convert from beta' to beta polymorphs over one week of storage, which was not the case for the pure fat. Bricknell and Hartel found differences in the polymorphic evolution when studying chocolates with crystalline or glassy sugar over the 22 days. In contrast, in our study, within one hour of isothermal crystallisation time, no differences in the polymorphic pathways were encountered with the different carbohydrate particles added (crystalline sucrose vs. glassy inulin).

Table 2 summarizes the quantitative data obtained from WAXS and SAXS. For WAXS, the start of crystallisation is reported. For SAXS, the long spacing (d001) and the average number of lamellae in a CNP are specified. The average number of lamellae was calculated via two methods: (1) via the Scherrer equation and (2) via the BWA method.

The long spacings (d001) found for PO, POE, and all suspensions range from 42.2 to 42.8 A. These values indicate a 2L-structure. The long spacing was not influenced by temperature (20 or 25  C), nor by SE or carbohydrate particle addition (sucrose or inulin).

Scherrer analysis was applied to study the CNP thickness, i.e., the number of lamellae stacked on top of each other (Table 2). For all suspensions, the Scherrer number was higher for samples crystallized at 25  C compared to at 20  C, in line with the slower growth kinetics at 25  C. The number of lamellae was in line with those reported elsewhere for chocolate (10-18 lamellae), taking into consideration another measurement setup. Differences encountered were however, limited (1 or 2 lamellae) and might thus not be of great importance. The general trend is that the carbohydrate particles reduce the number of lamellae slightly, but to a lesser extent than the SE addition (with or without carbohydrate particles). It is hypothesized that this result relates to the enhanced nucleation upon SE or carbohydrate particle addition.

Bertaut-Warren-Averbach (BWA) analysis (Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5) reveals broad CNP thickness distributions, ranging approximately from 3 to 25 lamellae stacked on top of each other, for all samples. At 20  C, the additions of carbohydrate particles and SE make the distributions more narrow. The addition of sucrose or inulin reduces the maximum number of lamellae with 3, while ester addition results in a decrease of 5 lamellae. For FC25, the addition of carbohydrate particles results in similar distributions for the suspensions and the bulk lipids. In contrast, combined carbohydrate particle and SE addition result in steeper cumulative distributions and hence lower average numbers of lamellae. The range of existing thicknesses was not modified (3-25). In general, although BWA analysis results in lower values, data obtained revealed the same trends as Scherrer analysis. This finding was also reported in literature.

Time-resolved ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering (USAXS) analysis was performed as proof-of-concept to study the mesoscale of palm oil-sucrose suspensions. The USAXS spectra of POS and POSE can be found in Supplementary Fig. 6. The quantitative data obtained from the USAXS spectra are displayed in Table 3. For comparison, the data obtained for the reference samples PO and POE have also been displayed in Table 3. With respect to the analysis of suspensions, the profiles could only be obtained up to the range of q = 0.0067 A-1. This is the result of an overexposure of the detector due to the intensity coming from the carbohydrate particles and the need for a larger beam-stop area. Nonetheless, the part of interest for this research (CNP dimensions) is situated below 1 microm (q > 6*10-4 A-1) and is still available. In addition, the high q-region contains diffraction peaks coming from the (wide-angle) beam-stop. This phenomenon is often an issue, especially in USAXS studies, where Porod (q-4) scattering behaviour is encountered. The presence of these secondary scattering peaks could not be avoided with the set-up of the beamline and could only be correctly removed by additional measurements in the SAXS region to overlay all USAXS and SAXS data. Unfortunately, this was not possible in the timeframe of the experiment. Very recently, a method was developed to overcome this issue in future experiments. For the data presented in Supplementary Fig. 6, the peaks were mostly removed by subtraction, which was, at the time of data processing, the best available option. The data in this area must hence be cautiously interpreted, and hence, the data were found unsuited for further shape-dependent model fitting.

Table 3 gives an overview of the USAXS results obtained for the palm oil-sucrose-based suspensions, in comparison to pure PO and POE systems. Although possibly affected by the secondary scattering peaks, the slopes found for the high q-region (3.5-3.7) are in agreement with the slope obtained in the bulk fat. The slopes were found slightly higher for FC20 compared to FC25 in bulk and suspensions, but considering the small differences, these represent a similar scattering contrast between CNPs and liquid oil.

For the slopes in the low q region, indicative of the CNP shape, slightly bigger differences were found (1.6-2.0). For suspensions, the slopes are lower under FC25, which would indicate that the CNPs are more rod-like compared to their bulk counterparts or samples crystallized at 20  C. The differences might also be explained by the lower scattering intensity at 25  C compared to at 20  C in the lower q region, as for POS and POSE this region is less extended than for PO and POE, and thus more doubtful.

The cut-off points, indicative of CNP size, show clear trends. It was found that, independent of the cooling protocol, the addition of sucrose shifted the cut-off point towards a higher q-value, and hence it is assumed that sucrose addition decreased the CNP size. The shift in the cut-off point upon sucrose addition was, however, less than for SE addition. The combined addition of SE and carbohydrate particles decreased the CNP size equally to the SE addition alone.

In addition to USAXS analysis, de-oiling and subsequent cryo-SEM imaging were performed on all suspensions, crystallized following the FC20 and FC25 protocol. The reference samples, PO and POE, have been discussed earlier, and readers are invited to view the respective cryo-SEM images. The addition of carbohydrate particles (and ester) reduced the CNP size (length and width) severely when comparing with PO (Fig. 3). CNP lengths are well below 1 microm, confirming that the CNPs could be discovered by the USAXS range available for POS and POSE analysis. No clear differences were found between the different suspensions, which suggests a clear CNP size reduction by both carbohydrate particles and the carbohydrate particles and SE combination, both at 20  C and at 25  C. Rousseau and Sonwai used atomic force microscopy and found that CNP size was reduced in freshly crystallized chocolate, compared to in cocoa butter.

Polarized light microscopy images for palm oil (PO)-based suspensions with 10 wt% sucrose (POS) or inulin (POI) without or with 0.5 wt% of sucrose ester SP30 HLB-6 (POSE, or POIE) after one hour isothermal crystallisation at a 20x magnification. Scale bar = 100 mum.

Polarized light microscopy (PLM) was applied to study the microscale evolution during crystallisation. Figure 4 shows the fat crystal networks formed after one hour isothermal time. Although polarized light microscopy is not an ideal technique to study suspensions, the time-resolved static crystallisation makes it possible to identify differences over time. A first thing that stands out from the PLM images is that upon addition of the SE, the carbohydrate particles tend to cluster together. Although the suspensions were stirred and homogenized when applying them to the microscopy glass, reheating them on the plate often caused heterogeneity. In addition, the hygroscopic nature of sucrose and inulin might result in clustering of the carbohydrate particles. Secondly, for inulin dark spots can be found in the particles, which confirms that (some of) these particles remained hollow.

Upon the start of nucleation, more crystallites are found in all cases compared to bulk palm oil. This is in line with the hypothesis of heterogeneous nucleation as found from DSC data. On top, the time-resolved images suggest that nucleation starts at the surface of the carbohydrate particles, rather than between them. Over the time of one hour of isothermal crystallisation, all formed networks seemed to be finer than those obtained in bulk palm oil, both at 20  C and 25  C. The increased density of the network might be related not only to the increased number of nucleation points, but also to spatial hindrance caused by the carbohydrate particles themselves. Especially at 25  C, for all samples, the created networks are denser and more space-filling compared to the pure PO samples, indicating an increased degree of crystallisation, as was also detected by an increase in melting enthalpy by DSC (Supplementary Fig. 2).

In addition to PLM, cryo-SEM magnifications (250x, Supplementary Fig. 7) show the microstructure in more detail. Despite the necessary de-oiling, the results are more informative than PLM images. It can be seen that the addition of carbohydrate particles reduced the floc size present, but the different flocs can still be distinguished, in line with the results of West and Rousseau. West and Rousseau reported floc sizes of around 11 microm for palm oil-sucrose mixtures after 4 weeks of storage at 20  C, which is in line with the sizes encountered here. At 20  C, the combined addition of carbohydrate particles and SE resulted in a homogeneous and fine fat crystal network without the clear presence of flocs, indicating a loss in hierarchical structure for both sucrose and inulin addition. At 25  C, SE addition reduced floc size compared to the bulk oil, but separate flocs could still be discriminated. In general, the sucrose-based suspensions seem to have the most dense structure, which might be due to the presence of a higher number of very small particles. Carbohydrate particles are always embedded in the fat crystal network, and carbohydrate particle surfaces were covered with CNPs and their aggregates.
Raman spectra of reference materials (palm oil, tripalmitin (PPP, oil, sucrose ester, sucrose and inulin).
Data vertically shifted for readability. Vertical lines indicate the Raman shift at 1127 cm-1 (dotted line) and 1654 cm-1 (full line).

In addition to PLM and cryo-SEM, Raman spectroscopy is ideally suited to study the microstructure of complex fat matrices. It can be noted that the Raman scattering signal is rather weak, but it can be enhanced by addition of metal nanoparticles and carbon structure, while its spectral selectivity can be enhanced by applying machine learning algorithms. With the addition of carbohydrate particles to the fat matrix, Raman microscopy allows for a spatial localization of these particles, the solid fat, and the liquid oil. Figure 5 illustrates the reference profiles for palm oil (semi-solid at 20  C), liquid oil, tripalmitin (PPP, indicative for solid fat), sucrose, and inulin. The spectrum obtained for sucrose is in good agreement with those of Alinovi et al. and Dahlenborg et al., while the oil spectrum was in line with Andersen et al.. As discussed in De Witte et al., the Raman bands at 1654 cm-1 and 1127 cm-1 are indicative for the presence of oil and fat, respectively. However, as visualized, sucrose and inulin equally display peaks around 1127 cm-1 rendering the use of this band impossible. Other bands, at 1295 and 2860 cm-1, equally associated with the solid fat contribution, could not be used for similar reasons.

Despite the need for a different processing methodology, the carbohydrate particles showed Raman spectra clearly different from PPP and oil, and are therefore ideally suited for Euclidian Distance (ED) mapping. The Euclidian distance implies that the full Raman spectra of the sample are compared with the full Raman spectra of a reference. Each Raman shift gets an equal contribution in the comparison. A high resemblance between a spectrum and a reference results in a low value for the ED. For the aim of visual mapping interpretation, similarity (= 1/(1 + ED)) is plotted in Fig. 6. In this case, an intense colour (yellow) indicates a high similarity with the reference spectrum and thus the presence of a certain material.

The results of the so-called Raman heat mapping (Fig. 6 for FC20 and Supplementary Fig. 8 for FC25) clearly show that the technique is capable of localizing the presence of carbohydrate particles (sucrose and inulin). Nonetheless, we should consider that although focusing in one plane of the sample, the Raman laser has a certain penetration depth (few microm, but depending on opacity), which might complicate the carbohydrate particle location within the fat matrix. Localization of the SE is impossible for two reasons: (1) the bands indicative of SE are very similar to those of PPP, and (2) the size of the SE does not match the step size of the mapping.

Both for FC20 and FC25, it can be seen that the addition of carbohydrate particles decreases the floc size, visible by a spatial distinction between solid fat and liquid oil. In contrast, addition of carbohydrate particles combined with SE at 20  C, results, just like for SE alone, in the formation of a fine and dense network, where different clusters cannot be recognized anymore. In contrast, at 25  C, combined carbohydrate particle and SE addition results in the formation of small, but separate flocs. This is in clear agreement with the cryo-SEM images (Fig. 3).

To check the dense network found for POE samples, the number of mapping points in Raman analysis was increased, and an area of 40 microm x 40 microm was scanned with 1.5 pixels per microm. The inset showed that even with a smaller step size, a similar conclusion should be drawn. In the microscopy heatmaps with a smaller step size, horizontal lines seem to be present, which are a known defect of Raman mapping with high laser power or small step sizes.

In addition, some figures (e.g., POS - FC20, Fig. 6E) suggest that the solid fat is mainly located at the carbohydrate particles surface, which would be in line with the theory of heterogeneous nucleation. However, this could not be confirmed in all images. It might be that for this trend to be visible, a finer resolution of the mapping is necessary. For comparison: in this research, we used a step size of 2 microm (40x objective), in the research conducted by Dahlenborg et al. 0.43 microm (50x objective) was used and Nikolaeva et al. were able to use 0.23 microm (100x objective). Step sizes of above a microm are common to use, as the laser spot size is often larger.

PPP was identified as the main high-melting TAG for PO crystallization. The similarity with PPP serves as an indicator for the localization of the solid fat, rather than an indication of the solid fat content. The visualization of PPP-similarity alone is an oversimplification. Other TAGs, e.g., POP, might also be solid and will have Raman spectra corresponding to bands of both PPP and OOO. The melting enthalpy (Supplementary Table 1) indicates no differences between the solid fat contents of the samples.

From the Raman analysis, we conclude, in line with the findings of West and Rousseau and Yoshikawa, et al., that particle addition enhanced nucleation, but suppressed crystal growth, resulting in smaller crystal floc size and a distinct distribution of TAG crystals compared to the bulk counterpart.

Overall, in this study, it was found that for palm oil-based suspensions carbohydrate particle addition (10 wt%) and combined carbohydrate particle and SE SP30 (HLB-6) addition (0.5 wt%) affected the onset of crystallisation and the time of polymorphic transition, as well as the melting curve. Polymorphic pathways and long spacings were not affected. No differences between sucrose and inulin were found, in line with their carbohydrate-nature and their similar particle size distribution. Addition of the SE combined with the carbohydrate particles was in general most efficient.

On the mesoscale, a 10 wt% carbohydrate particle addition was found to decrease the CNP thickness, but less than the addition of a limited amount of SE. The USAXS study of the palm oil-sucrose mixtures revealed that CNP size was decreased most with sucrose and SE addition, and less with sucrose alone. Cryo-SEM analysis of all carbohydrate particles showed a significant decrease in CNP size for all suspensions. The study of the microscale with PLM was found to be complex when carbohydrate particles were present, even at a low concentration of 10 wt%. Cryo-SEM and Raman spectroscopy analysis could overcome this issue, revealing that the carbohydrate particle addition decreased the floc size severely. The addition of carbohydrate particles and SE together in combination with crystallisation at 20  C removed the visibility of separate flocs, while in the other conditions (25  C or particle addition alone) small flocs were found. The results presented in this study clearly illustrate that carbohydrate particles with a size in the order of micrometres affect the scales of a similar size. Similarly, the SE molecules, which are smaller in size, also manage to affect also the nanoscale. It must be stressed that the results obtained for crystallisation in suspension are only valid for the applied temperature conditions. It is the combined result of the sample composition, shape, and particle size distribution, the cooling protocol, and the isothermal temperature that forms the nano-, meso- and microscale structure.

From this study, it can be concluded that the effects of sucrose or inulin particle additions on palm oil crystallisation at most hierarchical structures are limited and clearly inferior to that of the applied sucrose ester. The overall conclusion is that crystallization in bulk differs widely from crystallization in suspensions. In general, the effects of (crystalline) sucrose and (glassy) inulin addition were similar, indicating no effects of solid state. Nonetheless, from an industrial perspective, this does not rule out effects of sucrose replacement by inulin at the macroscale, including effects on taste, preservation, mouthfeel, viscosity, and hardness.
Methods
Materials

Palm oil (PO) was kindly provided by Vandemoortele NV (Izegem, Belgium). The sample has been extensively described in De Witte et al.. The sucrose ester (SE SP30 HLB-6) was provided by Sisterna (Roosendaal, The Netherlands). Its effect at 0.5 wt% concentration on the crystallisation of PO has been unravelled earlier by De Witte et al..

Sucrose S0 (density 1.60 +- 0.02 g/cm3), which contained less than 1% moisture, was purchased from Sudzucker/Tiense Suiker NV via Ranson (Harelbeke, Belgium). This type of sucrose does not contain added starch. Inulin Orafti HP was kindly provided by BENEO-Orafti S.A. (Tienen, Belgium). Orafti HP has an average degree of polymerization (DP) of 23 (density 1.41 +- 0.02 g/cm3), ruling out the presence of remaining sugars. It contained 2.6% moisture. The bulk sucrose and inulin are referred to as the 'bulk carbohydrate particles'.
Refining of carbohydrate particles

To ensure for a suspension particle size relevant to industry, a refinement step was performed. To do this, a premix was made, containing one carbohydrate particle and part of the PO (25 wt%). This premix was mixed in a Vema mixer (Machinery Verhoest bvba, Izegem, Belgium) at 45  C, before being refined with a 3-roll refiner (Exakt 80S Apparatebau GmbH & Co. KG, Norderstedt, Germany) with a gap setting of 2:1 at 40  C and 400 rpm at Cacaolab bv (Ghent, Belgium). Refinement of the premix was stopped when the digital micrometre (Mitutoyo 0-25 mm 0.001 mm Model 293-230) indicated a maximum particle size <30 microm. For this digital micrometre measurement, a mixture of the suspension with rapeseed oil (1:1) was made.
Visualization via of carbohydrate particles (unrefined and refined) cryo-scanning electron microscopy

The bulk and refined carbohydrate particles were visualised by means of cryo-scanning electron microscopy (cryo-SEM). To compare the carbohydrate particles before and after refinement, the refined carbohydrate particles needed to be extracted from the premix to obtain the dry particles. A lipid extraction was performed. 0.5 g of suspension was mixed with 10 mL of isopropanol (VWR, Leuven, Belgium). The mixture was then put at 40  C in the oven for one hour. The sample was shaken to fully dilute the lipid phase. The solution was then filtered over a Whatman filter paper, rinsed with isopropanol and dried for 45 min at 40  C to obtain dry particles.

Cryo-SEM analysis was performed using a JEOL JSM 7100 F scanning electron microscope (JEOL Ltd, Tokyo, Japan). The carbohydrate particles were mounted on an aluminium stub, covered with a carbon tape. After vitrification in a nitrogen slush, samples were transferred under vacuum conditions into the cryo-preparation chamber (PP3010T Cryo-SEM Preparation System, Quorum Technologies, UK), conditioned at -140  C. A 30-minute sublimation at -70  C was performed, after which the stubs were sputter-coated for 60 s with platinum using argon gas, transferred to the SEM stage at -140  C and electron beam targeted at 3 keV.
Particle size distribution of carbohydrate particles (unrefined and refined) via laser diffraction

The particle size distribution (PSD) of the bulk and refined carbohydrate particles was measured in triplicate based on laser light diffraction and the Mie theory by means of a Malvern Mastersizer S (Malvern Instruments Ltd., Worcestershire, UK), equipped with a 300 RF lens to measure particles in the range of 0.05-900 microm. Bulk carbohydrate particles were measured in air. The refined carbohydrate particles were measured in the premix. 0.5 g of the premix was mixed with 10 mL of isopropanol and subjected to a sonication treatment using an ultrasound water bath (Elmasonic S, Elma Schmidbauer GmbH, Singen, Germany) at 45  C and 80 Hz for 15 min. The measurement was performed in isopropanol, in triplicate.
Characterization of thermal behaviour and solid state of carbohydrate particles (unrefined) via differential scanning calorimetry

The solid state of the bulk carbohydrate particles was determined using the Q1000 differential scanning calorimeter (TA Instruments, New Castle, Delaware, USA) equipped with a nitrogen cooling system. Indium (TA Instruments), azobenzene (Sigma-Aldrich, Bornem, Belgium), and undecane (Acros Organics, Geel, Belgium) were used for cell constant and temperature calibration. Samples (+-5 mg) were sealed in hermetic aluminium pans (TA Instruments). An empty pan was used as a reference. The following time-temperature protocol was applied: equilibration at 20  C and holding for 10 min followed by heating at a rate of 5  C/min to 200  C. Peak melting temperatures and glass transition temperature were determined using TA Universal Analysis (TA Instruments). Measurements were done in triplicate.
Solid state characterization of carbohydrate particles (unrefined) via wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering

Wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS & SAXS) profiles of the bulk carbohydrate particles were collected on a Xeuss 3.0 system (Grenoble, France), equipped with an Eiger 2 R 1 M detector from Dectris (Baden, Switzerland) and a Cu-source Genix 3D form Xenocs (Grenoble, France), providing a wavelength of 1.54 A. Voltage and current were 50 kV and 0.60 mA, respectively.

Two Kapton foils, placed around a metal spacer of 1 mm were filled with powder. SAXS data were acquired with a sample-to-detector distance of 360 mm, resulting in 0.05 A-1 < q < 0.65 A-1. WAXS data were acquired with a sample-to-detector distance of 55 mm, resulting in 0.15 A-1 < q < 3.50 A-1. The acquisition time was set at 60 s. Data were corrected for the contribution of the Kapton foils.
Production of suspensions

After refinement of the premix (75 wt% carbohydrate particle + 25 wt% PO), the amount of PO in the suspensions was adjusted to 90 wt%. The suspensions with 90 wt% PO were further the subject of this study. SE (0.5 wt%) was always added after refinement and PO quantity adjustment. Each sample (suspension) contained only one type of carbohydrate particle. Sample abbreviations are used as follows: 'PO' for palm oil, 'S' for sucrose, 'I' for inulin, and 'E' for sucrose ester addition. When referring to sucrose or inulin or both, we refer to the 'carbohydrate particles'.
Protocols for crystallisation of suspensions

All suspensions were preheated to 70  C for 10 minutes to erase PO crystal memory, then cooled at 20  C/min (fast cooling, FC) to 20  C or 25  C and kept isothermally for one hour. The temperature selection is based on clear microstructural differences found at these temperatures for PO. The following abbreviations are used: FC20 = fast cooling to 20  C and FC25 = fast cooling to 25  C. The protocols and related timing are displayed in Supplementary Fig. 9.
Differential scanning calorimetry of suspensions

The differential scanning calorimeter was used to evaluate the crystallisation and melting behaviour of the suspensions following the described cooling protocols. Melting was evaluated by heating the samples from 20  C or 25  C at 5  C/min to 70  C.
Wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering of suspensions

Simultaneous small- and wide-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS & WAXS) experiments were performed at the DUBBLE beamline (BM26) of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF, Grenoble, France). A wavelength lambda of 1.03 A was applied. Calibration was performed using LaB6 (WAXS) and AgBeh (SAXS). The sample-to-detector distance was 1.96 m and 0.28 m for SAXS and WAXS, respectively. Suspensions were put in borosilicate capillaries of 1.5 mm in diameter (WJM-Glas, Berlin, Germany), and analysed in a Linkam THMS600 heating/cooling stage, equipped with a liquid nitrogen Dewar and programmed with each of the temperature profiles. An acquisition time of 3 s was used, which resulted in a frame being collected every 3.65 s.

The intensity was corrected for transmission, beam exposure time, and Kapton foil scattering by means of a beamline-owned data processing program, called Bubble. The subcell (polymorph) was derived via the WAXS peaks.

From the SAXS data, different parameters were obtained. The reported values were obtained at the end of one hour crystallisation, and the results from the last three profiles were averaged. First, the lamellar spacing (d001) was derived from the position (q001) of the first-order (001) crystallisation peak following:

Secondly, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) from the first-order (001) crystallisation peak was obtained. The Scherrer equation was applied to derive the thickness tau (domain) of the nanoplatelet and thus the number of lamellae stacked on top of each otherwhere K is a numerical constant with a value close to 1, lambda is the wavelength, FWHM001 is the full width at half maximum from the first-order crystallisation peak (radians), and theta is the Bragg angle (radians). In this research, a factor K of 0.9 was applied since it is often used for platelets. An extended review of this factor is available in Langford and Wilson. These data were not corrected for instrumental broadening, as the goal was only the comparison between samples.

Thirdly, the Bertaut-Warren-Averbach method (BWA) was applied to obtain the CNP thickness distribution by taking into account the full SAXS peak shape as described in den Adel et al. and Rondou et al.. The BWA-method starts from the 001 reflection, that has not been corrected for strain. In short, the method assumes that the 001 reflection is the sum of the scattering coming from a large number of scatterers of a certain size and hence it can be seen as a Fourier series. An inverse Fourier transformation is used to obtain information about the size of the scatterers. To start, the SAXS peak was fitted with a Gaussian profile of multiple terms. Within the range of -0.5 < s* <0.5, 15 equally spaced peaks were used. The number of lamellae was allowed to vary between 0 and 30.
Wide- and ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering of suspensions

Crystal nanoplatelet size and morphology, and polymorphism were obtained by measuring simultaneous ultra-small and wide-angle X-ray scattering (USAXS & WAXS) profiles on the TRUSAXS instrument of the ESRF (ID02) using a wavelength lambda of 1.03 A and at a sample-to-detector distance of 31 m. The detector used for USAXS was the EIGER2-4M, on which the range of the scattering vector (q) was 0.0002 A-1 < q < 0.02 A-1. The WAXS detector used was a Rayonix LX-170HS, which was located at the top of the cone of the 34 m evacuated USAXS tube. The q-range recorded on this detector was 0.7 A-1 < q < 3.7 A-1. The beamline setup has been described in detail by Narayanan et al.. Each suspension was put in a quartz glass capillary of 1.5 mm in diameter (WJM-Glas, Berlin, Germany) and left unsealed. The temperature protocols specified above were applied using a Linkam THMS600 stage (Linkam, Redhill, UK). For each frame, 10 acquisitions were taken and averaged. The exposure time was set to 0.02 s. Due to background calculations, there was 17 s time between 2 acquisitions. From each of the USAXS profiles, the background of the capillary filled with the liquid oil was subtracted, as it was aimed to measure the scattering coming from the solid fat.

The USAXS slopes at low and high q were fitted in the range of 0.0008 A-1 < q < 0.002 A-1 and 0.008 A-1 < q < 0.015 A-1, respectively. Please note that the values reported for the 'slope' are the absolute values of the exponents, i.e., if the decay of the curve behaves as 10-4, a value of 4 is reported as the slope. The lowest q-value for which the I(q) curve is straight and accords with the slope at high q is called the cut-off point. To determine the cut-off point, the fit in the range of 0.008 A-1 < q < 0.015 A-1 was extrapolated over the full q-range, and the difference with I(q) was determined. The cut-off point was defined as the point where the deviation was at zero, before the I(q) bends back and the deviation starts to increase continuously. WAXS data were corrected by the subtraction of an empty capillary. The polymorphic form over time was derived via a comparison of peak positions to existing literature.
Cryo-scanning electron microscopy of suspensions

Cryo-scanning electron microscopy (cryo-SEM) was applied to unravel the 3D morphology of the fat crystal flocs. The samples were crystallized following the protocols described on a PE120 Peltier system (Linkam, Redhill, UK). After one hour isothermal time, the sample (about the volume of a droplet) was transferred to a pre-tempered aluminium cryo-SEM stub covered with carbon tape. The sample was de-oiled by dripping 1 ml of isobutanol on top and letting it evaporate at the crystallisation temperature. This was repeated four times. Similarly to the carbohydrate particles, the de-oiled suspensions were visualized in the cryo-SEM. For suspensions, sublimation time and sputter-coating time were 45 min and 90 s, respectively.
Polarized light microscopy of suspensions

A Leica DM2500 device (PLM Leica, Wetzlar, Germany) was used as a polarized light microscope. Applying a polarizer allowed to distinguish the liquid from the crystalline fat phase and to visualize the fat crystal network on the microscale. A drop of liquid suspensions was added on a microscopy slide and covered by a cover slip. The temperature protocols specified above were applied via a water-cooled PE120 Peltier system (Linkam, Redhill, UK) attached to the microscope. A 20x magnification lens (type HC PL Fluotar, dry, NA 0.5, WD 3.4 mm) was used. PLM images were collected in a time-resolved manner by making a video recording.
Raman spectroscopy of suspensions

Samples were statically crystallized in a shear cell CSS450 (Linkam, Redhill, UK) and moved to a CaF2 glass plate for analysis after one hour isothermal time. A XTRA II laser diode (wavelength 785 nm, TOPTICA Photonics, Grafelfing, Germany) coupled to a WiTec Alpha 300 Raman microscope (Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK) was used. The spectrometer used was a UHTS 300 (Oxford Instruments), equipped with a CCD camera cooled to -60 C (ANDOR iDus 401 BR-DD, DU401A-BR-DD-352, Oxford Instruments). WiTec Control FIVE Plus was used as operational software.

For the data acquisition, a 40x long-working distance, air objective (CFI S Plan Fluor ELWD 40x, NA 0.6, Nikon, Tokyo, Japan) and 300 gratings with a spectral center of 2000 were used. The laser was set at 54 mW. For every sample, an area of 80 microm x 80 microm was scanned, acquiring one spectrum every 2 microm using an acquisition time of 0.5 s. Using Project FIVE software, data were corrected for cosmic rays. Baseline corrections were made with Matlab by means of an asymmetric least squares (ALS) fitting. Furthermore, each spectrum was min-max normalized. The spectra of PO were considered a combination of those of oil and tripalmitin (PPP). In every point, the obtained spectrum was compared to the spectra of its pure constituents (oil, PPP, sucrose or inulin) via Euclidian distance mapping:
To make data interpretation more intuitive, the similarity (= 1/(1 + ED)) was plotted in the heatmaps.
Graphs and statistics

All graphs were obtained using Matlab R2023a. If relevant, statistics were performed in RStudio 2025.05.1. Data was tested for homogeneity of variances and normality by using a Levene's and Shapiro-Wilk test, respectively. A Kruskal-Wallis test was used to compare the means in case more than two groups were present. A Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction was applied for pair-wise comparison. Comparison between the means of two groups was performed with a Man-Whitney U test. A significance level of 5% was selected.

passages.text: A multi-granularity feature fusion approach with attention for facial expression recognition

Facial expression recognition (FER) has been challenged by insufficient sensitivity to fine-grained local variations and limited feature representation capabilities in existing methods. To address these issues, we propose a novel FER method MGFA based on multi-granularity feature fusion with attention mechanism. MGFA enhances facial expression feature representation by combining both global and local multi-scale features. In the Global Multi-scale Feature Extraction Module (GMFEM), different multi-scale sampling methods and channel attention mechanisms are employed to extract and enhance the global feature information. In the Local Multi-granularity Feature Extraction Module (LMFEM), spatial segmentation is first applied to the facial image to capture local information at different granularities. Subsequently, the Multi-scale Lightweight Spatial Attention Module is introduced to enhance attention to local key features. Furthermore, the Cross-Fusion Module (CFM) simulates the relationship between feature information extracted from regions with different granularities, improving the model's ability to capture both local and global details of facial expressions. Experimental results on three widely-used public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly enhances the accuracy and robustness of FER.
Introduction

Facial Expression Recognition (FER) is a crucial form of emotional expression, widely applied in areas such as human-computer interaction, security surveillance, consumer payment, and medical diagnosis. With the rapid advancements in computer vision and artificial intelligence, automated facial expression recognition has become a prominent research focus. The goal of FER is to analyze facial expressions in images or videos and classify them into basic emotional categories, such as anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise.

Traditional FER methods often rely on handcrafted feature extraction techniques, such as Local Binary Patterns (LBP), Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG), and Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF). While these methods can capture some local facial information, they lack robustness in handling real-world variations, such as lighting changes, facial occlusion, and pose variations. Additionally, they struggle with processing large-scale data and learning high-dimensional features, leading to suboptimal performance in complex environments. In contrast, with the rapid advancements in deep learning technologies, FER methods based on deep neural networks have become the mainstream approach. These methods automatically extract features through an end-to-end learning process, significantly improving facial expression recognition performance. On controlled datasets like CK + and JAFFE, deep learning models have shown remarkable results. However, when applied to "wild" datasets (e.g., RAF-DB, FER2013), their performance tends to drop significantly. This performance gap is primarily due to the uncertainty factors in real-world scenarios, such as expression occlusion, pose variations, low-resolution images, and diverse lighting conditions.

To address these challenges, recent research has increasingly focused on methods that combine local and global features. By integrating both types of features, researchers aim to capture detailed facial expression information while maintaining overall facial changes, thereby improving recognition robustness. For example, Zhao et al. proposed a global multi-scale and local attention network (MA-Net), which extracts global features through multi-scale modules and uses an attention mechanism to capture local key features. This approach effectively handles occlusion and pose variations by fusing global and local features at the decision level. Similarly, Xie et al. employed convolution at different scales to extract global multi-scale features and used attention mechanisms to capture local key features. They also introduced a feature fusion module that adaptively combines features at different levels, improving the discriminative power of facial expression features. In addition, to address issues of global feature contamination and improper local feature cropping, Zhang et al. proposed enhanced discriminative global-local feature learning with priority (EDGL-FLP). This method uses a unified mixed multi-scale module to traverse subsets of global features for enhanced fusion, while a saliency and statistical perception attention module extracts channel and spatial attention of local features, preventing confusion from early fusion. Moreover, EDGL-FLP combines core facial regions and half-face features to improve global feature discriminability using facial symmetry. Xiong et al. also proposed a model that fuses local and global features, incorporating multiple attention mechanisms in the Res18-LG module to enhance local-global reasoning and using graph neural networks (GNNs) to extract spatial distribution features of facial key points. Although these approaches address certain issues, challenges such as insufficient local feature fusion, information redundancy, and suboptimal feature selection remain.

To capture complex relationships between different facial regions and improve performance under occlusion, Devasena et al. proposed a Twinned Attention Network (Twinned-Att), integrating a dual coordinate attention block (Dual-CA) and a cross-convolution block (Cross-conv). This model focuses on both global and local features, enhancing robustness against occlusions. In this paper, we propose a method for FER based on multi-granularity feature fusion to address the limitations of traditional and current deep learning models in complex environments. Our approach combines global multi-scale feature extraction with local multi-granularity feature capture, which better adapts to the complexity of facial expression changes. Specifically, we design a Global Multi-scale Feature Extraction Module (GMFEM) with different sampling methods and apply ordinary and dilated convolutions across two multi-scale branches to capture facial expression information. A channel attention mechanism further enhances the model's ability to focus on important features. For local feature extraction, the Local Multi-granularity Feature Extraction Module (LMFEM) captures fine-grained local details, while the Multi-scale Lightweight Spatial Attention Module (MLSAM) optimizes local features to improve expression recognition. A Cross-Fusion Module (CFM) is used to model the relationship between features at different granularities, promoting feature interaction and improving overall recognition. Our experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, significantly improving classification accuracy in complex scenes and enhancing robustness. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

We propose a FER method MGFA based on multi-granularity feature fusion, which enhances the model's ability to perceive both local facial details and global structures. By combining feature information from different granularities, the method improves robustness and recognition accuracy for various facial expression changes.

We introduce a Global Multi-scale Feature Extraction Module (GMFEM) that extracts multi-scale information through different sampling methods and fuses them. This module integrates channel attention and channel shuffling operations to enhance the model's ability to capture detailed facial expression features.

We propose a Local Multi-granularity Feature Extraction Module (LMFEM) that extracts and fuses fine-grained and coarse-grained features across different granularity scales, achieving complementary feature fusion. A Cross-Fusion Module (CFM) is also introduced to facilitate interaction between local features at different granularities, further enhancing recognition accuracy and robustness.

We introduce a Multi-scale Lightweight Spatial Attention Module (MLSAM) that captures the importance of spatial features at different scales. This module adaptively weights local regions, focusing on key areas and suppressing irrelevant background information. Additionally, we use depthwise separable convolution instead of traditional convolution to reduce computational overhead while maintaining feature extraction efficiency.
Related work

In recent years, with the rapid advancement of deep learning, convolutional neural network (CNN)-based FER methods have made significant strides on controlled datasets. However, due to the complexity of facial expression variations and the influence of external factors like lighting changes, occlusions, and pose variations, existing methods still face substantial challenges. To overcome these issues, researchers have introduced techniques such as multi-scale feature extraction, attention mechanisms, and multi-granularity approaches to improve model performance and robustness.
Multi-scale feature extraction

Multi-scale feature extraction has been extensively studied in FER to enhance model robustness against pose variations, occlusions, and differences in expression intensity. Traditional CNN-based FER models typically rely on a fixed receptive field, limiting their ability to capture both local details and global contextual information. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various multi-scale feature extraction methods. In, Zhang et al. introduced a facial expression recognition method based on a multi-scale efficient channel attention mechanism, which extracts rich multi-scale facial features through multi-scale feature extraction layers, while incorporating an attention mechanism to improve the model's focus on critical features. To facilitate multi-scale feature extraction and prevent overfitting, Shi et al. proposed a pure convolutional model with a hybrid attention mechanism and a multi-scale receptive field. By integrating Inception modules in the middle layers, their approach aggregates visual information at different scales, while the CBAM attention mechanism enhances the model's ability to focus on the most relevant features for recognition.

To address the challenge of extracting features from face regions with significant scale variations, He et al. proposed a facial expression recognition method that integrates multi-scale region awareness with multi-level feature fusion. They employed an inverse residual structure to enhance feature extraction in high-dimensional space, introduced multi-scale modules to capture features from diverse receptive fields, and incorporated attention mechanisms to suppress irrelevant regions. Adaptive multi-level feature fusion was utilized to maximize feature information while maintaining consistency across network depths. Their approach significantly improved model performance, demonstrating superior accuracy across multiple benchmark datasets. In, Xie et al. proposed a facial expression recognition method that integrates multi-level feature extraction and fusion. They introduced a feature extraction module with different convolutional kernel scales to capture multi-level features, which are then adaptively fused using a feature fusion module with global and local attention mechanisms in a top-down manner. This approach constructs a new facial expression feature representation, effectively handling the complexity and diversity of real-world facial expressions.

Although these methods effectively extract multi-scale features, challenges remain in feature extraction when facial information is incomplete. To address this, Qi et al. proposed a pyramidal convolutional attention residual network (PCARNet) based on ResNet18. This approach extracts multi-scale features of facial expressions through pyramid convolution, capturing global and local facial information to overcome the limitations of existing methods. At the same time, an improved attention mechanism weights the multi-scale features in the channel and spatial dimensions, further optimizing feature representation and achieving excellent performance on public datasets. To improve FER performance under occluded conditions, Kang et al. proposed an interweaved autoencoder network, integrating CNN and Transformer layers into a multi-scale structure using designed Residual Connection Union (RCU) blocks. This architecture analyzes the relationships between different regions, accurately identifies and emphasizes information-rich but often overlooked image blocks, thereby enhancing model performance and generalization ability.

In addition to these approaches, RUL-C tackles data uncertainty in FER by utilizing multi-scale feature extraction through an embedding proximity approach. This method ensures that feature representations remain close to newly assigned class centers during the relabeling process, improving model stability and performance.

Similarly, GLA-FERNet proposes a gradient-based lightweight network design that focuses on multi-scale feature extraction for FER. It leverages a gradient optimization algorithm to select features at different scales, which improves the model's recognition accuracy by capturing multi-level features. This method effectively enhances the feature extraction process while maintaining computational efficiency, making it particularly suitable for complex FER tasks.

Although these methods enhance feature extraction capabilities, challenges remain in balancing local details and global context. Standard convolution captures local features but struggles with long-range dependencies due to its fixed receptive field, while dilated convolution expands the receptive field but can lose fine-grained details due to sparse sampling. Furthermore, effectively fusing multi-scale features while avoiding redundancy and cross-scale feature imbalance remains a key challenge. To address these issues, we propose the Global Multi-scale Feature Extraction Module (GMFEM), which combines two different feature extraction pathways, using standard convolution and dilated convolution to expand the receptive field in different ways. This ensures the effective integration of local and global information. Additionally, we use channel attention and channel shuffling operations during the multi-scale feature extraction process to optimize cross-scale feature fusion. Finally, local, global, and original features are integrated through a weighted fusion strategy, enhancing the model's ability to represent facial expression features and improving robustness in FER tasks.
Attention mechanism

In FER, attention mechanisms have been widely utilized to enhance a model's ability to focus on critical facial features, particularly in complex scenarios such as occlusions, pose variations, and lighting changes. Traditional CNN-based methods are often constrained by fixed receptive fields, making it difficult to adaptively highlight the most discriminative features. To address this, various attention mechanisms have been incorporated into FER models, especially to improve both local and global feature extraction.

For example, Li et al. proposed a novel Slide-Patch and Whole-Face Attention model (SPWFA-SE) using squeeze-and-excitation (SE) blocks to adjust the significance of each channel, enhancing feature representation. Pu et al. incorporated channel attention into their CNN-based FER model, emphasizing useful feature channels while suppressing redundant information, which improved classification accuracy. In FerNeXt, Omar et al. used efficient channel attention (ECA) within the ConvNeXt architecture to enhance the model's ability to capture critical facial features. Meanwhile, Shen et al. designed a multi-head self-attention mechanism (MCA) that highlights important facial expression features while suppressing irrelevant information, improving recognition performance through enhanced class separability.

In addition to channel attention, spatial attention mechanisms have been introduced to enhance FER by focusing on crucial facial regions. Gan et al. proposed a densely connected convolutional network with hierarchical spatial attention, which adapts to locate salient regions and enhances emotion-related features. Wang et al. introduced a Spatial Attention (SA) mechanism, refining spatial feature maps dynamically based on expression-relevant cues, enabling the model to focus on key facial regions. Akram et al. incorporated spatial attention into residual blocks, allowing the model to focus on key regions such as the eyes and mouth while maintaining facial texture and color integrity.

While channel and spatial attention mechanisms have been successful, each comes with its limitations. Channel attention focuses on global feature distribution but may miss spatial relationships, while spatial attention excels in localizing important features but struggles to model cross-channel dependencies. To leverage both, Qian et al. introduced a hybrid attention approach in the Ventral-Dorsal Attention Capsule Network (VDACaps), where channel and spatial attention mechanisms were integrated into separate streams, enhancing FER performance. Similarly, Xia et al. combined channel and spatial attention within ResNet18, improving FER under complex lighting and backgrounds. CAGNet combines channel attention and spatial attention, sequentially emphasizing important facial regions. This dual attention system helps the network focus on discriminative features, improving FER accuracy on standard datasets.

Additionally, DRFN introduces a dynamic attention mechanism, assigning varying importance to different regions of the face. This enables the model to focus on the most relevant features for expression classification, improving robustness under varying poses and occlusions. Pazandeh et al. proposed a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based FER model incorporating attention to improve local and global feature extraction. Their two-stream representation, with class tokens and weighted global average pooling (WGAP), adjusts the importance of facial regions, enhancing feature learning, especially for subtle facial expressions in challenging real-world scenarios. Moreover, HFE-Net integrates convolutional kernels and transformers, using a hybrid attention mechanism to prioritize expression-related features. The model refines feature extraction by focusing on relevant facial areas, improving FER performance. MHAN further enhanced attention mechanisms by integrating multi-head attention with convolutional and global pooling layers, capturing facial features across multiple scales and improving the recognition of subtle expressions and poses. Finally, Zhu et al. introduced an attention map consistency method to address class imbalance in FER. By rebalancing attention maps based on class importance, the model focuses on critical features for each class, improving the ability to recognize both primary and difficult expressions.

Our method integrates both channel attention and spatial attention to optimize facial expression feature extraction. We incorporate channel attention in the Global Multi-scale Feature Extraction Module (GMFEM) to focus on crucial global features, while using a Multi-scale Lightweight Spatial Attention Module (MLSAM) to capture fine-grained local details through multi-scale convolutions. This hybrid attention mechanism effectively fuses local and global information, improving recognition accuracy and robustness in FER tasks.
Multi-granularity

Multi-granularity feature extraction has gained significant attention in FER tasks in recent years. It aims to enhance the model's ability to recognize facial expressions by extracting feature information from local regions at varying granularities. These methods enable a more comprehensive representation of facial expressions, from fine-grained local details to global information, thereby improving the model's robustness and accuracy across different expression types [39-341].

For example, Guo et al. proposed a dynamic sequence facial expression recognition network based on multi-granularity feature fusion. Their approach extracts both coarse-grained features, such as the offset distances between frames, and fine-grained features from individual frames. A dual-channel neural network is employed to learn these multi-granularity features, improving FER accuracy. Zhang et al. developed a method based on multi-scale grid attention and spatial-channel attention. Their Multi-Scale Grid Attention (MSGA) module captures relationships between facial regions at different granularities, while the Multi-Scale Spatial-Channel Attention (MSSCA) module refines high-level image features. This approach significantly enhances the model's ability to capture both global and detailed facial expression features, improving performance across different datasets. Similarly, Wang et al. proposed the Multi-granularity Region Relation Representation Network (MGR3Net). The network processes the facial image into three granularities and models the relationships between each region through a region attention unit. It then aggregates global and regional embeddings and uses hybrid-level fusion to combine these multi-granularity features, achieving better classification results. Beyond the field of FER, several recent works have explored global and local feature fusion in other visual domains. C2T-Net introduces a channel-aware cross-fused transformer to jointly leverage global semantics and local discriminative cues for pedestrian attribute recognition. CLEAR integrates pre-trained language models with cross-transformer interactions to enhance global-local alignment across modalities. HiGDA employs a hierarchical graph of nodes to capture local-to-global topology for semi-supervised domain adaptation. These studies demonstrate the general effectiveness of integrating multi-level or cross-scale representations.

While extracting features from different granularities significantly enhances a model's perception of local details, traditional methods often overlook the synergistic effect between these features. Consequently, the integration of local and global information remains insufficient, which can hinder recognition accuracy. In our work, this limitation is addressed by enhancing the expression of local and global features through spatial and channel attention mechanisms, enabling the model to capture both fine-grained local details and overall facial structure. Moreover, a multi-level feature extraction strategy is introduced to progressively refine local features while modeling global relationships. This design allows for a comprehensive exploration of the complementarity between different granularity features, significantly improving the accuracy and robustness of facial expression recognition.
Proposed approach

The proposed FER method MGFA is based on multi-granularity feature fusion, and its overall architecture is illustrated in Fig. 1 (the sample image is from the publicly available RAF-DB dataset). The method consists of three main components: the feature pre-extraction module, the global multi-scale feature extraction module, and the local feature extraction block.

In the feature pre-extraction module, Gabor filters are applied to extract texture and edge features from the input image. These filters help capture fine-grained local structures which are essential for recognizing subtle facial expressions. Following this, the initial layers of ResNet50 are used to generate preliminary feature maps, which lay the foundation for the subsequent global and local feature extraction processes.

In the global multi-scale feature extraction module (GMFEM), a multi-scale feature extraction technique is applied alongside a channel attention mechanism. The multi-scale module captures global facial features at different scales, enhancing the model's ability to perceive the overall structure of facial expressions. The channel attention mechanism is incorporated to emphasize the most critical feature channels, improving the model's ability to focus on relevant facial expression details, and thus boosting classification performance.

The local feature extraction block extracts detailed local features at varying granularities through spatial partitioning. A Multi-scale Lightweight Spatial Attention Module (MLSAM) is used to further refine these local features by focusing on the most important regions, effectively enhancing the model's ability to capture subtle changes in facial expressions. Additionally, a Cross-Fusion Module (CFM) is employed to model the relationships between local features at different granularities and global features, ensuring effective interaction between the features and improving recognition accuracy.
The overall architecture of the proposed MGFA.
Global multi-scale feature extraction module

In facial expression recognition, features at different scales contribute differently to representing emotional cues. To capture both fine-grained details and global structural patterns, we design a Global Multi-scale Feature Extraction Module (GMFEM), as shown in Fig. 2. The module consists of two parallel branches. The first branch employs standard convolutions with kernel sizes of 3 x 3, 5 x 5, and 7 x 7 to extract multi-scale representations of local and global information. The second branch adopts dilated convolutions with dilation rates of 1, 2, and 3 to enlarge the receptive field and capture contextual dependencies at different scales. Each convolutional output is refined through a channel attention mechanism to emphasize critical features while suppressing irrelevant information. Finally, the features from both branches are concatenated, processed with channel shuffle for cross-scale interaction, and fused through weighted coefficients (alpha, beta, gamma) to generate the final multi-scale representation.

Local feature extraction block

In the Local Feature Extraction Block, the input feature map is first processed by the Local Multi-Granularity Feature Extraction Module (LMFEM), which captures local features at multiple granularity levels to enhance sensitivity to subtle facial expression variations. To further refine these features, a Multi-scale Lightweight Spatial Attention Module (MLSAM) is employed to compute spatial attention weights across different scales, effectively highlighting key local regions while reducing computational complexity through depthwise separable convolutions. Finally, a Cross-Fusion Module (CFM) integrates the feature maps obtained from different granularity levels, promoting complementary information exchange and producing the final output of the Local Feature Extraction Block.
Local multi-granularity feature extraction module

To enhance the feature extraction capability of facial expression recognition models, we propose a Local Multi-granularity Feature Extraction Module (LMFEM). Traditional deep learning methods often struggle with illumination variations, occlusions, and pose changes, which limit their ability to capture fine-grained local details and consequently degrade classification performance. To overcome these limitations, we adopt a hierarchical local feature extraction strategy in which the input image is partitioned into multiple local regions, and features are extracted at different granularity levels through spatial partitioning of varying scales. To further refine these multi-granularity representations, we incorporate a Multi-scale Lightweight Spatial Attention Module (MLSAM), which computes spatial attention weights across scales while utilizing depthwise separable convolutions to reduce computational overhead without sacrificing critical information. This design enhances the model's sensitivity to subtle facial expression variations. Together, these components strengthen both the accuracy and robustness of facial expression recognition. The structure of this module is illustrated in Fig. 3.
Structure of the proposed LMFEM.
