infons.kwd: Spondylarthritis ASAS-NSAID Biotherapy NSAID

passages.text: Use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in patients with axial spondyloarthritis receiving biotherapy and associated factors: a prospective cohort study
Background

The objectives of this study were to evaluate NSAID use over time in patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) receiving biologic therapy, to determine the prevalence of axSpA remission without NSAIDs, and to identify factors associated with continued NSAID use after one year of follow-up.
Methods

This is a prospective longitudinal study included 85 patients with axSpA who were diagnosed according to the ASAS criteria and treated with biologics. Assessments were performed at baseline and at 3,6, and 12 months, and disease activity was evaluated with the ASDAS-CRP, BASDAI, and CRP. Data on NSAID use and type were collected, and the ASAS-NSAID index was calculated. This prospective longitudinal study included 85 patients with axSpA, diagnosed according to the ASAS criteria and treated with targeted therapies, regardless of the duration of prior exposure. All patients received targeted therapies. Assessments were conducted at baseline and at 3, 6, and 12 months. Disease activity was evaluated using the ASDAS-CRP, BASDAI, and CRP. Data on NSAID use, type, and dosage were collected, and the ASAS-NSAID index was calculated. At baseline, patients were categorized into two groups according to their NSAID use status, and baseline characteristics were compared accordingly.
Results

The mean age was 37.46 +- 11 years, with a male predominance (69.4%). Axial radiographic involvement was present in 87.1% of patients. The mean disease duration was 12 years [9-19.25], with a median time from diagnosis to biologic initiation of 3 years [1-8.5]. Thirty-four patients (40%) were in remission. At baseline, 42.3% of the participants used NSAIDs, which significantly declined to 11.5% at M12 (p < 0.001). At M12, 36.1% of patients achieved remission, all without NSAIDs. The ASAS-NSAID score significantly decreased over time. Persistent NSAID use at M12 was due primarily to mechanical pain (57.1%) rather than to inflammatory activity (42.9%). Multivariate analysis revealed that mechanical pain was the main factor associated with continued NSAID use.
Conclusion

Biologic therapy significantly reduces NSAID use and ASAS-NSAID scores in axSpA patients, highlighting the NSAID-sparing effect of bDMARDs. Additionally, NSAID use is not always linked to SpA activity but may be driven by mechanical pain.
Clinical trial number
Not applicable.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s41927-025-00599-4.
Highlights
There was a significant reduction in NSAID use among SpA patients recieving biologic therapy: 42.35% at baseline and 11.5% at M12 (p < 0.001).
A significant decrease in the ASAS-NSAID score (p < 0.001) was observed.
Mechanical pain was linked to continued NSAID use, regardless of disease activity.
At M12, 36.1% of patients were in remission, all of whom were NSAID-free.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s41927-025-00599-4.
Introduction

Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a heterogeneous group of chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases characterized by common clinical and genetic features. Despite their clinical diversity, they share a common anatomical substrate: the enthesis. Manifestations can be axial, involving the sacroiliac joints and spine, and/or peripheral, presenting as arthritis, enthesitis, or dactylitis. Additionally, extra-articular manifestations, such as anterior uveitis, psoriasis, and chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), may also be present.

The primary therapeutic objective is to achieve and maintain clinical remission or, if remission is not possible, a low disease activity (LDA) level. A personalized treatment strategy should be implemented and regularly adjusted to achieve this objective in accordance with the treat-to-target approach.

In the updated guidelines of the Moroccan Society of Rheumatology on the therapeutic management of SpA, published in 2023, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) remain the first-line treatment for axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) in the absence of contraindications. The efficacy of NSAIDs in treating SpA is well documented and supported by numerous randomized clinical trials.

Furthermore, advances in the understanding of SpA have led to the development of targeted therapies. Following more than 30 years of experience with tumor necrosis factor alpha inhibitors (anti-TNF) in the management of SpA, Interleukin 17-inhibitors (anti-IL-17) and, more recently, Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKis) have expanded therapeutic options.

In clinical practice, the combination of NSAIDs with biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) is common. However, given the potential side effects, it is recommended to consider a gradual reduction or discontinuation of NSAIDs once remission or, if not possible, if LDA has been achieved in patients on biological treatment. Several clinical trials have shown that anti-TNF can facilitate the successful reduction of NSAID use in patients with SpA.
However, data concerning NSAID dosage regimens and the factors associated with their maintenance in SpA patients treated with bDMARDs remain limited.

The primary objective of our study was to evaluate the use of NSAIDs in patients with axSpA undergoing advanced therapies, including biologic and targeted synthetic treatment. The secondary objectives were to determine the prevalence of axSpA in remission without NSAID use and to identify factors associated with continued NSAID use after one year of follow-up.
Methods
Study design and setting

We conducted a prospective cohort study including patients with axSpA according to the Assessment of Spondyloarthritis International Society (ASAS) classification criteria. Patients were recruited from the Rheumatology Department at El Ayachi University Hospital in Rabat between August 2022 and February 2023.
Participants

All patients meeting the following inclusion criteria were included in the study: aged over 18 years, had an established diagnosis of axSpA according to ASAS criteria, and were considered refractory to NSAIDs while receiving targeted therapies, including either biologic agents or JAK inhibitors, regardless of the duration of exposure. Patients with contraindications to NSAIDs were excluded. Visits were scheduled at baseline and at 3, 6 and 12 months. The participants were categorized and compared at baseline into two groups: the NSAID group, which included patients taking NSAIDs in combination with targeted therapies, and the NSAID-free group, received targeted therapy without any NSAID use.
Data collection

Sociodemographic characteristics, as well as clinical and paraclinical data related to the disease, were collected. These included age, sex, comorbidities, characteristics of SpA, and treatments received. Disease activity was assessed at baseline and at 3, 6, and 12 months using the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) and the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score based on C-reactive protein (ASDAS-CRP). Inflammatory markers, namely erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), were also measured at each visit.

Pain was clinically characterized as either mechanical or inflammatory. Mechanical pain was defined as pain localized to an anatomic structure, exacerbated by movement or mechanical load, relieved by rest, accompanied by less than 30 min of morning stiffness, and showing limited improvement with anti-inflammatory therapy. Inflammatory pain was inferred when symptoms improved with activity, were associated with 30 min or more of morning stiffness, or coincided with elevated ESR/CRP or high disease activity scores. No systematic imaging was performed to confirm the origin of pain; this pragmatic, clinically driven approach reflects routine real-world practice and is acknowledged as a limitation.

To assess NSAID use, the ASAS-NSAID score was calculated at each visit. This is a standardized tool for evaluating NSAID use in clinical trials, ranging from 0 (no use) to >= 100 (maximum use). The score was calculated over a 3-month period, taking into account the type of NSAID, the total daily dose, and the number of days of usage during this timeframe. It reflects both the daily NSAID dose and the percentage of days that NSAIDs were used within the 3-month period.
The presence of fibromyalgia was also assessed at baseline using the Fibromyalgia Rapid Screening Tool (FiRST). A score >= 5 was considered indicative of fibromyalgia.
Sampling and statistical analysis

No formal sample size calculation was performed. Instead, we adopted an exhaustive sampling strategy: all patients who met the inclusion criteria and attended the day hospital during the recruitment period were consecutively included. This approach reflects the real-life clinical practice and ensures representativeness of the target population.

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS. The normally distributed parameters are presented as the means +- standard deviations, while nonnormally distributed parameters are presented as medians. Qualitative data are expressed as frequencies (numbers and percentages). Comparisons between independent groups were made using the t-test for normally distributed quantitative variables and the Mann-Whitney test for nonnormally distributed variables. The chi-square test was used to compare qualitative variables between groups.

Intragroup comparisons of quantitative variables during follow-up were performed using Student's t-test for normally distributed variables and Wilcoxon's nonparametric test for nonnormally distributed variables. For qualitative variables, the McNemar test was applied.

To account for missing data at the 12-month follow-up, we applied an imputation method to handle the loss to follow-up. This approach enabled us to estimate and substitute the missing values with available data, minimizing the bias caused by incomplete information. The imputation was performed using an appropriate statistical technique to maintain the accuracy and integrity of the analysis, ensuring more reliable results in evaluating the study outcomes.
Results
Patient characteristics

Eighty-five patients were included, with a mean age of 37.46 +- 11 years, and 69.4% were male. The median disease duration was 12 years [9-19.25]. Among them, 6 patients (7.1%) had hypertension, and 6 (7.1%) had diabetes. All patients had axSpA. Radiographic axial involvement was predominant, affecting 74 (87.1%) of patients, whereas peripheral joint involvement was observed in 53 (62.4%) patients. In addition, 21 out of 46 the patients tested for HLA-B27 were positive, and 64.7% had coxitis. The extra-articular manifestations included uveitis in 13 patients (15.3%), psoriasis in 4 patients 55 (64.7%), and IBD in 8 patients (9.4%) (Table S1).

In terms of disease activity at baseline, the median BASDAI score was 1.35 [0.65-2], and the mean ASDAS-CRP score was 1.68 +- 1.02. Thirty-four patients (40%) were in remission. Thirty-six patients (42.3%) were taking NSAIDs at baseline. Diclofenac was the most frequently prescribed agent, reported by 15 patients (41.7%). This was followed by indomethacin in 8 patients (22.2%), ketoprofen in 5 patients (13.9%), coxibs in 4 patients (11.1%), meloxicam in 3 patients (8.3%), and piroxicam in 1 patient (2.8%). In terms of biological therapy, 68 patients (80%) were receiving anti-TNF, 16 (18.82%) were receiving anti-IL-17, and 1 was receiving anti-JAK (1.18%) (Table S2).

The comparison between the NSAID group and the NSAID-free group revealed no significant differences in age, sex, or disease duration (p = 0.29, p = 0.25, and p = 0.79, respectively). The prevalence rates of comorbidities such as hypertension and diabetes were similar between the two groups. Regarding disease characteristics, no significant differences were observed between the groups in terms of the type of SpA, the presence of coxitis, or extra-articular manifestations (Table S1).

The analysis revealed differences in disease activity markers between the two groups. Patients taking NSAIDs had a significantly higher median BASDAI score compared to those not taking NSAIDs (p = 0.005). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was significantly greater than in the NSAID group compared to the NSAID-free group (p = 0.007). Similarly, the ASDAS-CRP score was significantly higher in the NSAID group than in the NSAID-free group (p = 0.027) (Table S2).
Variations in NSAID use and ASAS-NSAID scores during follow-up
Between M0 and M3 (Table S3)

Between M0 and M3, the SpA activity parameters remained stable (ASDAS-CRP: 1.65 +- 1.02 at M3 vs. 1.68 +- 1.02 at M0, p = 0.167; BASDAI: 1.77 [0.6-2] at M3 vs. 1.35 [0.65-2] at M0, p = 0.642; CRP: 5.8 [2-13.9] mg/L at M3 vs. 5.4 [1.8-11] mg/L at M0, p = 0.587). The proportion of patients using NSAIDs significantly decreased from 36 (42.35%) patients to 17 (20%) patients (p < 0.0001). The ASAS-NSAID score did not decrease. (DeltaM3-M0: 0.23, p = 0.79).
Between M0 and M6 (Table S4)

Between M0 and M6, BASDAI and ASDAS-CRP scores remained stable. NSAID use continued to decline, with 13 patients (15.29%) still using NSAIDs at M6, compared to 17 (20%) at M3 and 36 (42.35%) at baseline. The ASAS-NSAID score showed a significant reduction (DeltaM6-M0: -4.3; p < 0.001).
Between M0 and M12 (Table S4)

Between M0 and M12, 25 patients were excluded from the study because of the discontinuation of biologic therapy, either due to health insurance coverage, treatment intolerance, or other problems requiring the discontinuation of biologics for further investigation. An imputability analysis was performed. Similar results were observed, with 7 (8.23%) patients using NSAIDs at M12, and a DeltaASAS-NSAID M12-M0 of - 3.07 (p < 0.001).
At M12, 36.1% of patients were in remission according to the ASDAS-CRP, all of whom were NSAID-free.
Reasons for NSAID use during follow-up

At baseline (M0), mechanical pain was the primary reason for NSAID use, accounting for 41% of cases, and included mechanical talalgia, lumbar radiculalgia, and mechanical gonalgia, among others. Inflammatory pain was the second most common reason, reported by 26% of patients. Hip pain, which was observed in 12% of patients, was specifically related to advanced coxitis at the surgical stage, whereas 15% of patients continued using NSAIDs due to fear that stopping them could trigger an inflammatory flare. Less frequently, stiffness and nonrheumatic issues were mentioned, each representing 3% of the cases (Table S6).
The reasons for NSAID use at M3 and M6 are presented in Table S6. At M12, the reasons for NSAID use were an inflammatory flare of SpA (42.9%) and mechanical pain (57.1%) (Table S6).
Factors associated with NSAID use at M12

According to the univariate analysis, the ASDAS-CRP score, BASDAI score, and mechanical pain were associated with continued NSAID use. Multivariate analysis, adjusting for confounding factors, identified mechanical pain as the only factor significantly associated with persistent NSAID use (Table S7).
Discussion

Our results suggest a significant decrease in NSAID use among patients with axSpA receiving targeted therapies: 42.35% at baseline and 11.5% at M12 (p < 0.001), as well as a reduction in the ASAS-NSAID score (p < 0.001). This decrease was not correlated with disease activity, although NSAID use was initially associated with disease activity at baseline. However, the presence of mechanical pain was associated with the continued use of NSAIDs in patients.

Similar to our results, in patients with axial SpA treated with anti-TNF, the use and dosage of NSAIDs decreased significantly during follow-up in the Groningen Leeuwarden Ankylosing Spondylitis (GLAS) cohort of 254 patients. 79% were using NSAIDs at the start of the study and this proportion decreased significantly to 38% after 52 weeks. The ASAS-NSAID index also decreased significantly. However, in contrast to our study the analysis over time revealed that NSAID use was significantly associated with disease activity.

Furthermore, a two-year clinical trial (12 weeks in blind and 12 weeks in open) of etanercept versus placebo in 82 patients with axial SpA reported a statistically significant decrease in the ASAS-NSAID score during the second part of the trial for patients switching from placebo to etanercept.
In the SPARSE study, NSAID use was reduced or discontinued by week 8 in patients treated with etanercept.

The proportion of SpA patients whose NSAID scores decreased or whose NSAID treatment was discontinued was greater in the anti-TNF treatment group. Moreover, etanercept was associated with a significantly greater improvement in the ASDAS-CRP score, physician global assessment of disease activity, and BASDAI.

In addition, a recent retrospective longitudinal study, including 429 patients with axial SpA, observed a significant reduction in the use of NSAIDs in patients treated with bDMARDs (p < 0.001). This reduction remained stable throughout the 52-week follow-up. However, in patients treated with bDMARDs, the ASDAS-CRP and BASFI scores were independent determinants of NSAID use, while BASDAI and Patient Global Assessment (PGA) scores were determinants of NSAID dosage. No significant independent predictor was found for ASAS-NSAID scores.

Also, a post hoc analysis combined data from three secukinumab trials (MEASURE 2-4), including 562 patients for each maintenance dose of secukinumab at 150 and 300 mg. The mean ASAS-NSAID score decreased over time in both the 150 mg and 300 mg secukinumab dose groups. The proportion of patients who achieved a 50% reduction in the ASAS-NSAID score and a clinically significant reduction in the ASAS-NSAID score to < 10 increased over time in both dose groups and among patients with low and high NSAID consumption.

In our study, at M12, 36.1% of patients were in remission, all of whom were NSAID-free. Conversely, a study conducted using data from the Moroccan Biotherapy Registry (RBSMR) including 194 patients aimed to evaluate the concomitant use of symptomatic treatments, particularly NSAIDs, with biologics in patients with SpA revealed that 48% of patients in remission according to the BASDAI and 36% in remission according to ASDAS-CRP continued to take NSAIDs.

To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has explored the reasons for NSAID use in patients with axSpA receiving targeted therapies. During the initial assessment, our study identified several distinct motivations for NSAID use, including inflammatory pain related to SpA, as well as mechanical pain that was independent of disease activity. Additionally, some patients expressed a sense of psychological dependence, driven by the concern that stopping NSAIDs could trigger an inflammatory flare.

This is also, to our knowledge, the first study conducted in North Africa to evaluate NSAID use among patients on biologics using the standardized ASAS-NSAID score. A major strength of this work is its real-world design: patients were not given any recommendations to reduce or discontinue NSAIDs, allowing for an authentic assessment of actual clinical behaviors.

However, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the sample size was relatively small (n = 85) and recruitment was limited to a single center, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. Second, there was a substantial loss to follow-up by month 12 mainly related to the discontinuation of biologic therapy for reasons such as lack of insurance coverage, treatment intolerance, or the need for further evaluation. Although imputation methods were used to address missing data, this may have introduced bias, particularly if patients lost to follow-up had different outcomes.

Finally, the classification of pain as mechanical or inflammatory was based on clinical assessment. Although standard radiographs were available for most patients, they were not systematically performed at the time of the study, and thus were not used to confirm the nature of the pain. This approach reflects routine clinical practice, but highlights the need for future studies to consider more structured approaches to pain assessment.

Lastly, due to the single-arm observational design of our study, all participants received targeted therapies without a contemporaneous control group of patients not receiving biologics. As such, our results reflect observed associations rather than causal relationships. In particular, the observed reduction in NSAID use over time cannot be attributed exclusively to targeted therapy, as spontaneous NSAID tapering may also occur in clinical practice, independent of treatment. This limitation should be considered when interpreting the clinical implications of our findings.

These observations potentially have clinical implications, particularly related to management of residual pain in patients with axSpA who use targeted therapies. The continued NSAID requirement despite clinical remission tends towards factors other than inflammation (mechanical dysfunction, fear of a flare). This draws attention to the importance of a holistic and patient-specific assessment of pain and may be an impetus for clinicians to consider non- (or alternative) pharmacological pain management strategies, such as physical therapy, psychosocial support, or referral to pain specialist services. Recognition and treatment of alternative causes of pain in these patients may improve their outcome and reduce prolonged NSAID therapy when not warranted.
Conclusion

Our study offers important insights into how targeted therapies affect NSAID use in patients with axSpA. We found a clear reduction in both NSAID consumption and ASAS-NSAID scores, showing that these treatments can effectively reduce the need for NSAIDs. However, NSAID use was not only linked to disease activity but also to mechanical pain and patients' concerns about flares. This highlights the importance of looking beyond inflammation when managing pain in axSpA. A more personalized, comprehensive approach that includes alternative pain management strategies could help improve patients' quality of life while minimizing unnecessary NSAID use.

passages.text: Toward Understanding Ligand-Directed Excited-State Electron Flow in Bridged Ruthenium(II) Complexes

Effectively and efficiently capturing and directing light to drive chemical reactions in molecular systems remains a challenge. A series of tpphz (tetrapyrido[3,2-a:2',3'-c:3'',2''-h:2''',3'''-j]phenazine)-bridged bimetallic Ru complexes was prepared using substituted polypyridyl distal ligands with a range of electron-withdrawing (EW) and electron-donating (ED) substituents to investigate the flow of electrons within the complex. The excited state is localized on the distal ligand with the most EW substituent, while charge transfer to the tpphz bridge is promoted by ED substituents. Density functional theory and time-dependent density functional theory were employed to identify the electronic transitions in the visible region of the spectrum and are supported by electrochemical and spectroscopic measurements. Cyclic voltammetry showed a two-electron oxidation of the ruthenium metal centers that correlates with the EW or ED nature of the substituents. Transient absorption spectroscopy revealed a trend in the excited-state lifetimes based on the EW or ED nature of the distal ligands. Computational and experimental results were used to propose an excited-state mechanism involving electron transfer to the tpphz bridge in all complexes except with the most EW substituent. The results provide molecular-level understanding of how excited-state electron transfer can be controlled in bridged transition metal complexes through choice of distal ligands.
Introduction

Electron transfer reactions are among the most common and important reactions in chemistry and biology. Developing electron transport systems and quality redox catalysts for reactions such as water oxidation, carbon dioxide reduction, and nitrogen fixation are critical to our quest for a more sustainable world.   A significant challenge with many redox reactions of interest is the need to transfer multiple electrons in a controlled way. As a result, many catalysts take advantage of transition metals that can access multiple oxidation states and therefore participate in multielectron transfer reactions.

Developing a fundamental understanding of electron transfer has been a goal of chemists for decades. -    From the electron transport chain to photosynthesis, electron transfer is ubiquitous throughout biological systems. The design of model systems to develop intuition about electron transfer processes has resulted in the linking of multiple redox centers with bridging ligands to form a molecular donor-acceptor system that has resulted in significant interest due to implications in photochemical electron and energy transfer. A wide array of studies involving transition metal dyads with a focus on the bridging ligand have been reported. -     Much of this work centered on intervalence charge transfer (CT) between the two mixed-valent metal atoms to describe how charge is either more localized or delocalized about the metal atoms and bridge classifying these complexes using the Robin-Day classification system.

In addition to the need to transfer multiple electrons in controlled ways, redox catalysts also need significant energy input to drive these energy intensive reactions.   An attractive goal is to use readily available solar photons to drive these redox reactions. Transition metal complexes are compelling targets for such applications because they can absorb photons and form excited states that can ultimately drive these reactions of interest. For example, a rich history of ruthenium polypyridyl chemistry describes utilization of such light energy to drive water oxidation.   Understanding the mechanism of how these catalysts utilize light energy to drive these reactions is of critical interest to design and improve upon current catalyst design. In recent years, many laboratories have developed single-site ruthenium catalysts that are capable of oxidizing water. -   Mechanistic studies reveal that a high oxidation state build-up on the metal center to RuV must be obtained for the water oxidation reaction to occur. This has led to a significant focus on ligand design to help the catalysts reach this high oxidation state, while being cognizant of how stabilizing the high oxidation state may also impact reactivity.

While a single metal center does provide the ability for multielectron transfer processes, coupling multiple metal centers together can lower the need to achieve high oxidation states at a single metal site. Such metal centers can be linked by conjugated bridges. One bridge is the tetrapyrido[3,2-a:2',3'-c:3'',2''-h:2''',3'''-j]phenazine (tpphz) bridge. The first reported synthesis of the bridging ligand tpphz and its complexation to form a bimetallic ruthenium complex was reported in a communication by Bolger in 1995. This work was followed up in 1996 with a full article reporting a series of mono- and bimetallic complexes containing ruthenium and osmium with 2,2'-bipyridine (bpy) primarily used as the distal ligands. The tpphz ligand is rigid, planar, and conjugated allowing for less structural distortion of bimetallic coordination complexes formed with tpphz as a bridge. Shortly after these initial synthetic reports, the photophysical properties of this class of bimetallic complexes with the tpphz bridging ligand were reported. -   That work identified that the two lowest lying metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) states involved transitions to the tpphz ligand; namely the higher-energy state (MLCT1) had the electron density located primarily within the phenanthroline portion of the tpphz ligand and the lower energy state (MLCT0) had the electron density located on the pyrazine portion of the tpphz ligand.

However, with inclusion of the bridging unit and the increasing number of metal centers, there is a logical complication in tracking electron transfer processes upon photoexcitation of these types of complexes. Past work attempted to track the flow of electrons in these systems. In 2003, Chiorboli reported a thorough study of the ultrafast spectroscopy of the tpphz-bridged bimetallic complexes with Ru-Ru, Ru-Os, and Os-Os metal centers with bpy distal ligands. These ultrafast studies attempted to identify the formation of the lowest energy MLCT0 state. The work reported an early fast process (~2 ps) in dichloromethane with unknown origin, although it was hypothesized to be a fast intraligand electron transfer process from an electron localized on the distal bpy ligands of a high-energy MLCT state to the MLCT1 state. This fast process was followed by a longer "slow" process of 140 ps that was assigned to the transition from the MLCT1 state to the MLCT0. This rate is solvent dependent with the rate increasing by 2 orders of magnitude when the polar solvent acetonitrile is used. The significance of making a mixed Ru-Os complex adds complexity but yields insight into donor-acceptor chemistry in which each half has significant electronic differences. The authors demonstrated by introducing asymmetry in the molecule with this mixed-metal system, the energy and electron transfer relaxation dynamics could be altered based on changes in polarity of the solvent.

Previous work on tpphz-bridged dinuclear Ru-Ru complexes provided critical insights on the photophysical properties based on different ligand substitutions. -   Another study by Hayes demonstrated the photoinduced dynamics of electron and energy transfer in dinuclear Cu-Cu and Cu-Ru complexes with the tpphz bridging ligand. Both ultrafast optical and X-ray absorption spectroscopies (XAS) were employed, yielding insight about which atoms were involved in the charge and energy transfer. In the dinuclear Cu complexes, both energy and electron transfer between the asymmetric metal centers were observed when the difference in ground-state redox potentials were greater than 310 meV. The direction of electron transfer also followed what was expected based on the electrochemical properties of the metals. This work demonstrated that CT across metal complexes can be predicted by the ground-state redox potentials of the metal centers. It also introduced the possibility of shuttling energy between different metal centers of a complex. Further work on mixed-metal systems reported utilizing K-edge XAS to track the electronic structure of tpphz-bridged multimetallic complexes including Ru, Os, Cu, Pt, Pd, and Rh as the transition metals of choice. The XAS results show a distinct energy difference between the N atoms connected to the metal (the phenanthroline-component of the ligand) and lower energy N atoms of the phenazine portion of the tpphz ligand that can be used to distinguish between CT to either of these sites. Other work has shown that the properties of different distal ligands can be used to change the nature of the excited states and the deactivation pathways in other metalated systems. -

Recently, mixed metal RuII-tpphz-RhI catalysts were employed to identify the excited-state dynamics induced by exciting into two distinct MLCT states (one photoexcitation process into an MLCT state with the RuII component as the electron donor and a second photoexcitation process into an MLCT state with RhI as the donor). The authors detangled a complicated mechanism of energy and electron transfer between the Ru and Rh metal centers, which the authors proposed both ultimately reach a charge-separated state in which the electron is localized on the phenazine portion of tpphz and a formally oxidized RhII state that then decays by LMCT back to the ground state. In contrast to the design principle of those bimetallic complexes, photoexcitation ultimately leads to undesired charge transfer to the RhII metal center, which inhibits catalysis. In a different bimetallic system, photoinduced electron transfer is proposed to result in electron transfer to the second metal center to initiate reductive catalysis. -    However, recent unpublished work has examined these complexes using time-resolved XAS to track the dynamics of the electron transfer that suggests a different path for the electron. In fact, there is a much more complex catalytic mechanism at play that is still under investigation.

In this work, we report upon a series of five bimetallic ruthenium complexes that are bridged by the aromatic and planar tpphz ligand. The five complexes studied are [(R2-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(R2-bpy)2](PF6)4, where R2-bpy = MeO-bpy (4,4'-dimethoxy-2,2'-bipyridine), Me-bpy (4,4'-dimethyl-2,2'-bipyridine), bpy (2,2'-bipyridine), phen (1,10-phenanthroline), and CF3-bpy (4,4'-bis(trifluoromethyl)-2,2'-bipyridine). The bimetallic complexes are symmetrical, containing a series of bidentate polypyridyl ligands on the periphery with varying electron-donating (ED) and -withdrawing (EW) groups in the 4 and 4' positions. We describe the spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and excited-state dynamics of these systems, and provide mechanistic insight from density functional theory calculations. The redox properties are controlled by the ED and EW nature of the substituents on the polypyridyl ligands. We show that we can direct the flow of electrons within the bimetallic complex, whether driving charge transfer toward the bridging unit with ED substituents or holding electron density on the distal ligands, away from the bridging unit with EW substituents. Gaining an understanding of how altering the ED or EW nature of the distal ligand changes the excited-state properties of these complexes will lead to insight into the development of catalysts for photoredox reactions of interest.

Cyclic Voltammetry

Cyclic voltammetry measurements were obtained on a Pine Research WaveNow Wireless Potentiostat and collected at sweep rates of 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 1000, and 2000 mV/s. Concentrations of the metal complexes ranged between 1.0 and 2.0 mM. A standard three electrode setup was used with an Ag/Ag+ pseudo-reference electrode, platinum wire distal electrode, and glassy carbon working electrode. The working electrode was polished on a polishing pad with alumina before each scan. All measurements were collected in 0.1 M tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate (TBAPF6) in MeCN electrolyte solution. Solutions were sparged with argon for approximately 15 to 20 min before data collection and then left under a blanket of argon for all studies. Ferrocene was used as an internal standard.
UV-Visible Spectroscopy

UV-visible absorption spectra were collected on a Cary 5000 UV-vis-NIR or a JASCO V-750 UV-visible spectrophotometer. UV-visible samples were prepared in dry MeCN but were otherwise open to ambient conditions during measurement. Concentrations of the metal complexes ranged between 0.002 and 0.02 mM. Measurements were conducted in a 1 cm quartz cell.
Emission Spectroscopy

All samples were prepared such that the absorption of each sample was kept below 0.1 AU at the excitation wavelength to limit reabsorption of emitted light. All experiments were performed in 2 mm quartz cuvettes, where the optical path length was 10 mm in the direction of the excitation beam and 2 mm in the direction of emission detection (perpendicular to the excitation). UV-visible phosphorescence data (500-800 nm range) were obtained on an ISS Chronos BH fluorescence lifetime spectrometer with a steady-state upgrade at an excitation wavelength of 470 nm. NIR phosphorescence spectra (1200-1350 nm) were collected at an excitation wavelength of 470 nm with a Horiba Fluorolog-3 spectrofluorometer fit with a Xe lamp and an 800 nm long-pass filter. An IR detector (DSS-IGA010L InGaAs) was used to observe emission in the IR region. The IR detector was cooled to liquid nitrogen temperature prior to measurement. Phosphorescence data were collected both in ambient air-exposed conditions and with the samples degassed on a high-vacuum line in 2 mm quartz high-vacuum cuvettes using the freeze-pump-thaw method.

Photoluminescence lifetimes were measured on an ISS Chronos BH fluorescence lifetime spectrometer equipped with a pulsed LED used as the excitation source of lambdaex = 470 nm and a repetition rate of 10 MHz or lambdaex = 370 nm with a repetition rate of 1.54 MHz. A 370 or 470 nm bandpass filter was equipped after the excitation for the 370 nm LED and 470 nm LED, respectively, and a 515 nm long-pass filter was placed before the emission detector for all samples. The data were collected in high-vacuum cuvettes and degassed using the freeze-pump-thaw method as described above. The instrument response function (IRF) was collected on distilled water. The emission data were fit in one of two ways: (1) using a monoexponential function and deconvolving the IRF or (2) using a monoexponential function on the data trace alone beginning after the IRF signal decayed (Figures S65-S70). The best fit (i.e., the fit with the lowest chi2) was chosen.

Quantum yields were calculated using fluorescein as a reference fluorophore. The fluorescein standard was prepared in 0.10 M NaOH, in which fluorescein has a quantum yield of 0.91 +- 0.05 at the excitation wavelength of 470 nm. UV-visible spectra for quantum yield calculations were acquired on a Cary 5000 UV-vis spectrometer. Quantum yields were calculated using the following equationwhere I is the integrated fluorescence intensity, A is the absorption at the excitation wavelength, and eta is the index of refraction of the solvent. Quantum yields represent the average of three trials of the samples in acetonitrile.
Transient Absorption Spectroscopy

Femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (fs-TAS) was performed using an Ultrafast Systems Helios spectrometer. One-hundred-fifty femtosecond pulses of 800 nm laser light were generated with a Coherent Libra amplified Ti:sapphire system at 1.3 W and 1 kHz repetition rate. A beam splitter was used to send approximately 80% of each 800 nm pulse to a Topas-C optical parametric amplifier used to generate the excitation wavelength of 325 nm that was attenuated to 1.0 mW to prevent decomposition of the sample. The other 20% of each 800 nm pulse was sent through a CaF2 crystal to generate a white-light continuum for use as the probe pulse with a wavelength window of 340-680 nm. The setup of the transient absorption experiments is described in detail elsewhere. -   For these measurements, transient absorption spectra were measured over a 5.5 ns window. For each scan, 250 exponentially-spaced timepoints and each sample was subjected to three scans. At least three separate samples were measured for each complex. Nanosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (ns-TAS) was performed using an Ultrafast Systems EOS spectrometer. The pump pulses were the same as those used in the fs-TAS experiment. The white light for the probe beam was generated using a pulsed PCF-based fiber optic laser. The time windows for ns-TAS ranged from 1 to 5 mus. Time delays in the ns-TAS experiment were sampled randomly using an electronically controlled delay, with 400 time points recorded over a 20 min collection period. The sample was stirred with a magnetic stir bar during each fs- and ns-TAS run.

Samples for TAS were prepared on a high-vacuum line in a 2 mm quartz high-vacuum cuvette. The concentration of each sample was ~50 muM. UV-visible absorption spectra were recorded before and after each TAS experiment to verify that no decomposition had occurred. The UV-vis spectrometer was set up with acquisition parameters of 5 ms integration time, 100 scans to average, and a boxcar width of 3. Samples were prepared so that the absorption at 325 nm was ~0.2 AU.

Data was prepared using the global analysis software Surface Xplorer, provided free of charge by Ultrafast Systems, following a protocol described in detail elsewhere. A chirp correction was applied prior to analysis of each data set (Figures S32, S34, S36, S38, and S40). Data fitting was performed using a Python-based fitting software coded in-house. Fitting was done by using a set of guess lifetimes and linear algebra to construct a set of guess decay-associated difference spectra (DADS). The number of principal components necessary to approximate the data surface through global lifetime analysis (GLA) was determined (Figures S33, S35, S37, S39, and S41). Principal component kinetic traces were then fit, and DADS and their corresponding lifetimes were generated. The extracted modeled lifetimes and DADS were then used to reconstruct a fit surface that was compared with the original data set and are shown in the fit reports provided in Figures S33, S35, S37, S39, and S41. The quality of the fitting was assessed by subtracting the fit surface from the original data surface, generating a residual surface. Each residual was also assessed with a residual standard error to facilitate comparison between fit models. In every set of the fs-TAS data, the longest lifetime was too long to be resolved on the 5.5 ns window, so it was allowed to fit as an "infinite". The "infinite" lifetime was determined using single-wavelength fitting of the ns-TAS data at the triplet absorption peak at ~600 nm or the ground-state bleach of ~470 nm (Figures S42-S51). The triplet lifetime obtained from this fitting is shown as the lifetime of the longest-lived DADS in the GLA results.
X-ray Crystallography

X-ray structural analysis for [(CF3-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(CF3-bpy)2](PF6)4 and [(MeO-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(MeO-bpy)2](PF6)4: Crystal data and refinement details are presented in Table S8. Crystals were mounted using viscous oil onto a plastic mesh and cooled to the data collection temperature. Data were collected on a D8 Venture Photon III diffractometer with Cu-Kalpha radiation (lambda = 1.54178 A) focused with Goebel mirrors. Unit cell parameters were obtained from fast scan data frames, 1 /s omega, of an Ewald hemisphere. No symmetry higher than triclinic was observed and solution in the centrosymmetric space group option, P-1, yielded chemically reasonable and computationally stable results of refinement. The data were treated with multiscan absorption corrections. Structures were solved in Olex2 using intrinsic phasing methods and refined with full-matrix, least-squares procedures on F 2.

Instead of one entire cation in a general position as in [(CF3-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(CF3-bpy)2](PF6)4, the structure in [(MeO-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(MeO-bpy)2](PF6)4 has two cations, each at a center of inversion, at half-occupancy in the asymmetric unit. Five acetonitrile molecules were found cocrystallized in the asymmetric unit of CF3-bpy. Another 5.5 molecules of acetonitrile in CF3-bpy, and five molecules of benzonitrile in [(MeO-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(MeO-bpy)2](PF6)4, per asymmetric unit, were found severely disordered and treated as diffused contributions using a solvent mask. Five -CF3 moieties and three PF6 - ions were found disordered in two positions in [(CF3-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(CF3-bpy)2](PF6)4 with refined site occupancy ratios of 50/50, 59/41, 60/40, 58/42, 52/48, 84/16, 67/33, and 62/38, respectively. One cation in [(MeO-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(MeO-bpy)2](PF6)4 has a methoxy group that is sterically geared intermolecularly and shares the disordered configuration in two positions with another methoxy group on the second cation with a refined distribution of 72/28. Another methoxy group in [(MeO-bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(MeO-bpy)2](PF6)4 was found disordered in two positions with a refined site occupancy distribution of 52/48. Geometrical and rigid-body displacement restraints and constraints were applied as they make chemical sense to model the disordered moieties.

Non-hydrogen atoms were refined with isotropic displacement parameters. Hydrogen atoms were treated as idealized contributions with geometrically calculated positions and with U iso equal to 1.2U eq (1.5U eq for methyl) of the attached atom. Atomic scattering factors are contained in the SHELXTL program library. The structures have been deposited at the Cambridge Structural Database under the following CCDC depositary numbers: CCDC 2449699, 2449700.
Mass Spectrometry

Mass spectrometry data was collected using an AB Sciex Triple TOF 5600 + via direct infusion of acetonitrile solutions with electrospray ionization (ESI). Mass differences are reported for the most intense peak in the isotopic window for the ruthenium complexes.
Computational Studies

All calculations were performed using the Gaussian09 suite of software programs. The M06-L density functional method was used for geometry optimization and analytical frequency calculations, with all structures reported being minima (no imaginary vibrational modes). The basis set used for main group elements was 6-31G and for ruthenium the def2-SVP basis set was used. All geometries and frequencies were calculated under the influence of solvent (water) via the CPCM technique and utilized the default parameters set in Gaussian09. The numerical integration grid for density functional theory (DFT) calculations was set to UltraFine.

Vertical excitation energies were determined using time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) at the optimized geometries utilizing the same DFT method and basis set. All transitions were calculated under the influence of solvent via the CPCM method. Orbital diagrams presented in this work were generated using Gauss View 5 (Figure  , Figures S56-60).

Results and Discussion
Synthesis

Several attempts were made to synthesize [(bpy)2Ru(tpphz)Ru(bpy)2](PF6)4, which for clarity in this manuscript is labeled as [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+, utilizing conventional synthetic methods, all of which resulted in long reaction times (greater than 72 h) and poor yields (less than 35%). Using a microwave reactor resulted in near quantitative yields in most cases and a reduction in reaction times to 11-30 min. Microwave reactors provide rapid, focused heating leading to increased reaction rates compared to conventional methods. -   Solvent volumes were reduced from an average of 80 to 5 mL and ethylene glycol was replaced with an ethanol/water mixture, leading to less waste and providing a more environmentally friendly procedure.

Once [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+ was obtained and the protocol was refined, four additional complexes were prepared with four different distal ligands (Scheme  ): 4,4'-dimethoxy-2,2'-bipyridine (MeO-bpy), 4,4'-dimethyl-2,2'-bipyridine (Me-bpy), 1,10-phenanthroline (phen), and 4,4'-bis(trifluoromethyl)-2,2'-bipyridine (CF3-bpy). The bimetallic complexes prepared with these ligands are labeled in this work as [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+, [Ru2(tpphz)(Me-bpy)4]4+, [Ru2(tpphz)(phen)4]4+, and [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+.
Overview Synthetic Scheme and Structure

Although a diastereomeric mixture of racemic (DeltaDelta/LambdaLambda)- and meso (DeltaLambda) isomers will form during synthesis of the homoleptic tpphz complexes, they are not expected to have different electronic or spectroscopic properties. Fletcher et al., separated racemic (DeltaDelta/LambdaLambda)- from meso (DeltaLambda)-[{Ru(dmbpy)2}2(mu-bipym)]4+ (dmbpy = 4,4'-dimethyl-2,2'-bypyridine; bipym = 2,2'-bipyrimidine); the 1H NMR spectra of the diastereomers were distinctly different given the proximity of the chiral metal centers (~5.6 A). In contrast, Fairbanks et al., similarly resolved DeltaDelta-, LambdaLambda-, and DeltaLambda-[{Ru(bpy)2}2(tpphz)]4+ and observed no differences in the NMR spectra of the isomers (Ru-Ru separation ~12.8 A). Resolution of the diastereomers was not pursued in this work as electronic differences between the isomers were not expected.
Structure Comparison

Figure   shows crystal structures of the complexes [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ and [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ (this work). Labeling for the comparison of the average bond lengths between these and [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+ (previously published) are shown in Figure S62, Table S9. -   Bond types are assigned to include Ru-N bonds between either ruthenium metal center and the tpphz ligand (Ru-Nt), Ru-N bonds between either ruthenium metal center and a distal ligand pyridyl oriented axially with respect to an octahedral geometry about a ruthenium (Ru-Na), Ru-N bonds between either ruthenium metal center and a distal ligand pyridyl oriented equatorially with respect to an octahedral geometry about a ruthenium (Ru-Ne), and N-C bonds found within the central pyrazine ring of the tpphz ligand (Np and Cp, respectively). Absolute labeling of atoms in the structures for comparison is ambiguous, e.g., assignment of Ru1 relative to N1 when multiple Ru-N bonds are present, etc. To address this ambiguity, average bond lengths of similar geometry are used for comparisons. A summary table of collected bond lengths is available with the Supporting Information (Table S9). The average Ru-Nt bond lengths for [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ and [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ are 2.066 and 2.069 A respectively, compared to the known structure of [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+, which has a bond length of 2.074 A. Modest bond contractions of 0.007 and 0.004 A respectively for the [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ and [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ complexes were observed. The average Ru-Na bond lengths for [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ and [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ are 2.057 and 2.052 A, respectively, while [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+ has a corresponding average bond length of 2.081 A, resulting in bond contractions of 0.024 and 0.029 A, respectively. The average Ru-Ne bond lengths for [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ and [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ are 2.054 and 2.053 A, respectively, while the associated bond average in [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+ is 2.051 A. The average bond lengths for the central pyrazine moieties in each compound (Np-Cp) for [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ and [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ are 1.324 and 1.328 A, respectively, compared to [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+, which has a bond length of 1.347 A. Structural differences in bond lengths for the electron donating and withdrawing bipyridine ligands are modest overall and unlikely to forecast the large electronic effects observed elsewhere.
Computational Structural Analysis

Structural analysis of the five complexes was performed using computational methods. Selected bond lengths and angles are reported in Table S1. All complexes adopt a distorted octahedral shape around each ruthenium metal center. All Ru-N bond lengths range from 2.06 to 2.10 A, which is typical of ruthenium polypyridyl complexes. -    Subtle impacts of adding ED and EW substituents to the bipyridine framework are observed. For example, the ruthenium-tpphz nitrogen bond lengths decrease slightly from the most EW substituents (2.093 A for CF3-bpy) to the most ED substituents (2.072 A for MeO-bpy). Likewise, the ruthenium-bipyridine nitrogen bond lengths increase slightly from the most EW substituents (2.062 and 2.07 A for CF3-bpy) to the most ED substituents (2.077 and 2.08 A for MeO-bpy). The outlier occurs when a phenanthroline ligand is substituted for a bipyridine derivative. The ruthenium-tpphz nitrogen bond lengths for the phenanthroline substituted metal complex are 2.077 A, falling in the middle of the complexes studied. However, the ruthenium-phenanthroline nitrogen bond distances are 2.081 and 2.083 A, which are slightly longer than any of the ruthenium-bipyridine bond distances. The longer Ru-N bond length in the phenanthroline may be due to the more rigid phenanthroline ligand compared to bipyridine and substituted bipyridines. While all the bond length changes are modest, they are reflective of the ED and EW nature of the substitutions in the 4- and 4'-positions on the bipyridine framework.

All the corresponding bond angles are similar among the five complexes, each of which resulted in the distorted octahedral geometry around the metal centers. Comparing the ruthenium-nitrogen bond angles reveals that the largest variation is only 2.5 . While these changes are small, corresponding ruthenium-nitrogen bond angles increase in a systematic manner as the nature of the bipyridine substituents is varied from EW to ED. The bond angles in [Ru2(tpphz)(phen)4]4+ remain an outlier to this trend for reasons similar to those identified for the bond lengths.
UV-Visible Spectroscopy Studies/Computational Analysis of Electronic Transitions

The electronic structure of the five bimetallic complexes was explored using computational and spectroscopic methods. The maximum wavelengths (lambdamax) of each bimetallic complex along with their molar absorptivity (epsilon) found by UV-visible spectroscopy are reported in Table  . DFT and TDDFT were used to compute the electronic structure, molecular orbitals (Figures S55-S60) and the nature of the singlet electronic transitions below 3.5 eV (Figure  , Figure  , Figure S55, and Tables S2-S6). Analysis of the Ru-tpphz bimetallic complexes revealed three primary types of electronic transitions in the visible region of the absorption spectra, as shown in Figure  . The first metal-to-ligand transition (ML1) occurs from a primarily metal-centered orbital into an empty pi* molecular orbital on the tpphz ligand. The second metal-to-ligand transition (ML2) occurs from the metal to an empty pi* orbital on the  distal  bipyridine or phenanthroline ligands. The third ligand-localized transition (LL) is a localized pi   pi* transition on the tpphz ligand. The ML1 and ML2 type transitions are lower in energy and comprise the MLCT band that is common to these types of transition metal complexes (Figure  ) overlapping well with the experimental absorption spectra in this region. The LL type transition is higher in energy as expected for pi   pi* transitions falling to the blue end of the MLCT band.

TDDFT excitations of the bimetallic complexes from the ground state (vertical sticks) overlaid with their corresponding experimental absorption spectra (solid line) measured in MeCN. Each spectrum is labeled by the complex's distal ligand. Navy, gold, and lime green excitations represent the ML1, ML2, and LL transitions, respectively. The absorption spectrum for the tpphz ligand (pink line) overlays the spectrum with bpy ligands. The overlay of the experimental data in MeCN with computed (M06-L/DZ) transitions shows good agreement between calculated and experimental spectra.

The pi   pi* LL transition serves as a useful reference point from which to begin the interpretation of the computational and spectroscopic data because this transition is present in the free tpphz ligand. By starting with the free tpphz ligand the experimental and computational analysis can be verified to yield significant insight into the electronic structure of these complexes. In the free tpphz ligand, a clear LL transition occurs at ~380 nm in MeCN/TFA in the UV-visible spectrum (Figure  , pink spectrum and Supporting Information Figure S55, bottom tile). While computational modeling predicts a single transition, the experimental results yield multiple transitions that are attributed to the Franck-Condon progression. The Franck-Condon vibrational effect has been previously observed and reported for the tpphz ligand. -   For the bimetallic tpphz complexes, the LL transition along with Franck-Condon effects are still observed at ~350 to 400 nm. Likewise, the LL transition appears in the same region for all complexes with only modest shifts. The LL transitions computed for each metal complex are red-shifted by approximately 10 nm from the experimental results. Further, the LL transition for each of the complexes appears within 7 nm of each other in the experimental data and within 4 nm of each other in the computational data. As a result of the consistent energy of the LL transition, it became the comparison point for the spectral and computational data analysis.

Despite the modest shifts, rough trends in the energy of the transition with ED and EW nature of the substituents are observed experimentally. The complex with the most EW CF3-bpy has the highest energy LL transition occurring at 366 nm. As the distal ligands become more electron-donating, the LL transition trends toward higher wavelengths (lower energies) with [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ exhibiting the LL transition at 373 nm. While the experimental results show this modest trend, the computational results of the LL transition have no discernible trend. Importantly, the LL transition provides a clear comparison point for the following analysis of the ML1 and ML2 transitions.

The ML1 and ML2 MLCT transitions are lower-energy transitions compared to the LL. In these transitions, the electron is transferred from a metal-centered orbital to pi* molecular orbitals residing on the tpphz (ML1) or substituted-bipyridine/phenanthroline ligands (ML2). The ML1 and ML2 transitions are all relatively close in energy to each other, suggesting that any photoexcitation likely results in the population of the pi* orbitals of both the tpphz and distal ligands. In examining the experimental data, there are no clear trends in lambdamax values for the transition, which is likely due to these multiple overlapping ML1 and ML2 transitions.

Although there is experimental ambiguity in the spectral shifts of the MLCT band, the computational data yields important insight into the nature of the lowest energy transition in each complex. Notably, for the bipyridine-substituted complexes, the lowest energy electronic transition red shifts (decreases in energy) as the distal bipyridine ligands become more electron-donating. As already demonstrated, as the ED ability of the distal ligands increases, the pi-backbonding decreases. -    As the pi-backbonding decreases, the energy of the t2g metal orbitals increases, resulting in lower-energy MLCT transitions. One critical observation of the ML1 and ML2 energies is that all the complexes except for [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ show the ML1 type transition, in which the electron is excited directly into a pi* of the tpphz ligand as the lowest-energy transition. For [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+, the lowest-energy MLCT changes to a ML2 transition in which the excited electron transitions into a pi* molecular orbital on the distal CF3-bpy ligand. The EW nature of the CF3 groups lower the CF3-bpy ligand energy below the tpphz ligand pi* molecular orbitals. Interestingly, these results support the drastic difference in the excited-state transient absorption spectra of [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ compared to the other complexes in this study, vide infra. It should be noted that all the lowest observed ML1 transitions are not transitions into the lowest tpphz unoccupied orbital, i.e., the LUMO, but to higher lying tpphz orbitals. In the case of the [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ complex the lowest energy transition is of ML2 type to the distal orbitals because they are now lower in energy than all of the tpphz orbitals except for the LUMO. Since the low-lying electronic transitions are not to the LUMO, which are localized to the tpphz ligand for all complexes, the relationship between electronic transitions and the electrochemical data are not directly correlated (Figure S56-S60, Tables S2-S6).
Photoluminescence Measurements

Photoluminescence studies were performed on the five bimetallic complexes to uncover their emissive properties. The phosphorescence spectrum of each complex is shown in Figures  , S63, and S64. Each complex shows phosphorescence in the spectral range of 600-700 nm and upon exposure to air in the range of 1200-1350 nm from singlet oxygen, confirming the assignment of emission from the triplet state. These peaks were confirmed as phosphorescence because in the presence of oxygen, the photoluminescence is quenched and a new peak attributed to singlet oxygen phosphorescence is observed (~1270 nm), indicative of energy transfer from the triplet state to ground-state O2 (Figure S63). [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ demonstrated a phosphorescence quantum yield (Phiph) ~4 times greater than that of the next most emissive complex. No other discernible trends are found in the phosphorescence wavelengths (lambdaph) or in the Phiph based on the EW or ED nature of the ligand (Table  ). The measured phosphorescence lifetime (tauph) of each of the bimetallic complexes is also reported in Table  .
Normalized photoluminescence spectra of the bimetallic complexes at lambdaex = 470 nm. Each spectrum is labeled by the complex's distal ligand.
Electrochemical Studies

Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was carried out in 0.1 M TBAPF6 as the supporting electrolyte in MeCN. With the use of an Ag/Ag+ pseudoreference electrode, all data was referenced to the ferrocenium/ferrocene (Fc+/0) couple added as an internal standard. Relevant redox couples are reported in Table  , and the CV scans are shown in Figures  , , and S21-S25.
Cyclic voltammograms of [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+, [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+, and [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ in 0.1 M TBAPF6 in MeCN. CV traces are labeled by the complex's distal ligand.

Cyclic voltammogram of [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ and [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ in 0.1 M TBAPF6 in MeCN. CV traces are labeled by the complex's distal ligand. Gray shading and the dashed line represent the shifting of reduction peaks.

A quasi-reversible redox wave is observed at ~0.6 to 1.2 V vs Fc+/0 that is attributed to the RuIII/II couple of the metal centers. Owing to the bimetallic nature of the complexes, the RuIII/II couple is a two-electron couple, in which each ruthenium atom in the complex is reduced by one electron. The observation that the RuIII/II redox couples appear as a single two-electron peak indicates that the two metal centers are relatively decoupled and operate as two distinct metal centers. The RuIII/II redox couple is impacted by the ED and EW nature of the substituents on the distal ligands. The bpy and phen distal ligands produce comparable RuIII/II reduction potentials of ~0.95 V vs Fc+/0, indicating that these ligands have similar electronic properties, which is supported by previous work.   Addition of ED or EW substituents to the bpy ligands significantly impacts the RuIII/II couples. Installation of the more ED substituents, Me-bpy and MeO-bpy, decreases the RuIII/II couple to 0.84 and 0.71 V vs Fc+/0, respectively. The more ED substituents on the distal ligands push electron density onto the metal center, stabilizing the more positively charged oxidation state. -   Conversely, installation of more EW CF3 substituents on the bpy distal ligands increases the RuIII/II couple to 1.23 V vs Fc+/0, indicating the metal centers of the complex are more difficult to oxidize. This more challenging oxidation results from a shift in electron density away from the metal center, which requires more energy to reach a higher oxidation state on the metal.

Several quasi-reversible reduction peaks are observed in the CV scans below -1.0 V vs Fc+/0. The first reduction process observed in the CV data for all complexes is assigned to reduction of the tpphz ligand. This assignment is supported by our computational work (vide infra and Figures S56-S60) and previous work, revealing that the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital resides primarily on the tpphz ligand.   This reduction potential does not shift as dramatically with the ED or EW nature of the R-group substituent on the bpy ligand when compared to the RuIII/II reduction potential. That is, the reduction of the tpphz ligand shifts by only 0.07 V from the most EW CF3-bpy ligand to the most ED MeO-bpy ligand. As expected, this modest shift does correlate with the EW or ED nature of R-groups, decreasing from EW to ED distal ligands. This trend indicates that there is a small degree of electronic communication between the distal ligands and central tpphz ligand in which electron density can be pushed onto the tpphz ligand, making it slightly more difficult to reduce.

Additional reduction waves are observed in the bimetallic complexes, and are assigned to reduction processes on the distal ligands.   These follow a clear trend for which reduction of the distal ligand occurs most readily onto the ligands with EW substituents. Notably, the reduction peaks of CF3-bpy ligand shift very close in energy to the tpphz LUMO reduction, further demonstrating the significant difference between the CF3-bpy complex compared to the others. That is, the CF3-bpy ligand orbitals are lower in energy than in other complexes where higher energy tpphz orbitals are lower in energy than the distal ligand orbitals, vide infra.
Transient Absorption Spectroscopy

Transient absorption spectroscopy (TAS) was used to quantify the excited-state evolution for each complex. Figure   (left column) shows the representative TAS spectra of the five bimetallic complexes. For four of the five bimetallic complexes (not [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+) photoinduced absorption indicative of the excited state are observed across the entire spectrum convolved with bleaching of the ground-state absorption features. These representative spectra show fast spectral shifting (~200 fs-3 ps) of the induced absorption at ~600 nm. The peak grows in and blue shifts for each complex before beginning to decay. Generally the peak is broader for the complexes with more electron-donating substituents on the bipyridine ligands. A ground-state bleach is observed in the representative spectra of these complexes in the 450-500 nm range. However, the bleach is not the same shape as the absorption spectrum as can be seen in the left column of Figure  , which shows the ground-state absorption spectrum overlaid as a black dotted line on top of the TAS representative spectra. Instead, two distinct peaks are observed in each bleach signal. The relative intensity of these two bleach features changes over the 5.5 ns TAS window. For the complexes with more ED substituents on the bipyridine ligands (i.e., MeO-bpy), the higher-energy (shorter-wavelength) peak remains more prominent over the 5.5 ns window. However, for the complexes with the less ED substituents, the ratio of the two bleach features changes relative to each other, with the lower-energy (longer-wavelength) bleach feature ending up more prominent by the end of the 5.5 ns fs-TAS window. At wavelengths below ~425 nm, the bleach of the ground-state features is seen overlaid on a broad excited-state absorption.

The representative spectra for [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ show different spectral evolution than those of the other bimetallic complexes. The [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ representative spectra lack the broad photoinduced absorption at ~600 nm observed in the other complexes. In this region only a small excited-state absorption is observed reminiscent of the parent [Ru(bpy)3]2+ complex (see Figure S53). The primary ground-state bleach feature retains the same spectral shape as the steady-state absorption spectrum and shows no shifting. A sharp excited-state absorption peak ~375 nm is observed, in contrast to the other bimetallic complexes.

Figure   (middle column) shows the results of global analysis fitting (GLA), which produced decay-associated difference spectra (DADS) for each liftime. The best fit to the data produced three lifetimes along with the corresponding DADS. Negative-going features in the DADS (seen between 550-650 nm Figure   (middle column)) are indicative of the amplitude of the exponential function that contributes to the respective lifetime at that wavelength. A negative-going DADS signal represents a growth of the TAS signal at that wavelength and is not the same as a bleach commonly described in representative TAS spectra such as those in the left column of Figure  . The longest lifetime was determined using the ns-TAS system (Figures S42-S51) because the dynamics exceeded that which can be measured within the fs-TAS temporal window. This lifetime was quantified using a single-wavelength fit for the peak at 600 nm for [Ru2(tpphz)(phen)4]4+, [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+, [Ru2(tpphz)(Me-bpy)4]4+, and [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+or at 470 nm for [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+. The fits obtained for [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ (tau1 = 10.8 ps, tau2 = 280 ps, tau3 = 1080 ns) show lifetimes similar to those of the parent [Ru(bpy)3]2+ (tau1 = 20 ps, tau2 = 740 ns) but do contain an additional lifetime component.

Figure   (right column) shows single-wavelength kinetics at multiple wavelengths. The data points shown are the actual data points collected by the TAS experiment at several different wavelengths. The solid lines over the data points represent the single-wavelength trace reproduced by the results of the GLA fit. The kinetic traces are presented in this way to confirm that the GLA fit reproduces the data well. In each set of data and for each fit, the model captures the data points well across the entire temporal window.

Figure   plots each lifetime as a function of the Hammett parameters for each ligand. For the series including [Ru2(tpphz)(MeO-bpy)4]4+ to [Ru2(tpphz)(bpy)4]4+, the shortest lifetime, tau1 (Figure   left), increases slightly with less ED/more EW substituents on the distal ligands, the intermediate lifetime, tau2 (Figure  , center), decreases slightly with less ED/more EW substituents on the distal ligands, and the third lifetime, tau3 (Figure  , right), increases with less ED/more EW substituents on the distal ligands. The trends observed for tau1 and tau2 are marginal as the lifetimes are within the error bars of the measurements. The lifetimes associated with [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+ (Figure  , greyed out portion of each tile), however do not fall onto the trendline of the other complexes, indicating that this complex undergoes a different photophysical mechanism for deactivation. This observation is most likely due to the triplet excitation profile, where the lowest TDDFT triplet excitation for all but the CF3-bpy complex are metal-LUMO transitions. The CF3-bpy transitions lead to multiple low-lying triplet states involving either the tpphz or the distal CF3-bpy ligands (Table S7). Table   summarizes the lifetimes for each of the five bimetallic complexes found by TAS.

Photophysical Mechanism

Based on the TAS, CV, emission and TDDFT results, an excited-state mechanism for this series of complexes is proposed in Figure  . In this discussion, intraligand electron transfer is defined as movement of the electron from the phenanthroline portion of the tpphz bridge to the phenazine portion of the bridge, and interligand electron transfer is defined as electron movement from either one bpy ligand to another bpy ligand or from a bpy ligand to the tpphz bridge. Previous work on [Ru2(tpphz)(phen)4]4+ reported that the first lifetime (tau1) is rapid intersystem crossing (ISC) to the triplet MLCT1 state followed by relaxation to a lower energy triplet MLCT0 state.   This relaxation occurs by either interligand electron transfer for [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+, or through a combination of both intra- and interligand electron transfer for the other four complexes. The second lifetime (tau2) is assigned to the geometry reorganization of the molecule while the electron sits in a "sink" on the tpphz bridge. The last lifetime (tau3) is then designated as the relaxation of the triplet state back to the singlet ground state. The values of tau3 found by TAS and tauph are similar to each other for each complex (Table  ), indicating that the longest process represents relaxation from the triplet state back to the ground state.

The higher phosphorescence quantum yield observed for [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+, relative to the other complexes, also supports the assignment of this mechanism, specifically the localization and retention of the MLCT excited state on the distal ligands. Figure  b,c are designed to show the difference in the electron population and electron flow on the tpphz bridge in the excited state for all complexes compared to [Ru2(tpphz)(CF  3  -bpy)4]4+, for which the electrons remain on the distal ligands in the excited state.
Conclusions

In summary, we have synthesized and fully characterized a new series of tpphz-bridged ruthenium complexes containing varying ED or EW substituents on the distal bipyridyl ligands. Both the ground-state characteristics and excited-state evolutions were quantified through DFT, electrochemistry, emission spectroscopy and transient absorption spectroscopy. Taken together, these results were used to propose an excited-state mechanism describing the electron flow within this series of bimetallic complexes. When the complexes possess more ED substituents on the distal ligands, the electron flow is pushed onto the tpphz bridge, whereas with EW substituents on the distal ligands, the electron can be directed to localize on the distal ligands. This work opens the door to further control the flow of electrons through bridged metallic complexes by altering the EW and ED nature of the distal ligands as the excited-state mechanism has been elucidated.
