Skyrmions are topologies defined by a mapping from one sphere to another, and have conventionally required at least two DoFs, one for each sphere. In the case of optical Skyrmions, one of the DoFs has traditionally been polarisation or spin angular momentum (SAM) for spin-textured fields, borrowing concepts from topologies in magnetism. We abandon this limiting notion and report optical Skyrmions using only the OAM of light, with results shown in Fig. 1.

The concept is shown in Fig. 1a, where the Skyrmionic topology is defined by a mapping from one OAM sphere (2-spheres embedded in 3D space) to another, each representing the two-dimensional space of their respective photons. The Skyrmion number (N) is defined as usual, counting how many times we wrap the OAM sphere of photon B when measuring all possible spatial positions of photon A. To verify this concept, we generated an OAM entangled state from a spontaneous parametric downconversion (SPDC) source, with full experimental details provided in the "Experiment and Data Analysis" section within the Supplementary Information. The state produced can be described by  where cl are complex scalar coefficients and  is the photonic state with OAM of lhbar per photon, with the correlations  cl 2 shown in Fig. 1b. The Hilbert space of the entangled pair can be sub-divided into multiple qubit states of the form, , each giving rise to a topological number of N =  Deltal = l0 - l1. Our experimental range admits topological numbers up to    +- 15. We experimentally construct all 30 such topological states (N = 0 has no topology so is discounted), inferring their topological number through a quantum state tomography for qubits, finding excellent agreement between theory (Nthe) and experiment , as shown in Fig. 1c. The switch from a positive to negative Skyrmion number is achieved by altering which photon sphere is wrapped, A or B. Some example topologies are shown in Fig. 1d for N = -1, 5 and  -8, together with the experimentally reconstructed profiles and topological numbers. The left panel reveals a Bloch vector field with a Neel-type texture, with the middle and right panels showing two higher-order vector textures. The full sphere coverage confirms the mapping, i.e., that every possible OAM state for photon B is in correspondence with photon A's position. The magnitude of the wrapping number can be discerned from the two adjacent panels, which show the Bloch phases phi12 and phi23, reminiscent of Stokes phases. Here, the number of times the positive (or negative) singularities appear in phi12 or phi23 returns the wrapping number, while its sign can be inferred using product of the polarity and vorticity of the vector representation given below each panel (the polarity is  + 1 if the vectors point up at the origin and down far away from the origin and  - 1 for the opposite case; the vorticity is  + 1 if the vector field rotates in the same direction as the azimuthal direction, and  - 1 if it rotates in the opposite direction). All are in good agreement with the theory, confirming the topology within the same DoF. In all these examples, the sphere we map to has coordinates  defined by the OAM-OAM projections, acting as the equivalent of the Stokes parameters for OAM-SAM quantum skyrmions. The order of these three coordinates can be considered a matter of convention, with no new topological invariants found by permutation.

The form of these biphoton states are identical to the asymptotic behaviour of monopole solutions in non-Abelian gauge theories, thus allowing for the experimental realisation of monopole-like topological structures in photonic configurations, which we now outline in more detail.

Our biphoton configurations, such as the entangled qubit state shown in Fig. 2a, emulate the behaviour of magnetic monopole solutions of Yang-Mills theories at large distances from the monopole core, shown conceptually in Fig. 2b, establishing the correspondence between our experimentally measured biphoton state  and the 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole solution. At first glance, there is a clear distinction between the two systems; our biphoton state is defined by the nonlocal correlations that encode a topological field configuration, whereas the 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole, too, is a field configuration (the Higgs field), but physically mimics a magnetic monopole that carries an enclosed magnetic charge. However, the mapping functions make evident a clear resemblance of their equivalence: notice that the state-dependent map , between the spatial sphere of photon A,  (derived from stereographically projecting  onto ), and the OAM Bloch sphere of photon B, , closely mirrors the monopole's topological map , obtained from the Higgs field's components , connecting the spatial sphere at infinity, , to the vacuum manifold . This is because the mapping function for the Higgs field is computed in the same way as our mapping function for the entangled state, i.e., mj ~ phij = tr(sigmajphi). In the third panel of Fig. 2a,b, we show a graphical representation of our biphoton state mapping function on the parameter sphere and an equivalent monopole configuration from Yang-Mills theory (See Supplementary Equation S.70 in the Supplementary Information for the expression of the equivalent asymptotic Higgs potential). In electromagnetism, charge is specified by a single number, positive or negative. In Yang-Mills theory, there are multiple independent charges - for example, the three colours of quarks in QCD - which are each described by a vector. The space of these vectors is called the internal space. We see that the Higgs field takes on the configuration of a hedgehog-like structure in this internal space. Evidently, the graphical representation of these seemingly desperate but equivalent fields configurations on their corresponding parameter spaces also reveals their topological equivalence. It follows that the corresponding wrapping numbers or topological charges proceed in exactly the same way (see "Non-Abelian Higgs Potential" section of Supplementary Information for derivation):quantifying the number of times the field configurations wraps the parameter space, with dOmegai representing the area element. The measured topological wrapping number for our biphoton state is N = 0.99, matching the wrapping number of the monopole configuration (+ 1), which is directly related to the monopole's charge. Therefore, the above establishes the equivalence between the topological features of our biphoton OAM state and that of the Higgs field.

Our analysis, though framed in two-dimensional OAM states, extends naturally to higher-dimensional OAM spaces, where topological charges generalise to a spectrum of charges for SU(d). This parallels Yang-Mills-Higgs theory, where monopole charges arise from distinct SU(2) embeddings within SU(d). We show that these embeddings correspond directly to the various S2   S2 mappings in the higher-dimensional topological space of our states.

Higher-dimensional spaces possess a spectrum of topological invariants arising from the winding numbers of maps to distinct embedded submanifolds. To systematically uncover these submanifolds, we establish a theoretical framework leveraging the Lie algebra of SU(d) as a powerful tool. This approach generalises the Pauli projections used in Stokes measurements for qubits to higher-dimensional analogous Gell-Mann projections for d = 3, and more generally, projections onto the SU(d) basis {Ta} a = 1, 2,    , d2 - 1 defining a generalised Lie algebra (GLA) vector . Within this framework, the topological structure emerges from an intrinsic manifold of d2 - 1 dimensions. To probe this topology, we construct explicit maps from a reference two-sphere (in our case, the OAM sphere of photon A) to the embedded submanifolds, as shown conceptually in Fig. 3a, each defined by a triplet of Lie algebra basis projections (see "Topological landscape for higher-dimensional states" in Supplementary Information). This yields  possible maps, each with an associated wrapping number quantifying how the reference sphere envelops the embedded sphere. In certain cases, this process first generates a disk-to-disk map, which we then extend to a sphere-to-sphere mapping, ensuring a well-defined topological invariant. The optimal choice of triples aligns with an SU(2) subgroup embedded within SU(d), paralleling the classification of monopole charges in non-Abelian Yang-Mills theory, where distinct SU(2) subgroups correspond to different topological charges. These invariants form a topological spectrum, as shown in Fig. 3b, encoding essential features of the space's topology.

The reason for the appearance of both disks and spheres is that, topologically, the infinite two-dimensional plane can be associated either with a sphere S2 or a disk D2, depending on the class of functions under consideration. If we restrict to functions that approach a fixed value at infinite radius, all points at infinity can be identified, and a one-point compactification maps the plane to a sphere. In contrast, if the functions retain nontrivial theta-dependence even at infinite radius, the boundary cannot be collapsed to a single point, and the topology is that of a disk.

As we saw in the case of the two-dimensional quantum state of the preceding part, the relevant observables are given by the Pauli-spin matrices, which form a basis for su(2) and determine the components of the state vector, whose tip moves along the surface of the Bloch sphere. Similarly, for a d-dimensional state, any triple {mi, mj, mk} selected from the spatially varying GLA vector defines a vector whose tip traces points on an embedded two-dimensional submanifold. Maps between spheres can exhibit non-trivial topology, characterised by a wrapping number N that counts how many times one sphere covers the other. This leads to a spectrum of topological invariants, potentially one per embedded submanifold, with their number growing as the quantum state dimension d increases. Defining the topological invariants reduces to identifying the triples (mi, mj, mk) that generate meaningful submanifolds. With d2 - 1 available components mi,j,k, there are  possible mappings, while the subset of non-trivial and independent invariants depends on the specific quantum state. Which submanifolds embedded within SU(d) to select? As argued in the Supplementary Information (See "Topological invariants for Qudit (any d) states" section), this can be answered by leveraging the identity between the Higgs potential in the vacuum sector of Yang-Mills-Higgs theory and the density matrix. This identification arises from the fact that the triplet {mi, mj, mk} defines a Higgs field in the vacuum sector, whose wrapping number precisely matches the magnetic charge of the corresponding 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole. In Yang-Mills-Higgs theory, monopoles carry a spectrum of charges, each linked to distinct embeddings of SU(2) subgroups within the larger SU(d) gauge group. Under our framework, these different embeddings correspond directly to the many possible S2   S2 mappings.

Our theory predicts the properties of the topological spectrum for any given state, in any dimension, and posits that complex high-dimensional quantum states can be classified by their topological spectrum. There will be  maps in the spectrum, of which  are in general non-trivial, i.e., depending on the exact state, they are the "window" in which one would expect to see a non-zero topological number. By way of example, consider the case of d = 3, a quantum qutrit. The topological manifold is 8-dimensional, allowing 56 possible maps. Of these, 18 could have non-trivial and independent topological invariants, depending on the state. Unlike qubits, where the single invariant determines whether the states  and  are entangled, for qutrits, certain nonzero invariants indicate that  is entangled with both  and , demonstrating sensitivity beyond simple bipartite entanglement.

Here, we investigate the resilience of the topological spectrum in the presence of noise, recognising that quantum states inevitably degrade due to various realistic noisy scenarios such as noisy detectors (e.g., shot and thermal noise), stray light (such as daylight), accidental multi-photon pair generation, photon loss, etc. In such settings, the channels map the pure state,  where p scales the purity of the state, ranging from 0 (maximally mixed) to 1 (pure). In Fig. 5 we investigate the behaviour of the topological spectrum for the input pure state  under generic isotropic noise, a standard approach to test quantum states in noise. Figure 5a (i) shows the spectrum, displaying only the theoretically predicted non-trivial signals (N   0), for the state with purity 0.8 measured under ideal experimental conditions. Figure 5a (ii) similarly shows only the non-trivial topological signals under isotropic noise, while (iii) and (iv) display the full spectrum, explicitly partitioned into non-trivial and trivial contributions, for increasing levels of isotropic noise. The degree of increasing noise is quantified by the corresponding reduction in signal-to-noise ratio and yields a degradation of the state here seen as a diminishing state purity of 0.72, 0.58 and 0.51 for the states represented in (ii), (iii) and (iv), respectively. Here, the purity was measured from the reconstructed density matrix (rho), following the definition, Tr(rho2). Empirically, we find that the topological spectra remain largely unchanged relative to the initial experimental spectrum, (i). This robustness is further supported by an average residual of less than 0.1 when compared to the ideal experimental case. A comprehensive dataset illustrating the behaviour under varying noise conditions is presented in Fig. 5b. The experimentally measured state purity (shown as data points) of the state decreases monotonically, matching theory (shown as dashed lines) with decreasing signal-to-noise ratio. However, the average residuals when comparing the noisy state against its ideal experimental counterpart remains close to zero (reaching a max of 0.14 for a purity (0.12) close to the theoretical minimum indicating a completely mixed state) closely matching the theoretical prediction. These results along with additional examples such as variations in state amplitudes and phases (shown in the SI) confirm that the underlying topological structure remains robust under a wide range of perturbations. Now, we note in Fig. 4b small signatures in some spaces that should have no topology, a feature that we also observe in Fig. 5a (iii) and (iv). It is clear that the emergence of these topological signals do not arise with the introduction of isotropic noise or variations in the amplitudes and phases of the state coefficients as the full spectra remains unaltered regardless of the amount of noise that is present. Rather as we deliberately introduce entanglement into subspaces within the larger Hilbert space, the theoretically predicted trivial part of the spectrum reveals emergent topology as a result of the introduction of entanglement, as seen by the emergence of new signatures in Fig. 5a (iii) and (iv). In a real-world scenario, this could be due to an eavesdropper introducing errors into the original state. We have included explicit examples in the SI that highlight the emergence of topological information with the introduction of entanglement into new subspaces. This is a notable advantage over low-dimensional systems: observing the entire spectrum opens the possibility to remain robust to perturbations yet also probe for them.

Having used d = 2 to highlight the possibility of topology with one DoF, and d = 3 to introduce the notion of a topological spectrum, we now show that indeed this approach can be pushed to high dimensions with a potentially enormous encoding alphabet, with the results shown in Fig. 6.
Towards higher dimensions

The predicted growth in the size of the topological spectrum with dimension is dramatic as shown in Fig. 6a. While the specific non-zero and independent invariants depend on the quantum state, this scaling highlights the rapidly increasing complexity of the topological spectrum. We confirm this in Fig. 6b, c where we show experimentally measured spectra corresponding to d = 5 and d = 7, for topological manifolds of dimension 24 and 48, respectively. We observe 2024 candidate invariants for d = 5, rising to 17,296 for d = 7, a clear indication that this approach is highly scalable. These results represent the highest dimensions reported in any topological system.
DISCUSSION

Intriguingly, using OAM entangled photons to access high-dimensional spaces has been extensively explored, but the topological features seem to have been hidden from view. Here we have shown that ubiquitous spatial entanglement, such as OAM correlations from SPDC, has an underlying topological tapestry that is very rich, with potentially many thousands of signatures to be found. In general, there will be  non-zero topological numbers in a given spectrum, and have deduced that for OAM states,  of these invariants are independent (see "Topological invariants for Qudit (any d) states" section in the Supplementary Information). Could this exciting potential be harnessed as a topological alphabet (which in general is not orthogonal) for quantum communication? To do so will require the development of quantum operators, gates and detectors that are topology specific, none of which presently exist, a situation that can be likened to the state of OAM as a resource two decades ago. There is potential for sensing and robustness simultaneously, as we have shown in the experimental example of robustness of the topological spectrum to environmental noise while probing for emergent topology in the initially trivial part of the spectrum, the latter due to the introduction of entanglement into new subspaces.

In the quantum context, both dimensionality and topology have attractive benefits. The harnessing of topology in quantum systems is mooted to overcome the fragility of such systems to external perturbation, facilitating the robust sharing and storing of quantum information. Higher dimensions in quantum states too has benefits, such as noise resilience, higher bounds for eavesdropping and security against cloning. The mutual benefits are very attractive and remain to be explored, particularly in cases where information must be distributed by entanglement as a resource, such as in teleportation, quantum networks, and quantum computers.

It is possible that this work has scope to expand even further, for instance, the existence of other invariants not yet discovered, which could distinguish states beyond those we have identified, and the ability to shape the topological spectrum by SPDC pump shaping. Note that in our work, the topology is a property of the entanglement itself, the map from the space of one photon to the other, and as such it has no direct resemblance to quantum simulation with synthetic dimensions of condensed matter phenomena, e.g., by emulating the Harper-Hofstadter Hamiltonian by some lattice and an interaction through a tight-binding model. Moving to higher dimensions in such systems also gives rise to a spectrum of topological invariants, experimentally observed in d = 4 for additional Chern numbers, so there are similarities in the underlying physics that deserve to be explored. OAM too has proven useful here, for instance, simulating 2D topological physics with 1D coupled OAM cavities and used as a building block for quantum devices. But in our work, we are not realising interesting physics in an analogue system that would require some interpretation between the two: the topology we uncover is a direct characterisation of the entangled photon state itself, not emulating other systems but rather probing the intrinsic structure of our physical system directly. Further, our work offers a unique approach to accessing Non-Abelian gauge fields, a powerful tool for studying complex physical systems. Our direct link of the OAM biphoton's topology to the monopole charge and Higgs field texture opens different directions to explore this link further.

In conclusion, our report represents a unique realisation of skyrmionic states with just the OAM degree of freedom, derived directly from the spatial entanglement without any quantum state engineering. Our generalisation to high dimensions has shown a unique paradigm to achieve high-dimensional topological states of light, necessitating a new theoretical and experimental framework, while introducing the notion of a topological spectrum, which we have experimentally confirmed with the highest reported dimensions and topological maps to date. The implication is a rich topological signature for identifying high-dimensional quantum states, potentially opening unique paths to communication and sensing with topology.

passages.text: Small fiber neuropathy in pediatric female heterozygotes of Fabry disease: a twin case report
Background

Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder, is associated with significant multisystem involvement, including small fiber neuropathy. While neuropathic pain is well-documented in females with Fabry disease, the objective confirmation of small fiber dysfunction in pediatric heterozygotes remains underreported. This study highlights the role of quantitative sensory testing (QST) in diagnosing small fiber neuropathy in young female patients.
Case report

We present twin sisters, heterozygous for a pathogenic GLA variant (c.298 A > T), who exhibited symptoms of small fiber neuropathy, including acroparesthesia and gastrointestinal dysfunction. QST revealed altered thermoalgesic and vibratory thresholds in one twin and isolated vibratory hyposensitivity in the other, supporting the diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy.
Discussion

These cases highlight the diagnostic challenge of Fabry disease, as neuropathic symptoms may be overlooked or attributed to other conditions in pediatric patients. The findings emphasize the need for early identification of small fiber dysfunction in heterozygous females, who are increasingly recognized as being clinically affected. The complex alterations in sensory processing reinforce the importance of integrating QST as an objective assessment tool for small fiber function in Fabry disease.
Conclusions

Small fiber neuropathy is an early and clinically relevant manifestation of Fabry disease in pediatric heterozygotes. Early recognition and intervention, including enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), are essential to mitigating disease progression and improving clinical outcomes. These cases underscore the utility of QST in confirming small fiber neuropathy and highlight its potential role in the early diagnosis and monitoring of Fabry-related neuropathy in pediatric patients.
Introduction

Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the GLA gene. These variants result in deficient activity of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A (AGA) and the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3), and other alpha-galactosyl derivatives in vascular endothelial cells. The multisystem effects of these accumulations lead to a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, including neuropathic, ocular, cardiovascular, renal, gastrointestinal, and dermatologic involvement. The systemic impact of Fabry disease necessitates a comprehensive understanding to reduce the significant morbidity and mortality associated with delayed diagnosis and treatment. While Fabry disease follows an X-linked inheritance pattern and has traditionally been considered more severe in males, female heterozygotes can also exhibit a wide range of symptoms due to X-chromosome inactivation, often presenting with variable disease severity.

Small fiber neuropathy is a recognized complication of Fabry disease and significantly contributes to disease-related morbidity. It is characterized by symptoms such as limb paresthesias, hypohidrosis, abdominal pain, cold hypoesthesia, and diarrhea. These symptoms typically emerge in childhood and progressively worsen over time, adversely affecting quality of life and long-term prognosis. Importantly, small fiber neuropathy and neuropathic pain are primarily associated with the classic phenotype of Fabry disease and do not occur in late-onset forms.

The diagnosis of Fabry disease is often delayed due to its rarity and the nonspecific nature of its early clinical signs. While the definitive diagnosis is established through genetic testing of the GLA gene, small fiber neuropathy can be confirmed using diagnostic techniques such as quantitative sensory testing (QST), skin biopsy, or pain-related evoked potentials (PREP). These advanced diagnostic tools require specialized equipment and expertise, which are often limited to specialized reference centers. Early recognition of this underdiagnosed condition is crucial, particularly given the availability of targeted therapies such as enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) and chaperone therapy, which can alter disease progression when initiated promptly.

In this report, we describe the case of twin sisters diagnosed with Fabry disease, genetically confirmed by the presence of a pathogenic GLA variant. Despite being female heterozygotes, they exhibit symptoms indicative of small fiber neuropathy, reinforcing the importance of considering Fabry disease in the differential diagnosis of pediatric neuropathic pain. We focus on their clinical presentation, the diagnostic challenges encountered, and the utility of QST and functional assessments in identifying small fiber neuropathy in affected individuals.
Case reports

The first twin exhibited initial symptoms at the age of four, including acroparesthesia, neuropathic pain in the feet, and abdominal discomfort. These episodes occurred 2 to 4 times per week with severe intensity, frequently associated with constipation. Physical examination revealed distal coldness but no other significant abnormalities. Despite normal nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography, quantitative sensory testing (QST) using CASE IV  software (4,2,1 algorithm with null stimuli) demonstrated a significant elevation in Vibratory Detection Thresholds (VDT) in both upper and lower extremities, with percentiles exceeding 97.5, indicating hyposensitivity. Additionally, Heat Pain Thresholds (HPT) were significantly reduced, with percentiles below 2.5 in response to moderate pain stimuli (HPT 5.0), alongside a leftward shift in the thermoalgesic curve, suggesting hyperalgesia. These findings supported the diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy (Figs. 1 and 2).
Vibratory Detection Threshold (VDT) performed at dorsum of left foot showing computed threshold 10.75, Calculated displacement 0.99 mum, Percentile 99.99, Deviate 3.72
Heat Pain Threshold (HPT) performed at dorsum of right hand showing computed threshold 18.85, Displacement 7.54  C from 34  C, Percentile 0.8 and Normal Deviate - 2.41

Further cardiac evaluation with 24-hour Holter monitoring indicated sinus tachycardia and reduced heart rate variability. However, additional assessments, including transthoracic echocardiography, pulmonary function studies, blood chemistries, and abdominal imaging, did not reveal any abnormalities.

The second twin developed symptoms at the age of five, initially presenting with abdominal pain localized in the hypogastrium, later becoming more diffuse. She experienced moderate to severe pain episodes 1-2 times per week, accompanied by diarrhea and acroparesthesia. Her physical examination was unremarkable, and nerve conduction studies along with needle electromyography yielded normal results. However, QST revealed significantly elevated VDT in both upper and lower extremities (Fig. 3), with calculated percentiles exceeding 97.5, indicating hyposensitivity. All other sensory thresholds remained within normal limits. Similar to her sister, Holter monitoring demonstrated decreased heart rate variability, though echocardiography, blood chemistry, and abdominal imaging were unremarkable.
Vibratory Detection Threshold (VDT) performed at dorsum of left foot showing computed threshold 8, Calculated displacement 0.33 mum, Percentile 99.99, Deviate 3.72

Both patients were confirmed to have a pathogenic GLA variant (c.298 A > T), which results in a premature stop codon and leads to a truncated alpha-galactosidase A enzyme. This pathogenic variant is associated with the classic phenotype of Fabry disease, characterized by early-onset symptoms and progressive multisystemic involvement. The clinical presentation and QST findings were consistent with small fiber neuropathy, leading to a definitive diagnosis of Fabry disease.

In accordance with international Fabry disease guidelines, enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with recombinant agalsidase beta (1 mg/kg every two weeks) was initiated in both patients due to the presence of small fiber neuropathy. The diagnosis was supported by clinical symptoms, objective quantitative sensory testing (QST) findings, and a pathogenic GLA variant (c.298 A > T), which is known to be associated with the classic phenotype of Fabry disease. Given the progressive nature of Fabry neuropathy, early therapeutic intervention was deemed necessary to mitigate disease progression and improve long-term outcomes. Additionally, neuropathic pain management was commenced with pregabalin at 5 mg/kg/day, divided into two doses. Following the initiation of enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) in combination with multimodal symptomatic pain management, both patients reported a subjective reduction in neuropathic and autonomic symptoms. Although this perceived improvement aligns with previously reported clinical trajectories in Fabry-associated small fiber neuropathy, these observations must be interpreted cautiously, as no validated pain or autonomic assessment scales were applied to objectively quantify change.
Discussion

We present two sisters diagnosed with Fabry disease who exhibited clinical signs of small fiber neuropathy, a condition increasingly recognized in pediatric female heterozygotes. Both experienced acroparesthesia and gastrointestinal symptoms, with one displaying altered thermoalgesic and vibratory sensitivity, while the other demonstrated decreased vibratory sensitivity.

The identified pathogenic GLA variant (c.298 A > T), resulting in a truncated protein, underscores the genetic heterogeneity of Fabry disease and its implications for phenotype severity. These cases highlight the diagnostic challenges posed by Fabry disease, particularly given its nonspecific early symptoms. The presence of acroparesthesia and abdominal pain aligns with prior reports and reinforces the necessity for heightened clinical suspicion. Neuropathic pain is a common manifestation in pediatric females with Fabry disease, affecting up to 40% of individuals under the age of 18. Additionally, severe and disabling neuropathic pain in female heterozygotes has been well documented, with pain attacks occurring in 58% of affected girls.

"Fabry neuropathy has been extensively studied using specific questionnaires, qualitative and quantitative peripheral nerve studies, functional sensory assessments, and tissue biopsies. While some pain questionnaires might be an alternative to measure the neuropathic pain, QST has been widely used to assess pediatric small fiber function, and abnormal QST findings in female heterozygotes with Fabry disease have been correlated with sensory symptom severity. Although sensory dysfunction in heterozygous females has been previously described, quantitative small fiber assessments in pediatric populations remain limited. In these cases, QST performed at age seven revealed significant abnormalities, reinforcing the potential role of QST in early diagnosis and monitoring of Fabry neuropathy."

Gastrointestinal symptoms are frequently reported in Fabry disease; however, their evaluation and monitoring remain challenging. In this study, gastrointestinal symptoms were assessed through clinical history and patient-reported complaints rather than a standardized evaluation scale. While this approach provided insight into symptom burden, the lack of a structured assessment tool represents a limitation. Recent literature suggests that validated scales such as the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS) or Fabry-specific questionnaires can provide objective measures of gastrointestinal dysfunction. Future studies should incorporate these tools to improve symptom quantification and assess treatment response more effectively.

In Fabry disease, early sensory dysfunction typically affects Adelta fibers, with cold detection thresholds being among the most consistently altered parameters. However, in these cases, both twins exhibited significantly elevated vibratory detection thresholds (VDT), suggesting hyposensitivity. While VDT abnormalities are not typically reported in early Fabry disease, potential explanations include broader small fiber impairment extending to Abeta fibers or secondary neuronal involvement due to progressive disease. Another possibility is the influence of central sensitization mechanisms, which have been reported in Fabry neuropathy and may contribute to altered sensory processing. Additionally, vibratory threshold testing can be subject to variability in pediatric patients, influenced by factors such as attention span, cognitive engagement, and response variability. Unlike cold detection thresholds, which rely on an immediate stimulus perception, vibrotactile assessments require sustained focus, making results potentially less reliable in young children. Future studies should incorporate repeated measures or complementary diagnostic tools to enhance the accuracy of sensory evaluations in pediatric Fabry disease patients.

The presence of small fiber neuropathy in these cases is particularly informative. The paradoxical findings of vibratory hyposensitivity and thermal hyperalgesia illustrate the complex alterations in sensory processing characteristic of Fabry disease. These results emphasize the necessity of incorporating objective measures such as QST to evaluate neuropathic pain and sensory dysfunction, particularly in young patients. Additionally, treatment selection in pediatric Fabry disease should consider both guideline recommendations and patient-specific factors.

In accordance with international guidelines, sodium channel blockers (such as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine) are generally recommended as first-line agents for the symptomatic treatment of Fabry neuropathy. However, in these cases, pregabalin was selected due to its established efficacy in treating small fiber neuropathy, its better safety profile in pediatric patients, and its ease of titration. Pregabalin has demonstrated benefits in Fabry-related neuropathic pain and has been widely used as a second-line option when sodium channel blockers are contraindicated or poorly tolerated. In our patients, pregabalin was chosen due to concerns regarding the potential side effects of sodium channel blockers, particularly in pediatric populations, including sedation, dizziness, and cognitive impairment. Additionally, the dosing flexibility of pregabalin allowed for better symptom control with fewer side effects, making it a more suitable choice for long-term management in young children.

In the present cases, both individuals reported a subjective improvement in neuropathic pain after the initiation of treatment. This clinical perception is consistent with prior literature suggesting that disease-specific therapy together with adjunctive pharmacologic interventions may attenuate neuropathic pain in Fabry disease. However, because no standardized instruments:such as the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), Douleur Neuropathique 4 (DN4), Small fiber neuropathy-symptoms inventory questionnaire (SFN-SIQ) (SFN-SIQ), or Composite Autonomic Symptom Score-31 (COMPASS-31):were used to document the course of symptoms over time, it is not possible to determine whether this reported change represents a true therapeutic effect or reflects spontaneous variability, natural disease course, or psychological adaptation. The clinical response observed here is therefore likely multifactorial, potentially involving effects of ERT, pharmacologic modulation of nociceptive pathways, nonpharmacological strategies, and patient-level coping mechanisms. Future studies would benefit from incorporating validated, quantitative measures of pain and autonomic dysfunction to better characterize treatment response and delineate the relative contribution of each therapeutic modality.

These findings reinforce the need for individualized treatment strategies that consider both symptom severity and the risk-benefit profile of available therapeutic options. Future studies should further evaluate the long-term efficacy of different pharmacological approaches in pediatric Fabry disease patients. Furthermore, since ERT response in Fabry neuropathy remains a controversial area, future studies should integrate both subjective measures (e.g., pain questionnaires) and objective evaluations such as post-treatment QST assessments to quantify the effects of therapy on small fiber function. This would help establish a clearer relationship between treatment intervention and sensory function improvements in pediatric Fabry patients.

Finally, practical considerations for QST in pediatric patients are crucial. The use of QST in children presents unique challenges, including cognitive engagement, attention span, and response accuracy. To improve test reliability, it is recommended that QST assessments in children incorporate repeated measures and standardized protocols that account for developmental differences in sensory processing. Additionally, the involvement of trained personnel experienced in pediatric neurophysiology can help optimize test accuracy. Despite these challenges, QST remains a valuable tool for identifying small fiber dysfunction in Fabry disease and should be considered in the evaluation of young patients presenting with neuropathic pain.
Conclusions

Small fiber neuropathy may be an early and prominent feature of Fabry disease, underscoring the need to consider this condition in the differential diagnosis of children presenting with neuropathic pain and autonomic symptoms. Early recognition and intervention are critical to slowing disease progression and optimizing patient outcomes. Further research is necessary to delineate the natural history of Fabry disease in pediatric populations and refine therapeutic approaches.

The findings from these twin cases, in conjunction with existing literature, suggest a need to reassess diagnostic and management strategies for Fabry disease, particularly in addressing neuropathic pain and gastrointestinal manifestations in affected females. These cases also reinforce the utility of QST as a valuable tool in detecting small fiber neuropathy in children with Fabry disease.

The patients described a subjective improvement in neuropathic symptoms after starting ERT in combination with symptomatic pain management. While this finding is clinically encouraging, the absence of validated outcome measures limits the ability to attribute this improvement to any specific intervention. These observations underscore the need for structured longitudinal follow-up using standardized sensory and pain assessment tools to more accurately evaluate therapeutic benefit in Fabry-related small fiber neuropathy.

passages.text: Effect of oil blends with near equal increases in 18 carbon n-3 and n-6 fatty acids on fatty acid profile of eggs

annotations.text: 18 carbon n-3 and n-6 fatty acids

passages.text: The present study aimed to compare the near equal substitution of 18 carbon omega-3 (n-3) and omega-6 (n-6) fatty acids (FA) on their elongation and deposition into the egg yolks and tissues of laying hens. Fifty 40 wk old Hy-line W-36 white leghorn hens were randomly allocated to five experimental groups (10 hens per group). The basal diet was a corn-soybean meal mash layer diet containing 3.14 % conventional soybean oil (SOY), control, and the experimental diets were prepared by substituting 1.25 % of the SOY for high-stearidonic acid (SDA; 18:4n-3) soybean oil or a high-alpha linolenic acid (ALA; 18:3n-3), a high-gamma linolenic acid (GLA; 18:3n-6), or a high-linoleic acid (LA; 18:2n-6) oil blend. No adverse effects on laying performance, egg components, and tissue weight were reported. Hens fed high-SDA and high-ALA diets showed higher levels of total n-3 FA than control and other treatments. Total n-3 highly unsaturated FA (HUFA) was increased in the yolk and breast muscle of hens fed high-SDA compared to the high-ALA. Similarly, the high-GLA and high-LA diets increased the total n-6 and total n-6 HUFA in yolk, liver, and breast than other diets. The total n-6 HUFA was the greatest in the yolk and breast muscle of hens fed high-GLA diet. The efficiency of synthesis and transfer of n-3 and n-6 HUFA was greater in the yolk of hens fed high-SDA and high-GLA diets than other treatments. Hepatic expression of FASN and ELOV2 was higher in SDA than the other UFA treatments. Overall, the high-SDA and high-GLA diets more efficiently enriched the yolk and body tissues with HUFA. Further investigation on the most efficient level of inclusion into the diet might be needed.
Introduction

Diets of laying hens are traditionally supplemented with vegetable oils to reduce dust, improve palatability, enhance energy intake to improve egg weight and production, and to meet the hen's essential fatty acid (FA) requirements. However, they can also be used to modify egg FA profile to produce specialty eggs with higher value. Extensive work has been done comparing oils enriched in 18 C n-3 and n-6 FA, but most are confounded by differences in the enrichment of the PUFA of interest, making interpretation difficult.

The 18 C n-3 and n-6 FA are elongated and desaturated to the highly unsaturated derivatives (HUFA), including the n-6 product arachidonic acid (ARA; 20:4n-6) and the n-3 products eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA; 20:5n-3) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA; 22:6n-3) as reviewed by. Many of the health benefits associated with n-3 FA are presumed to be through the HUFA. These can be directly enriched in eggs and chicken meat by feeding fish or algae oil supplements, but this approach is challenged by high costs, poor oxidative stability in feed, and possible contaminants. Elongation and desaturation of linoleic acid (LA; 18:2n-6) and gamma linolenic acid (GLA; 18:3n-6) to ARA and alpha linolenic acid (ALA; 18:3n-3) and stearidonic acid (SDA; 18:4n-3) to EPA and DHA is limited and differences in efficiency when fed at similar doses are not well described ( and).

There is an extensive literature on the ability of conventional flaxseed and flaxseed oil to increase 18 C and HUFA n-3 in eggs. We have previously compared genetically engineered soybeans enriched in SDA to flaxseed oil, but these oils differed in total n-3 content (37 vs 51 % total FA). We have also compared a high-SDA Ahiflower oil to a high-ALA flaxseed oil which contained similar levels of total n-3 FA (64 vs 66 % of total FA) although the oils were confounded by GLA concentration. Preparation of oil mixtures allows better control of FA treatments, and we recently reported the effect of nearly equal substitution of SDA for ALA, GLA, and LA on tissue FA profile in broilers. When provided at near equal dose levels, SDA resulted in 43, 45, and 60 % increases in n-3 HUFA compared to ALA and GLA resulted in 15, 11, and 16 % higher n-6 HUFA compared to LA in breast, liver, and thigh, respectively.

Gamma linolenic acid has garnered less attention than other PUFA but supplementation in poultry diets has been reported to increase GLA and total n-6 FA in both egg yolks and broiler meat. The effects of GLA on human health are not well understood. However, GLA appears to be efficiently converted in many cells and tissues, including some inflammatory cells, to dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA; 20:3n-6) and subsequently ARA. Dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid serves as a substrate for enzymes like COX and LOX, and its metabolites are reported to have mainly anti-inflammatory properties and inhibit platelet aggregation.

The present study aimed to directly compare the nearly equal substitution of 18 C n-3 and n-6 FA on their elongation and deposition into the egg yolks and tissues of laying hens. Oil blends were formulated to replace 23 percentage points of SDA in high SDA soybean oil for ALA, GLA, or LA while maintaining nearly equal concentrations of other FA. A control feeding conventional soybean oil was also included to allow comparison to previous literature. Our hypothesis was that SDA would raise total n-3 HUFA in the egg yolk and tissues more than ALA and GLA would increase n-6 HUFA more than LA.
Materials and methods
Animals and housing

Sixty Hy-line W-36 white leghorn hens were obtained from the Penn State university flock at 40 weeks of age and were housed individually in wire cages with sloping floors measuring 36 cm (height) x 43 cm (depth) x 30 cm (width). Each cage was equipped with a feeder and water nipple, and the hens were exposed to 16 hours of artificial light daily in a temperature-controlled and well-ventilated room at the Poultry Education and Research Center layer facility. Laying rate and egg weight was monitored for 5 d immediately before the experiment and the 50 best performers were chosen for the study (laying rate of 100 % and average egg weight of 61.8 +- 3.30 g, mean +- SD). The selected hens were individually weighed, wing-tagged, blocked by egg weight, and randomly allocated to five experimental groups (10 hens per treatment). All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of The Pennsylvania State University.

Diets were prepared by substitution of 1.25 % of conventional soybean oil in control diet (CON) with high-stearidonic acid soybean oil (High-SDA diet) or a high-alpha linolenic acid (High-ALA diet), high-gamma linolenic acid (High-GLA diet), or high-linoleic acid (High-LA diet) oil blends that increased each test FA ~22.5 percentage units.
SOY = conventional soybean oil, TSAA = Total sulfur amino acid, Limestone = calcium carbonate.
Nutrient composition is as balanced except total FA that was measured by gas chromatography.

The experimental diets, which varied only in treatment oils, were developed to meet, or exceed the nutrient requirements of Hy-line W-36 Leghorn hens. The control diet was a corn-soybean meal mash layer diet containing 3.14 % conventional soybean oil (Great Value , Walmart, PA) and the other treatments were prepared by substituting 1.25 % of the conventional soybean oil (SOY) for high-SDA soybean oil (Bayer Inc, Leverkusen, Germany) or a high-ALA, a high-GLA, or a high-LA oil blend (Table 1). The oil blends were created by blending palm oil (Jedwards International Inc, Braintree, MA), high-LA safflower oil (Jedwards International Inc), high-GLA safflower oil (Sonova, Arcadia Biosciences, Davis, CA), and high-ALA flaxseed oil (Polar Foods, Markham, Ontario, Canada) at various ratios to replace the 23 % SDA in high SDA soybean oil with GLA, ALA, or LA while maintaining other FA as close as possible (see Table 1). Thus, the oil mixtures provided equivalent enrichment of the n-3 and n-6 FA under investigation with minimal interference from other FA. An antioxidant was added to the diet at a rate of 0.25 g/kg (STABILON  4, Novus International). Feed and water were always available.
Production performance

The hens were weighed individually on day 0 and 30 and the body weight change (BWC) over the experiment was determined by difference. The eggs were collected daily, weighed, and stored at 4 C until processing. The amount of feed offered and remaining was monitored daily to calculate individual DFI. The hen-day egg production rate (HDEP) was calculated by dividing the total number of eggs produced by the number of days observed and then multiplying by 100. The egg mass (EM) was calculated by multiplying the egg weight and HDEP. Finally, the feed efficiency ratio (FER) was obtained by dividing DFI by EM.
Diets, eggs, and tissues collection and sampling

Representative samples from all experimental diets were collected at the time of diet preparation, stored at -20 C, finely ground using a coffee grinder, and analyzed for CP (16.6 %), ether extract (EE; 6.4 %), crude fiber (CF; 1.6 %), starch (46.4 %), calcium (Ca; 4.93 %), and available phosphorus (AP; 0.87 %) using AOAC methods (Cumberland Valley Analytical Lab, Waynesboro, PA). Total FA concentration was analyzed by gas-liquid chromatography (GC) as described below.

Eggs were obtained at the beginning (d 0), middle (d 15), and end of the experiment (d 30) and the weight of the whole egg and shell, albumen, and yolk were determined. Any missed eggs were replaced with those from the previous day. Briefly, the eggs were broken with a spatula, and the egg white separated from the yolk. The eggshell was washed, dried, and weighed, and the albumen weight was calculated by subtracting the sum of the shell and yolk weight from the egg weight. The yolks were frozen, freeze-dried, ground, and stored at -20 C for subsequent analysis.

On day 30, all hens were weighed and euthanized by electric stunning and exsanguination, followed by scalding and defeathering using a feather-picking machine. The liver and abdominal fat pad were collected, weighed, subsampled (~2 g), snap-frozen using liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80 C.
FA analysis

Fatty acid profile of the experimental oils, diets, yolks, and tissues (breast, thigh, liver, and abdominal fat) was determined using a two-step methylation procedure using 0.5 M sodium methoxide in methanol followed by 5 % methanolic HCl. The resulting FA methyl esters were quantified by GC as described by and). Briefly a GC (Agilent 6890 or 7890A; Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA) equipped with a fused-silica capillary column (SP2560; 100 m x 25 mm i.d. with 0.2-mum film thickness; Supelco, Inc., Bellefonte, PA) and a flame ionization detector. The oven program was 70 C for 4 min, 8 C/min ramp to 110 C, 5 C/min ramp to 170 C for 10 min, and 4 C/min ramp to 215 C for 23 min. Inlet and detector temperatures were 250 C with a 50:1 split ratio. Hydrogen carrier gas flow rate was 1 mL/min. Fatty acid concentration and methylation efficiencies were determined using multiple external standards (13:0 free FA, 17:1 free FA, and 19:0 methyl ester; Nu-Chek Prep, Inc., Elysian, MN). Peaks were identified based on purified standards (GLC780 and GLC461; Nu-Chek Prep), and 20:4 n-3 was identified using a purified stock (Caymen Chemical Company, Ann Arbor, MI). An equal weight standard (GLC461; Nu-Chek Prep) was used for calculation of recovery factors. Fatty acids were analyzed as mg/yolk and mg/100 g of fresh tissue.
Gene expression analysis

Hepatic expression of selected genes was measured as described by and. Briefly, total RNA was extracted using guanidinium thiocyanate-phenol-chloroform with a silica column with on-column DNase. Complementary DNA was synthesized using random primers (High Capacity cDNA Synthesis Kit, Applied Biosystems) and Real-Time PCR quantified gene expression with SYBR green and quantified relative to a standard curve. The geometric mean of two reference genes was used as a covariant in the statistical model (B2M and ACBT).
Statistical analysis

The statistical differences between treatments were analyzed using ANOVA in JMP Pro 16.2 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC). The model for egg yolks included the fixed effect of treatment, day on treatment (d 15 and 30), and their interaction with the pretrial observation of the parameter serving as a covariate. There was no interaction of treatment and day (P = 0.15) so only the main effect of treatment is reported. The model for production and tissue variables only included the effect of treatment. Data points outside of +- 3 Studentized residuals were treated as outliers and removed from the analysis. The means were compared using a Protected LSD test and significance declared at P <= 0.05.

passages.text: Diets were prepared by substitution of 1.25 % of conventional soybean oil (SOY) in control diet with high stearidonic acid (SDA) soybean oil or a high-alpha linolenic acid (ALA) oil blend [contained 52.3 % high-ALA flaxseed oil, 11.6 % high-gamma linolenic acid (GLA) safflower oil, 19.1 % high-linoleic (LA) safflower oil, and 17.0 % palm oil], a high-GLA oil blend [contained 61.8 % high-GLA safflower oil, 18.1 % high-ALA flaxseed oil, 13.8 % high-LA safflower oil, and 6.4 % palm oil], or a a high-LA oil blend [contained 60.0 % high-LA safflower oil, 18.1 % high-ALA flaxseed oil, 11.6 % high-GLA safflower oil, and 10.3 % palm oil].

PUFA= polyunsaturated FA, MUFA= monounsaturated FA, SFA= saturated FA, ALA= Alpha-linolenic acid, SDA= stearidonic acid, LA= linoleic acid, GLA= gamma-linolenic acid, OLA= oleic acid, ND= not detected.

The experimental diets were designed to have the same ingredient and nutritional composition as the treatment oils replaced 1.25 percentage units of conventional soybean oil in the control (Table 1). The treatment oil blends were carefully balanced to substitute approximately 23 % of the SDA (18:4n-3) found in High-SDA soybean oil with ALA (18:3n-3), GLA (18:3n-6), or LA (18:2n-6) in the high-ALA, high-GLA, and high-LA oil blends, respectively, while maintaining similar concentrations of other FA (Table 2). The treatments diets differed in FA profile but did not vary in total FA (ranging from 5255 to 5343 mg/100 g), total saturated FA (SFA; ranging from 870 to 913 mg/100 g), total monounsaturated FA (MUFA; ranging from 1167 to 1233 mg/100 g), and total polyunsaturated FA (PUFA; ranging from 3151 to 3212 mg/100 g) (Table 3).

The FA profile of the treatment diets reflected that of the oils. While the diets differed in terms of total n-3 and n-6 FA content, the total PUFA content was similar (60.2 to 61.6 % of FA). Additionally, the total MUFA ranged from 21.5 to 23.0 % of FA and total SFA ranged from 16.1 to 17.0 % of FA.

Treatment diets did not change total FA, total PUFA, total MUFA, and total SFA content of egg yolks (Table 7). The composition of FA in the egg yolks reflected the treatment FA profile. Yolks from hens fed the high-SDA, high-ALA, and high-GLA diets had higher contents of SDA, ALA, and GLA, respectively. The high-LA diet only numerically increased LA content relative to the other diets (P = 0.10; Table 7).

The total n-3 PUFA content was increased to a similar extent in high-SDA and high-ALA treatments (~178 mg per yolk) compared to the n-6 and CON diets (<113 mg per yolk; P < 0.001; Table 7). The high-SDA diet increased yolk n-3 HUFA content 39 % more than the high-ALA diet (114 vs. 82.3 mg per yolk; P < 0.001). Moreover, the ratio of n-3 HUFA to total n-3 PUFA was greater in yolks of hens fed high-SDA (0.648) than high-ALA (0.460), with the lowest ratio in high-GLA yolk (0.422).

The total n-6 HUFA content was more than 17 % higher in yolks from hens fed the high-GLA diet compared to those fed the high-LA diet (157 vs. 134 mg per yolk; P < 0.001; Table 7). The ratio of total n-6 HUFA to total n-6 PUFA was also higher in GLA than LA (14.8 vs. 12.6). The ratio of total n-6 to total n-3 was higher in yolks from the CON group hens (0.106) compared to the other treatments, with the lowest ratio observed in the n-3 treatments (~0.055; P < 0.001).

The treatment oils did not change liver total FA, total MUFA, and total SFA contents (Table 9). The FA composition of the experimental diets was also reflected in liver FA. Briefly, the livers of hens fed high-SDA, high-ALA, and high-GLA diets had increases in SDA, ALA, and GLA content, respectively (P < 0.001). However, LA content of the liver was not modified by treatment (P = 0.07).

The high-SDA diet increased the liver total n-3 by 13 % and total n-3 HUFA by 43 % compared to the high-ALA diet, respectively (P < 0.001). Similarly, individual n-3 HUFA were higher in the livers of hens fed the high-SDA diet compared to the high-ALA diet, with EPA increased 140 %, DPA increased 33 %, and DHA increased 41 %, respectively. Additionally, the ratio of total VLCn-3 to total n-3 was 19 % higher in the high-SDA livers compared to the high-ALA livers (79.1 vs 66.6 mg/100 g).

The high-GLA and high-LA treatments equally increased liver total n-6 and total n-6 HUFA (>1159 and 300 mg/100 g) compared to the n-3 treatments (<1006 and 244 mg/100 g) but were not different from the CON (1247 and 313 mg/100 g, respectively). The ratio of total n-6 to total n-3 PUFA was higher in the livers of hens fed the high-GLA diet (9.62) compared to the other treatments, with the lowest ratio observed in the high-SDA livers (4.91).

Discussion

The conventional approach to studying the impact of a specific FA on performance and tissue enrichment is to compare feeds or oils that differ in the FA of interest. This is common both in poultry nutrition and other animal models. However, these treatments are complex mixtures that differ in many FA that confound interpretation. For example, SDA has been commonly considered to have an equal effect on DHA as ALA and is commonly referred to as "pro-EPA" based on work with high-SDA soybean oil compared to flaxseed oil. However, flaxseed oil contains over 50 % more total n-3 FA and when compared at equal levels, SDA does increase DHA more than ALA as discussed below. The current experiment used a mixture of multiple oils to create test oils that predominantly differed in a single n-3 or n-6 FA. The amount of enrichment of the test FA was limited by the availability of oils. High-SDA soybean oil has the highest concentration of SDA, and the other blends were built to replace the 23 % SDA while maintaining the other FA and were successful in maintaining similar total SFA, MUFA, and PUFA levels between experimental diets. It is important to note that although FA profile was matched, the oils came from different plant sources and likely differed in phytosterols and other plant-specific compounds. An alternate approach that would allow higher enrichment of the n-3 and n-6 FA would be to saponify and enrich free FA or FA ethyl esters through fractionation. However, issues with palatability, oxidation, and digestibility may occur.

The conventional soybean oil control was included to allow comparison to previous literature. The feeding rate of 1.25 % of the diet delivered 0.57 % n-3 FA in the n-3 treatments and was based on previous dose experiments that have observed near-maximal effects of n-3 supplements on n-3 HUFA enrichment at between 0.6 and 1.3 % n-3 FA in the diet. Many previous studies were conducted with much higher levels of oils and oilseeds that likely saturate the elongation and desaturation pathway and limit the ability to observe differences, for example between efficiency of HUFA synthesis between SDA and ALA.

The lack of impacts on body weight, laying performance, or egg weight and composition indicates no major adverse effects of oil blends on hens' health and performance relative to the conventional soybean oil. It is important to recognize that the experiment was not powered to identify small changes in performance that are ecomically important to commercial production.

The lower liver weight of hens fed high-ALA and high-SDA diets in the current experiment was not observed in broilers exposed to similar oil blends or in other studies investigating the effect of high-ALA and high-SDA oils. The mechanism is not apparent, but the n-3 HUFAs are known to decrease hepatic lipid synthesis and stimulate oxidation. However, liver FA concentration was not different, so the weight difference does not appear to be due to steatosis (Table 9).

The FA profile of the egg yolk is rapidly and directly modified as it depends primarily on diet composition, especially the n-3 and n-6 PUFA that are not endogenously synthesized. The absorbed PUFA and their products are either deposited in body tissues or oxidized, although their concentration can be diluted by saturated and mono-unsaturated de novo synthesized FA.

The FA profile of egg yolks and tissues reflected the treatment oils as expected based on the ability of chicken to deposit the dietary FA body tissues further elongation and desaturation. The lack of enrichment of LA was may be attributed to the considerable level of this in all diets and possibly beta-oxidation.

Most common feed ingredients only contain near trace levels of GLA and its influence on egg FA profile has rarely been investigated. There is recent interest in GLA due to its moderate level in hempseed. For example, reported that hemp seed oil increased GLA in egg yolks to 1.09 % of FA and feeding evening primrose oil increased GLA to 4.87 %. Endogenously, GLA is synthesized from LA, which is consistently high in conventional corn-soy diets. Conventional sunflower oil is high in LA and has been reported to increase GLA and ARA (20:4 n-6) in the egg yolks. The High LA treatment in the current experiment did not change GLA in egg yolk compared to the n-3 treatments, although ARA was increased. The enrichment of GLA with LA feeding is expected to be dependent on the rate of GLA synthesis and utilization for further elongation. Conversion of LA to DGLA and ARA appears to be efficient in many cells and tissues as normally GLA is found in very low concentrations. Increasing GLA was more effective in increasing both GLA and HUFA n-6 FA, indicating that the desaturation of LA to GLA is a limiting step. The decrease in HUFA n-6 FA with n-3 FA was expected based on previous literature and it is interesting to note that SDA resulted in a slightly greater decrease, likely indicating a higher affinity for the shared desaturase and elongase enzymes. This is further supported by the sum of n-3 and n-6 HUFA was 219 mg/yolk in SDA and 205.5 mg/yolk in GLA.

Dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (20:3n-6) serves as a substrate for enzymes like COX and LOX, and its metabolites are reported to have mainly anti-inflammatory properties and inhibit platelet aggregation. Arachidonic acid has been of interest in brain development in early life and skin conditions. Although not currently a commercial market, future interest in GLA fortified foods could be efficiently met by GLA supplementation of laying hens rather than LA. However, the ability to enrich both n-3 and n-6 HUFA will require additional investigation.

The greater enrichment of total n-3 HUFA in liver and egg yolk of hens fed the high-SDA oil was due to increases in EPA, DPA, ETA, and DHA. Similarly, the egg yolk and breast muscle of high-GLA fed hens contained higher total n-6 HUFA than those of high-LA group due to increased concentrations of 20:3n-6, ARA, 22:4n-6, and 22:5n-6. In the liver and adipose tissue, the high-GLA and high-LA diets equally increased total n-6 HUFA. Furthermore, in liver and adipose tissue, the high-SDA and high-ALA diets equally increased total n-3 HUFA but the proportion of the total n-3 HUFA relative to total n-3 FA was greater in hens fed high-SDA diets. These findings were consistent with our previous research comparing ALA and SDA in broilers and laying hens. The increase in HUFA with SDA is commonly attributed to bypassing the first desaturation step, but SDA also maintained higher hepatic expression of ELOV2 compared to the ALA, GLA, and LA treatments in the current experiment (Table 12). If this transcriptional regulation is due to SDA or other possible bioactives, such as polyphenols and sterols, is not clear. It is interesting to note that CON and High-SDA were soybean oils while the other treatments contained flaxseed or safflower oil. Specifically, the High-LA oil that contained safflower oil decreased ELOV2 compared to control while it was reasonably similar in the high ALA and GLA that were from flaxseed and safflower oil.

The higher proportion of n-3 and n-6 HUFA in the egg yolk and breast muscle of hens fed high-SDA and high-GLA is likely explained by the synthesis of the HUFA requires conversion of ALA to SDA and LA to GLA as the first pathway step. The conversion process is catalyzed by delta-6-desaturase [FADS2; ]. Furthermore, 22:5n-3 and 24:4n-6 compete for the activity of FADS2 in synthesis of DHA and 22:5n-6, respectively. The higher concentration of total n-3 HUFA and all individual n-3 HUFA, including DHA, in the yolk and breast muscle of high-SDA fed hens confirms that SDA is metabolized more efficiently than ALA and demonstrates a rate limiting effect of FADS2 in HUFA synthesis. Feeding SDA bypasses this step and allows the elongase enzyme to convert SDA to ETA in the liver with subsequent deposition into the yolk and muscle.

Previously, SDA was considered to increase EPA but not DHA based on comparisons of SDA oils to flaxseed oil that contained much higher levels of n-3 FA. However, our previous work comparing high-SDA-ahiflower oil to high-ALA flaxseed that contained similar amounts of total n-3 FA reported greater enrichment of n-3 HUFA (98.9 vs. 85.1 mg/yolk) and DHA (82.7 vs 72.5 mg/yolk) when fed at 0.75 % of the diet. It is important to note that DHA enrichment was not different between Ahiflower and flaxseed when fed at 2.25 % of the diet (105 and 97.5 mg/yolk), highlighting the importance of dose and saturation of the system when interpreting efficiency of conversion. In the current study, the enrichment of n-3 HUFA was 114 and 82.3 mg and DHA was 97.2 and 71.7 mg for high-SDA and high-ALA oils, respectively. This is lower than the 143 and 105 mg of n-3 HUFA and DHA previously reported with 2.25 % Ahiflower oil indicating that the dose in the current trial was likely below the level of saturation allowing observation of differences between SDA and ALA enrichment.

Care is needed when interpreting the efficiency of PUFA conversion to HUFA as multiple factors have an impact including affinity of each PUFA for the desaturase and elongase enzymes and enzyme abundance but also the concentration of the PUFA and competing FA. The high efficiency of n-3 PUFA conversion to HUFA is higher at low concentrations and explains the high efficiency in the control in the current trial. Saturation of the enzymatic system by high treatment doses in previous work also likely limited ability to observe differences between SDA and ALA. The higher efficiency of SDA than ALA in increasing n-3 HUFA and higher efficiency of GLA than LA demonstrates the benefit of SDA and GLA. Additionally, the decreased efficiency of n-3 HUFA synthesis by GLA demonstrates the impact of competition.

The direction of treatment effects in liver and muscle FA profile were similar to the egg yolk. The experiment fed the treatment oils for only 30 d, so the impact on adipose and muscle FA profile is limited based on the rate of tissue turnover and is more limited compared to broilers that are rapidly depositing tissue. The liver is the main site of FA metabolism and packaging for support of egg yolk production. The FA content represents both the FA incorporated into plasma membranes and that undergoing metabolism and packaging. It is interesting to note that SDA increased DHA and total n-3 HUFA similarly in yolk and liver but both were greater than breast muscle. As expected, the HUFA were not efficiently stored in adipose tissue. It is interesting to note that adipose ALA was increased 7 mg/100 g by ALA compared to SDA and GLA was increased 6.2 mg/100 g by high GLA compared to LA, while adipose SDA was only increased 2.7 mg/100 g by SDA compared to ALA. This may be due to depletion of available SDA by the higher efficiency of conversion to HUFA. It is interesting to note that although SDA is synthesized in cells, it is only found in trace amounts in plasma and adipose tissue may not be adapted to its uptake and storage.

Overall, the experiment demonstrated that SDA and GLA are more efficiently elongated and desaturated then ALA and LA. However, observing these differences require comparison at equal levels while controlling for other FA and feeding at lower doses that do not saturate HUFA synthesis. The high repeatability of FA analysis and responsiveness of FA metabolism allowed observation of clear differences with a limited number of animals under controlled conditions, but larger experiments are necessary to determine if small, but economically important differences in egg production may exist. Additionally, plant oils are a complex matrix and the oils used were sourced from multiple sources and selected based on enrichment of FA of interest. Future work should also explore plant specific compounds in purified oil that may impact FA metabolism.

passages.text: Investigating interactions between macroinvertebrate indices, water quality parameters, and stream quality classifications in a Wisconsin agricultural watershed
Abstract

Increasing agricultural and urban land use poses a growing threat to freshwater ecosystems worldwide, contributing to nutrient loading and degradation of surface water quality. Stream restoration, such as riparian vegetation, can help mitigate nonpoint source pollution, yet its ecological outcomes remain variable. Aquatic macroinvertebrates are widely used as bioindicators for water quality due to their sensitivity to environmental change, but their responses to stream impairment and restoration in the context of ongoing land-use pressures are less well understood. This study investigates associations between water quality parameters, biotic indices, and stream classifications using macroinvertebrate and water quality data collected from stream sites within an intensively managed agricultural watershed in the Midwestern United States during the autumn seasons of 2021 and 2022. Numerical analyses were used for water quality and macroinvertebrate indices, while stream classifications:impairment status, nutrient thresholds, and habitat quality:were analyzed categorically. Nonmetric multidimensional scaling assessed macroinvertebrate correlations with water quality, while Kruskal-Wallis tests identified statistical differences across stream classifications. Findings show that sites with stream improvement projects exhibit higher macroinvertebrate index scores, with strong correlations between higher index scores, higher dissolved oxygen, and lower total phosphorus. These results suggest macroinvertebrates and water quality parameters are effective indicators of stream impairment and habitat quality, though long-term links to restoration require further study. Findings contribute to a broader understanding of how biological indicators can inform restoration success and impairment conditions in agriculturally impacted watersheds across temperate regions.
Core Ideas
Sample sites with stream improvement projects exhibit higher biotic index scores.
Higher macroinvertebrate index scores were associated with higher dissolved oxygen and lower total phosphorus.
Ecological indicators can be used to assess stream impairment.
Macroinvertebrates can be used to inform nutrient reduction strategies in agricultural watersheds.
Plain Language Summary

This study looked at how farming and city development affect streams in the US Midwest. When land is heavily used, it often adds nutrients, like phosphorus, to water, which can harm streams and the animals that live there. One way to help is by restoring streams, such as planting vegetation along their edges. Scientists use tiny water animals, called macroinvertebrates, to measure stream health because these creatures respond quickly to pollution. We studied seven streams during the fall of 2021 and 2022, checking water quality and the types of macroinvertebrates living there. We also compared streams that had been restored with those that had not. The results showed that streams with restoration projects had more types of healthy macroinvertebrates, higher oxygen levels, and less phosphorus. This means these small animals and water tests can help show how healthy streams are.
